It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scandal in recent history.

Christina Block, heir to a popular chain of steakhouses, is accused of ordering an Israeli security firm to carry out the violent abduction of her children from Denmark, following a bitter custody battle with her former husband.

There are allegedly connections with at least two former secret agents, from Germany and Israel.

In the latest twist, investigators in the case stumbled across evidence that has led to Germany's former intelligence chief, August Hanning, being arrested this month for treason and espionage.

Hanning's arrest stunned the intelligence community. Although his case has nothing to do with the Hamburg trial, he has denied allegations of involvement in an earlier attempted abduction of the children.

There was enormous media interest in Germany when Christina Block and six others went on trial in a high-security courtroom in Hamburg in July last year.

Block House restaurants, specialising in steak and baked potatoes, are a feature of many German towns. Their success over the past half century has helped make Christina Block's father Eugen a multimillionaire.

Prosecutors allege that she and a family lawyer, Andreas Costard, organised the forcible abduction of two of her children, who were staying with her former husband, Stephan Hensel, at his home in Denmark.

They say the operation was carried out by a 36-year-old Israeli citizen named only as Jonathan G and five others.

The abduction took place during the New Year celebrations of 2023-24, as the two children and their father were watching a firework display, according to the indictment.

Prosecutors say several men ambushed and beat up Stephan Hensel, and dragged the boy and the girl, then 10 and 13 years old, into a car.

On the approach to the border with Germany, they are alleged to have changed vehicles, taped up the children's mouths and tied the girl's hands.

The group are then said to have travelled on to Baden-Württemberg in a campervan. Prosecutors say the children were held there against their will until their mother arrived to pick them up on 2 January 2024 and took them to her home in Hamburg.

Christina Block, Andreas Costard and Jonathan G are charged with the abduction of minors, grievous bodily harm and unlawful detention.

Block's partner, a former TV sports presenter called Gerhard Delling, and three others are charged with aiding and abetting.

All of them deny wrongdoing, except for Jonathan G, who has admitted his involvement. However, he told the court he thought he was taking part in a rescue operation.

The trial comes after years of legal battles between Christina Block and her former husband, Stephan Hensel, over who had the right to look after the children.

Immediately after their separation, all four children lived with their mother in Hamburg. Hensel, who remarried, later moved to Denmark, where they regularly visited him.

In 2021, the two youngest children went to visit their father in Denmark, but then were not brought back to Hamburg as agreed.

A court in Hamburg ruled that Christina had custody and that the children should be returned. However, in February 2023, a Danish court ruled that, although the boy and the girl had been brought to Denmark unlawfully, they could not be taken back.

In May 2023, Hensel was charged with the abduction of minors, in a case which is still pending.

He has accused Christina of being violent with the children, charges she denies. She told the court Hensel wanted to take revenge on her.

She also denied knowing anything about plans for the abduction of the children from Denmark. Her defence argues that the Israeli security team had acted on its own initiative.

She told the court it was "a catastrophe" and that she had never wanted anything like that.

The head of the Israeli security team, David Barkay, who is not on trial but faces future legal proceedings, told the court that Christina Block and Costard had known about the planned repatriation operation.

Barkay, who was described by another witness as a former agent with Mossad, the Israeli secret service, said he had not shared all the details because he "didn't trust them."

The alleged connection with Germany's former spy chief, August Hanning, relates to accusations of an earlier attempt to abduct the children and bring them back from Denmark in 2022.

Prosecutors have said Hanning was responsible for arranging security staff sent to Denmark with Christina Block. His lawyer denies the accusations. Hanning has not been charged over the current Block court case.

However, while investigators were searching his home, they came across evidence to suggest Hanning was involved in buying some 2,000 documents from his former chief of staff and then passing on state secrets to foreign powers.

Which foreign power and who he is alleged to have given the secrets to is unspecified, but it has prompted widespread speculation.

Now 80, Hanning is in custody charged with treasonous espionage. His lawyer says he is being "unjustly persecuted" and that the charges are "unfounded".

Meanwhile the trial against Christina Block is currently on hold for two weeks - one of numerous delays and extensions over the course of the past 15 months.

The latest delay is because a witness, Stephan Hensel's new wife, failed to appear in court.

Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 18:11:29 GMT

Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder

Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.

Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.

Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.

"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.

"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."

Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.

It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.

The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommender content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.

It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.

Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier.

But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.

Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.

Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.

It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.

He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order.

"You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC.

"I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."

The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.

Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."

Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.

Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.

Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.

But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.

Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health, and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline.

Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line.

"The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.

While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change.

"Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.

Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.

More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.

The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off.

"This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said.

"If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them."

The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".

Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features – for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women – and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (£52m, $70m).

"The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC.

There's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation.

In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive – although a US jury recently ruled otherwise.

"I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' – like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' – and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney.

Right-wing parties in Australia – and the Trump administration – have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship.

But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake – they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week.

The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children.

However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far, it has been struggling to implement the ban? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued.

The EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 – after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds – is a cautionary tale.

Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that.

"Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation.

On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return.

The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act.

The rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app.

Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global.

"We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing."

Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them.

Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment."

Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms – though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off.

Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice.

"On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good."

If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line.

Antarctica’s ‘doomsday’ glacier will keep melting even if oceans cool

New Scientist October 15, 2026

The world’s widest glacier – Thwaites glacier in Antarctica – is already collapsing at an alarming rate due to ocean warming, with worrying implications for global sea-level rise. Now, a new study shows that it will continue to lose ice for at least the next 150 years, even under the impossible scenario of extremely cool oceans.

This means that future ice loss from the glacier is unavoidable, even under the most optimistic climate mitigation scenarios.

Dubbed the “doomsday glacier”, this vast mass of ice is roughly the size of Great Britain. Together with the neighbouring Pine Island glacier, it’s the area of Antarctica losing the most ice, mainly due to melting by the warmer ocean waters.

Advertisement

The race to understand how and when Thwaites glacier will collapse

“The Pine Island and Thwaites glaciers are the biggest contributors to sea-level rise in Antarctica at the moment, and they’re losing ice at an increasing rate,” says Rosie Williams at the British Antarctic Survey.

If Thwaites glacier collapses completely, it is expected to trigger a more widespread loss of the ice sheet covering West Antarctica, causing a calamitous sea-level rise of 5 metres. So determining how it behaves in future is crucial.

To explore this, Williams and her colleagues “did something quite wild”, she says. In three different computer models of the ice sheet, they turned off all ocean-driven melting – an impossible condition in reality, even under the most extreme ocean cooling scenarios – and watched what would happen over the next 150 years. The aim was to see the future trajectory of Thwaites glacier and Pine Island glacier, even without warming oceans.

Free newsletter

Surprisingly, the glaciers followed opposite paths. Pine Island glacier re-advanced and became more stable. “But with Thwaites glacier, we found something really different,” says Williams. Over the entire 150 years of the simulations, the glacier continued to lose ice, even though the rate of loss slowed over time. “Our general expectation was… if you turned off that ocean melting, the ice would be able to thicken and re-advance. It’s somewhat of a surprise that Thwaites glacier can’t do that.”

The researchers think that Thwaites is still being affected by extreme El Niño conditions in the 1940s which destabilised Antarctica’s glaciers and kick-started their retreat. “We’re still seeing some effect of that playing out today with Thwaites. [Glaciers] are really slow-moving. They have a long memory,” she says.

On top of this, human-induced climate change has probably accelerated the melt, says Ted Scambos at the University of Colorado Boulder. “Ocean heat delivered to the base of the ice … over the past four decades or so, as a result of anthropogenic warming, has pushed the Thwaites system into an inherently unstable configuration,” he says.

Warmer ocean is driving the Antarctic sea ice ‘regime shift’

But despite future ice loss being locked in, this doesn’t mean that strategies to reduce climate change and ocean warming are futile. “Almost the opposite,” says Williams. “Under the zero-melt scenario, [Thwaites glacier] still loses ice, but the more warming you have in the ocean, the faster that ice is lost, so it’s still really essential to bring down our emissions and control that rate of ice loss.”

“Every fraction of a degree really matters for trying to preserve these glaciers into the future, which matters for all of us, in terms of sea-level rise globally,” says Williams.

The temperature of the ocean adjacent to Thwaites glacier is projected to rise at triple the historical rate throughout the 21st century, leading to increased ice melting. The big worry is that this may trigger a doomsday scenario of run-away collapse of Thwaites glacier that, in turn, would trigger the collapse of the whole of the West Antarctic ice sheet in a process called marine ice sheet instability.

The floating ice shelf of world’s widest glacier – Thwaites glacier in Antarctica – is detaching, with worrying implications for global sea-level rise

Here, the study by Williams and her colleagues offers slight hope. “We haven’t crossed the point of no return,” says Mathieu Morlighem at Dartmouth College, New Hampshire. “In the best-case scenario…if melt from the ocean stops, Thwaites doesn’t… lead to a collapse of the West Antarctic ice sheet.”

The big question for the future is what happens with realistic ocean temperatures, says Williams, who is now working on this.

Meanwhile, another study published this week revealed other worrying news about Thwaites glacier. A more precise model of how the glacier interacts with the ocean indicates that it might retreat more rapidly than previously thought, potentially contributing to double the sea-level rise previously projected.

In January, Skyview High School in Virginia will become the first high school in the US to have a quantum computer on its premises. Made by the quantum computing and sensing firm XeedQ, it will be a teaching device aimed at inspiring the next generation of quantum innovators.

The quantum computing industry is in a period of expansion and both governments and private investors are increasing their focus on the field. Yet, many of the industry’s leaders agree that, in addition to investing in quantum technology, there ought to be a concerted effort to grow the quantum workforce as well. Fairfax County Public Schools (FCPS) in Virginia aims to meet this challenge by providing its high school students with hands-on access to a working quantum computer. FCPS Superintendent Michelle Reid says that this is a bet on a career pathway that is “globally exploding” and could set students up for pursuing one of the 800,000 quantum-related jobs projected to be created within the next decade.

The quantum computer, called XQ1, will contain four qubits, or basic building blocks of quantum computation, each of which will be based on a diamond imprinted with specifically designed defects. These types of qubits can operate at room temperature. Gopalakrishnan Balasubramanian at XeedQ says the firm designed XQ1 – which is about the size of a small refrigerator – to be robust enough to withstand the conditions of a classroom and run continuously for several years. He says that XQ1 will cost about $900,000. Reid says that this will still work out cheaper for FCPS than, for instance, a new programme to teach students welding skills.

Advertisement

The computational power of a quantum computer is related to its number of qubits, so XQ1 won’t enable students to run sophisticated programs. Instead, it will allow them to develop intuition for, for example, the probabilistic nature of qubits. Students will be able to test how repeatedly preparing a qubit in one quantum state, equivalent to giving the quantum computer the same inputs over and over, doesn’t necessarily always lead to the same result, or the same output, when the qubit is read out later, says Balasubramanian.

The world’s first fully 3D-printed microscope went big in 2025

In this way, some of the most fundamental ways in which quantum computers behave differently from conventional computers will become intuitive to students way before they enroll in college and undergo a rigorous formal education in quantum physics, he says. Additionally, students will be able to change electromagnetic pulses that control qubits as well as study the impacts of environmental noise on their functioning. They will work in teams of two or three and learn the coding language Python in the process.

Google showcases way to fix quantum computer errors more efficiently

New Scientist October 15, 2026

Making quantum computers error-proof is one of the biggest challenges currently facing the technology. Researchers at Google Quantum AI have now demonstrated one way to do so more efficiently. Their work suggests the smaller quantum computers that will be available in the next few years could be more impactful than expected.

Quantum computers can run mathematical operations, analogous to addition or multiplication, that conventional computers cannot. This makes them suitable for solving some problems that had previously been considered unsolvable, such as those that underpin cryptography.

Most important among the quantum operations the computers run are “non-Clifford gates”, which are the key ingredients for algorithms that transcend conventional computation.

Advertisement

We may finally have a way to rate a quantum computer’s usefulness

But there is a problem. Quantum computers are very error-prone, and their building blocks, called qubits, must be encoded into special groups, or “logical qubits”, before they can execute operations reliably. Executing non-Clifford gates in an error-corrected way requires large numbers of qubits, which means having to build very large quantum computers – a formidable engineering challenge.

Now, Emma Rosenfeld at Google Quantum AI and her colleagues have used the firm’s Willow quantum computer to show that the error-correction process can be made more efficient. Their new technique ultimately reduced Willow’s errors 40 times.

At the centre of their advance is the idea of a “magic state”, which is a special quantum state that qubits must assume before the quantum computer can run error-corrected non-Clifford operations. Creating these states had, so far, been a real bottleneck for quantum computing, says Rosenfeld. “It eats up a lot of qubits and a lot of time,” she says.

Free newsletter

In 2024, her colleagues at Google Quantum AI proposed a more efficient method for creating magic states called “magic state cultivation”. Here, instead of many imperfect qubits being repeatedly combined and manipulated into a magic state that is then put towards running an error-corrected operation, the magic state is “grown” within a smaller patch of qubits.

The Google researchers showed that magic state cultivation could, in theory, enable quantum computers to run consequential programs with just one-tenth the number of qubits we had expected they would need. The new experiment by Rosenfeld and her colleagues proves that magic state cultivation works in practice.

This is not the first time that new methods for making magic states have lowered a quantum computer’s error rates. Advances in creating magic states and error-correcting non-Clifford gates have also been achieved in experiments with quantum computers that have qubits based on ions. Willow’s qubits, which are based on tiny superconducting circuits, achieved error rates similar to those past experiments, but Rosenfeld says that they work more quickly, potentially reducing the quantum computer’s overall runtime.

A quantum computer made from extremely cold atoms can correct its own errors during long computations, an important prerequisite for becoming truly useful

“This is an impressive demonstration of a promising recent idea pioneered by Google,” says Isaac Kim at the University of California, Davis. “It’s an approach that can make fault-tolerant quantum computing substantially cheaper.” The new work demonstrates one of the building blocks necessary for universal quantum computing and could be a “gamechanger” in terms of building intermediately sized quantum computers with hundreds of logical qubits, says Dominik Hangleiter at ETH Zurich in Switzerland.

Zhenyu Cai at Imperial College London says that while this experiment is a significant step forward, Willow’s errors will need to be reduced further before it can tackle truly useful problems. Additionally, Kim says that in the experiment, Willow generated good magic states only for a fraction of its computational runs: only 8 per cent of Willow’s computations produced high-quality magic states that could then be put into further use.

Rosenfeld says that this percentage ought to increase as she and her colleagues refine the technique and improve Willow’s hardware. It is, in this case, also affected by a very careful benchmarking technique that the team used, which may not be used in future applications, she says. “This is the first demonstration that the concepts work. We’re not done.”

Towering glacial ice cliffs may collapse in fits and starts

New Scientist October 15, 2026

The world’s thickest glaciers may “calve” icebergs up to three times faster than previously predicted. However, such rapid retreat may not be sustained over long periods.

Instead, the large bodies of ice – which include Antarctica’s Thwaites glacier – may collapse in bursts, with intervening periods of stability.

The behaviour of tall ice cliffs is one of the biggest sources of uncertainty in predicting future sea level rise. Several of the world’s largest glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica extend out to sea, with their bases resting on the sea floor. Their coastal edges can form ice cliffs looming as high as 100 metres above the ocean’s surface.

Advertisement

The race to understand how and when Thwaites glacier will collapse

For years, researchers have feared that such marine-based glaciers might be vulnerable to runaway cliff collapse. The idea here is that each time an ice cliff collapses, it exposes a new, taller – and so potentially even less stable – ice cliff further towards the glacier’s interior. The loss of ice due to runaway collapse of these ever-taller cliffs could potentially double the amount of sea level rise expected over the next 100 years, according to an Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change report. But we don’t yet have enough empirical data to know how likely it is that runaway cliff collapse will occur, so previous studies have relied on ideal mathematical models to envision the process instead.

Caroline Needell at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology-Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute Joint Program and her colleagues used satellite data to provide the first direct, large-scale observations of how the tallest ice cliffs actually behave, offering a firmer basis for estimating the danger of runaway collapse – and the rapid sea level rise that could result.

According to the study, the risk of runaway collapse depends on two main factors: how steeply the sea floor beneath the glacial ice deepens, and how quickly the ice flows seawards. Imagine an up-ended jar of thick honey spilling onto a plate: it won’t remain in a tall, stable shape, but will thin outwards at the edges. In a similar way, if the viscous flow of ice is fast enough, it will thin out the edge of a glacier, reducing cliff height. Even if the glacier is thicker further towards its interior, sufficiently rapid ice flow appears able to compensate, lowering those ice cliffs and preventing a runaway effect.

This idea has been suggested by idealised mathematical models, but had never been systematically measured in real glaciers. “None of the glaciers we observed underwent unstable retreat, even though they did retreat much faster than our current models predict,” says Needell.

Free newsletter

That retreat could speed up even further in the future. Needell notes that most glaciers in the study are “buttressed” by sea-floor features. For instance, a series of underwater ridges currently help stabilise Thwaites from beneath.

“Over the next decades, it’s going to jump from one pinning ridge to another,” almost like “tripping” downhill, says Douglas Benn at the University of St Andrews in the UK. Eventually, Thwaites will reach a point where those ridges disappear. “The bed then begins to get real deep,” says Benn. At that point, which the glacier may reach within the current century, “the whole structural integrity of the ice becomes unviable”.

The floating ice shelf of world’s widest glacier – Thwaites glacier in Antarctica – is detaching, with worrying implications for global sea-level rise

That is when runaway collapse becomes a real possibility. However, those conditions may also speed up the flow of ice, thus thinning out any looming cliffs. The key question, says Needell, is whether thinning can outcompete rapid ice loss, restabilising the glacier. Her study suggests that it might – but the question remains open.

Robert Larter at the British Antarctic Survey points out that we haven’t yet seen this kind of runaway cliff collapse. One study suggests that it may have happened in the vicinity of Thwaites around 12,000 years ago. “The problem is, nobody was around to take observations at the time,” he says. “It’s a possibility we have to keep our eye on.”

This helps regulate involuntary bodily functions, such as heart rate, and interacts with the brainstem pathways involved in nausea and vomiting.

From dementia to heart attacks, hearing loss has been linked to a wide range of effects across the body, and the condition is on the rise. Fortunately, we’re learning how best to safeguard this crucial sense and how we might be able to reverse the damage

However, Liu stresses that the researchers didn’t look into the mechanism behind how ear defenders prevent nausea and vomiting, so the idea of them dampening this response “remains a hypothesis”.

Nevertheless, the results tell us more about brain activity under anaesthesia. “The biological plausibility is that general anaesthesia produces unconsciousness without necessarily eliminating all neural processing of sound,” says Liu.

Liu hopes to one day conduct a larger trial at multiple locations that measures noise exposure relative to nervous system activity among patients under general anaesthetic.

New Scientist October 16, 2026

We may be on the verge of solving the mystery of the Martian moons. On 20 October, the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft launches towards the larger of the two moons, Phobos, with the goal of bringing back a sample that may finally explain how Phobos and its sibling, Deimos, formed.

MMX will launch from Tanegashima Space Center in Japan. If all goes to plan, it should arrive at Mars in August 2027, entering an orbit that keeps it alongside Phobos so it can build a detailed map of the surface. Along the way, it will also observe the surface of Deimos.

Once the map is complete enough, the spacecraft’s operators at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) will use it to pick out a spot on Phobos for MMX to land. During one or two brief landings, it will take on two tasks: to drop off a small rover called IDEFIX and to pick up samples. The rover is the first anyone has ever placed on such a small cosmic body, so part of its purpose aside from scientific observations is to confirm that a wheeled rover even works on an object with such low gravity.

Possible signs of ancient life on Mars are rich in complex carbon

The samples, though, are the most important part of the mission. MMX has two different sampling devices: one that shoots a puff of gas onto the surface, blowing dust and pebbles back up into a sampling container, and another that blasts a hollow cylinder into the ground to take a sample a several centimetres deep. After the samples are taken, they will be stowed away inside the spacecraft, which will then head back towards Earth. It is expected to arrive home in 2031.

Once these samples get back to Earth and are analysed by scientists on the ground, they should finally solve the mystery of how Phobos and Deimos formed. For more than a century, researchers have debated whether the two are captured asteroids or formed from an impact on Mars, similar to how Earth’s moon formed. On first look, their shapes and surfaces resemble asteroids, but their circular orbits around Mars’s equator are more consistent with the impact hypothesis. Figuring out what they are made of should settle it once and for all.

This will also help illuminate what the solar system was like billions of years ago when these strange moons formed. “Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds,” said Tom Statler, part of the NASA team that is collaborating on the MMX mission, in a statement.

If we are very lucky, the samples from Phobos may even contain bonus bits of dust and debris from Mars itself. Impacts on the planet could have launched material into space, which would have collected on the moon’s surface and been preserved there for billions of years. That means that these samples could illuminate not just the history of Phobos and Deimos, but also of Mars.

El Niño has killed hundreds of children in Sudan

New Scientist October 16, 2026

Hundreds of children have died of starvation and disease in a drought in Sudan caused by the record-breaking El Niño. The risk of this leading to a full-blown famine is growing.

Almost half the country is experiencing drought, which in some areas is the worst in decades, according to a warning from the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), a partnership of the United Nations and charity organisations. As a result, crops are failing and people are dying in a “humanitarian catastrophe, already of historic proportions”, it said.

This El Niño will bring predictable disasters, so why aren’t we ready?

Hunger has reached famine levels in two refugee camps in Darfur, a region in western Sudan. While that’s not enough for the IPC to declare a famine across the region, the partnership said it has resulted in hundreds of deaths. Most of these are children, who are particularly vulnerable to malnutrition, as well as outbreaks of cholera and measles. At least 1800 people have died of malnutrition in three areas of Darfur controlled by a rebel faction led by Abdel Wahid al-Nur, according to the group.

Advertisement

Almost 29 million people, 62 per cent of the country’s population, are already being forced to eat less or go hungry. As the spotty harvest comes in, they won’t be able to store food or make money to buy it before the next rainy season in June, dramatically increasing the risk of widespread famine, says Manon Radosta at the non-governmental organisation CARE, a member of the IPC.

“Families are skipping meals. They’re not eating or they’re eating just porridge,” she says. “It would not take much to tip it. We cannot predict it, but we’re extremely worried that the situation will be so severe that people will be massively starving.”

Droughts and flooding brought by El Niño threaten crops around the world, raising the risk of increased prices and famines

In 2003, ethnic minorities in Darfur rebelled against Sudan’s largely Arab government, and government-backed Arab paramilitaries began killing civilians in a conflict that led to about 300,000 deaths. Twenty years later, the paramilitaries launched a civil war against Sudan’s new military government and killed thousands of non-Arab civilians in Darfur. Some of these massacres bore the “hallmarks of genocide”, the UN found.

The war has displaced 14 million people and disrupted farming and livestock herding. Prices of food and fuel have also shot up as the US-Iran conflict interrupts shipping on the Strait of Hormuz. Now, El Niño has reduced rainfall to crops including the main staple, sorghum, and withered vegetation for grazing. Ninety per cent of Sudan’s agriculture relies on rain rather than irrigation.

During this natural climate phase, weakened easterly trade winds allow warm water to slosh back eastwards across the tropical Pacific. A centre of rising, moist air that is heated by this water moves eastward as well, shifting atmospheric circulation.

A 2025 review paper suggested the rising air in the central-eastern Pacific transports heat to the east and west through atmospheric waves, encouraging air to descend rather than rise over the Sahel region across the continent, including in Sudan.

Free newsletter

“That descent warms and dries the air, inhibiting upward motion of the air masses that produces summer monsoon rainfall,” says Emily Black at the University of Reading, UK. The atmospheric waves promote easterly winds that blow against the movement of warm, moist air from the Atlantic Ocean into the heart of Africa, the paper added.

The El Niño is also forecast to bring potentially devastating drought to vulnerable countries in southern Africa, as well as heavy rainfall and flooding to the Horn of Africa. Nations including the US and the UK have cut foreign aid funding that could help prevent these extreme weather events from turning into humanitarian disasters.

High-income donor countries have given only $1.25 billion of the $2.87 billion in aid the UN has said is needed this year in Sudan. “The gap means right now we are unable to keep people alive,” says Radosta.

A monster El Niño is brewing in the Pacific Ocean – but there may be ways we can stop the worst impacts from occurring

Besides providing funds, other countries should pressure Sudan’s warring parties to stop targeting markets and water sources with drone strikes, she adds. The United Arab Emirates has been accused of arming the paramilitaries, while Turkey, Russia, Egypt and Iran are backing the armed forces.

The El Niño is still heating up and could exceed the previous sea-surface temperature record by 60 per cent. That will warm the atmosphere, and probably make 2027 the hottest year ever. It could also bring heatwaves across the tropics next March, April and May, say Liz Stephens, also at the University of Reading.

During the last El Niño in 2024, Sudan experienced prolonged temperatures above 40°C (104°F). “We’re loading the dice for some really extreme heat next year across the Sahel,” says Stephens. “We might expect to see increased mortality due to that as well.”

Scientists have just voted to abolish leap seconds

New Scientist October 16, 2026

Leap seconds, previously used to keep the world’s clocks in sync with Earth’s rotation, are to be abolished. Instead, universal time will be allowed to drift up to an hour from astronomical time before it is corrected. Representatives from 69 countries voted for the change on 15 October at a meeting of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) in Versailles, France.

As the gap between clock time and astronomical time slowly grows, the effect will eventually be “like living on daylight saving time”, but permanently, says Emily Akkermans, curator of time at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London.

For most of history, our clocks have been set by the apparent position of the sun in the sky. But in 1967, after the development of super-accurate atomic clocks, physicists defined an international time standard called coordinated universal time (UTC), based instead on the speed of a particular vibration of the caesium-133 atom.

Advertisement

The epic quest to redefine the second using the world’s best clocks

Natural fluctuations in Earth’s rate of rotation meant periodic corrections were needed to keep universal time in sync with the sky. As the rotation slowed, physicists added extra leap seconds. Twenty-seven have been added to UTC since they were introduced in 1972.

Now, that strategy is to be abandoned. This is partly because technological systems, from stock markets to telecommunications to GPS, have become much more reliant on precise timekeeping. That means introducing leap seconds is more complex, potentially risking the failure of mobile phone networks or electricity grids. Previous leap seconds have caused websites to crash and disrupted airlines’ booking systems, says Setnam Shemar at the National Physical Laboratory (NPL) in Teddington, UK.

“Time is now so much more important and integrated into these systems,” says Akkermans. “What once worked has become more problematic.”

Subscriber-only newsletter

What’s more, Earth’s rotation has recently begun to accelerate slightly, raising the daunting possibility of needing “a first-ever negative leap second”, said Noël Dimarcq, who heads the BIPM’s committee on time and frequency, in a statement. The practical consequences of such a jump backwards in time are hard to predict.

Physicists have been debating what to replace the leap second with for the past 30 years. At the BIPM meeting, they finally voted for a “leap hour”, which means that UTC will be allowed to diverge from astronomical time for up to an hour before being corrected. That should ensure an uninterrupted flow of time for “several centuries”, said Dimarcq. The change will take effect from 20 May 2027.

Once considered an oddity of quantum physics, time crystals could be a good building block for accurate clocks and sensors, according to new calculations

Shemar emphasises that the effects involved are very small: “It’ll be many hundreds or even thousands of years before a leap hour is needed.” He adds that physicists will still be accurately tracking Earth’s rotation to provide information for astronomy and celestial navigation.

The leap hour isn’t the only temporal innovation being planned, though. The BIPM meeting also asked for proposals on a new definition of the second – needed because optical clocks are now much more accurate than the caesium clock that time is currently based on – and called on international agencies to start considering how to define a universal time standard for the moon. Overall, the changes “will have a profound impact on future timekeeping both on Earth and other planets”, said Dimarcq.

Can a positive mindset protect us from the sniffles?

New Scientist October 16, 2026

The threat seems to be everywhere. On the tube, on the bus, as I the queue for coffee, I find that I am surrounded by coughs and sneezes, spreading diseases.

I eat healthily, exercise and try to get 8 hours of sleep to fend off the dreaded lurgy. It is only recently, however, that I started wondering whether our mental life might also play a part in our body’s defences. And the more I dug into the available literature, the more convinced I have become that it is critical.

Too busy to meditate? Microdosing mindfulness has big health benefits

Our attitudes, I have discovered, can subtly shape our immune system’s activity, which directly influences how likely we are to develop symptoms. If we want to fend off infection, we would do well to look after our minds as well as our bodies.

Advertisement

One of the first studies to explore this possibility arrived in the early 2000s, when Sheldon Cohen at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and his colleagues recruited 334 plucky volunteers who were willing to be infected with the common cold. In the month before the trial, they took regular questionnaires about their feelings throughout the day, noting emotions both positive (cheerful, at ease, energetic) and negative (sad, on edge, hostile).

On infection day, the scientists gave each participant a nasal drop containing one of two rhinoviruses known to cause sniffles, then held them in quarantine for five more days to observe whether any symptoms developed – quantified through objective measures. The team estimated the participants’ mucus production, for example, by collecting and weighing the snotty tissues they had used.

Cohen’s results were unequivocal. People with a sunnier emotional style were about a third less likely to develop symptoms than those who were less positive. Quite amazingly, the influence of the positive feelings was independent of the negative feelings – meaning that people who managed to feel both cheerful and anxious, for instance, were still less likely to develop symptoms than those who were neither cheerful nor anxious. This may sound counterintuitive, but it is perfectly possible to feel multiple emotions at the same time, and Cohen’s results seemed to suggest that positive feelings play the greatest role in our health.

I might have been sceptical if this were the only evidence, but multiple other studies have since confirmed and extended these findings. Cohen and his colleagues have shown that a so-called positive emotional style (PES) could also protect participants from influenza, for example – even after they controlled for a host of factors including age, sex, education, race and body mass.

While the exact mechanisms are unclear, it almost certainly comes down to stress, which is known to throw our defences into disarray. Someone under a lot of pressure may struggle to summon the resources to identify the virus when it first takes hold, leading to a suppressed immune response. Alternatively, the immune system may leap into action too quickly and too eagerly, bombarding the body with the inflammation that lies behind many of our symptoms.

How important is thinking about your breath for calming yourself down? We now know that slow breathing is effective even without conscious involvement

In the case of the common cold, it seems that the second potential mechanism is the most relevant. Someone with a more positive frame of mind may find it easier to cope with life’s stresses, meaning that the body becomes less inflamed when they face a pathogen. Along these lines, Cohen has found that people’s symptoms, such as a runny nose, are directly correlated with their levels of IL-6, a pro-inflammatory signalling protein called a cytokine, after infection. This was much lower among those with a PES. A group of researchers led by Sara Puig Pérez at Valencian National University, Spain, meanwhile, found that optimists have lower levels of another pro-inflammatory cytokine, TNFα, which has been linked to the fatigue and lethargy that often accompanies our sniffles, and this seemed to be reflected in fewer overall symptoms. It seems that the optimist’s body is simply better able to fine tune its response to the threat at hand.

As fascinating as this is, I’m mostly interested in the ways that I might use this information to protect myself, so I was delighted to find a trial of an eight-week mindfulness course by Bruce Barrett at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and his colleagues. Like Cohen, Barrett looked for objective evidence of infection, with blood tests, cheek swabs and nasal washes, rather than relying solely on reported symptoms.

The mindfulness course had previously been shown to cultivate a more positive mindset – and this had the desired effect on the participants’ health. The participants were generally less likely to develop a respiratory illness after practicing mindfulness. And for those who did develop signs of an infection, the symptoms were less severe. The benefits were comparable to those of exercise, which is also known to increase the efficiency of the immune system. The meditators were also less likely to take time off work due to illness than the control group, who had been put on a waiting list for the course.

Mindfulness may not be your thing. As I’ve written previously, I’ve personally struggled with it in the past, although I’m now finding new ways to incorporate it into my life. Given the very general link to good feelings, I’m sure that plenty of other kinds of self-care would bring similar protection. Social connection also seems to boost the immune response, so you might try to reach out to the people who matter most to you, for instance.

With the nights drawing in over the northern hemisphere, it is very easy to succumb to the winter blues, so now could be the perfect time to focus on the things that bring you comfort. A sneeze-free sniffle season may just be one of many benefits.

Will physics be the next field to be turned upside down by AI?

New Scientist October 16, 2026

AI has grown so adept at solving mathematical puzzles that critics fear the flood of new proofs it creates will overwhelm academics and actually set the field back. Until now, AI has had limited impact on other areas of science, but there are signs that physics may be about to experience a similar upset.

John Sous at Yale University says AI models may have an unfairly bad reputation when it comes to physics because of the way they are tested. Cutting-edge models have previously scored as low as 30 per cent on six different tests designed specifically to assess AI’s ability on tough physics problems, but this doesn’t square with the successes Sous and his colleagues have seen when using them, he says.

Checking the problems in the benchmark revealed a litany of errors and ambiguous definitions. Once corrected, scores soared to as high as 94 per cent. The problem didn’t lay with AI, but in the tests not providing the necessary information.

Advertisement

“I think anything that’s well defined, even if it’s very hard, I suspect that AI will be very good at it – arguably better than the best experts,” says Sous. “This is backed up by our data.”

But while some parts of physics can be very well defined – physicist Vladimir Arnold once said that mathematics is the part of physics where experiments are cheap – many aren’t. And it is in the new, uncharted, fuzzy and cutting-edge parts of physics where AI may struggle.

arXiv might not survive AI slop onslaught, warn mathematicians

Sous says that interesting physics comes when we find something confusing, some phenomenon we observe in nature, a material or the cosmos that we don’t understand. It is then a physicist’s job to create a model, an approximation or a simulation that captures and predicts that phenomenon.

“That’s a very artistic, a very creative process,” says Sous. “Can AI really take the next step and do the full job of a theoretical physicist? Do end-to-end research: define, create, explore, test? The picture is not clear yet.”

One reason mathematics has been at the tip of the spear of AI progress is formalisation. This technique turns a mathematical idea into computer code that can be methodically checked; the process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, it is considered correct beyond all reasonable doubt. It allows AI to process a problem and know when it has arrived at a correct solution.

Subscriber-only newsletter

While some advances have been made in using formalisation to test physics, it is early days in comparison to mathematics. And physics problems can often be messier and harder to pin down.

What is clear is that AI is already being used by physicists, not only to write computer code and do maths, but even to design and run experiments. Logan Wright, also at Yale University, is now teaching a course on using AI in physics research, and says that the syllabus is constantly changing to catch up with developments.

The key, says Wright, is to create experiments where the inputs and outputs can be computer controlled. Then that control can be handed over to an AI that is able to pull the appropriate levers to explore the problem space and arrive at meaningful results.

“It doesn’t have hands, it doesn’t have eyes, it just interacts with the world through language and code,” says Wright. “So if we can set up an experiment in which all the observations are reduced to code, and all the actions are reduced to code… then AI can actually be very helpful.”

Mathematicians and AI in behind-the-scenes battle over what’s true

One such experiment currently underway in Wright’s laboratory involves analysing how different shapes of laser pulses affect a rubidium atom. The researchers use Anthropic’s AI Claude to control the laser pulses and gather data on their effects.

“Claude can now basically say ‘I think this laser pulse is gonna produce this output’, right,” says Wright. “And it can test that.”

Wright says that such experiments can run overnight and complete as much work as a human would in a week – and human physicists can even use an app on their phone to suggest ideas that come to them while they are away from the lab, and get the results when they return.

“It’s not going to be [the case that] all of the universe can be explored in that way. It’ll be like very constrained domains,” says Wright. “I think part of the next frontier of physics will be to make as much progress as we can in those domains.”

Wright says that it is already entirely possible that AI will soon design an experiment that humans don’t understand, ask humans to build it and generate exciting new results. “But just to be clear, just like in math, there’s a debate about does it count as science if we get a result that we don’t understand anything about,” says Wright.

Jane Street and Auckland whiz kid Aarav Gupta: Why trading giant has its eye on 16-year-old

New Zealand Herald October 17, 2026

Aarav Gupta is just 16 but already studying maths and physics at the University of Auckland and planning to win a place at the heart of the global finance system with Jane Street, one of the world's biggest trading firms.

At 16, Aarav Gupta is too young to drink with his University of Auckland classmates, but old enough to have been flown to Hong Kong by one of the world’s richest trading firms to learn how it makes billions of dollars.

Leaving school last year at 15 with a university rank score of 310 out of 320, Aarav has since dived into his physics and maths degree, been elected class rep in one subject by about 150 classmates and even found time to win a prize in a uni poetry and photography competition.

If that doesn’t sound busy enough, he also applied to learn the secrets behind how Jane Street trades billions in split-second deals — being one of about 70 students from Asia-Pacific selected for its two-day programme.

Aarav, who only took up maths to help with his physics, said he was struck by how much equations help power a firm that made a reported US$39.6b from trading last year.

And he had surprisingly had a question that many of the less mathematically gifted among us might also hold.

“I always think: ‘What do math researchers even do?’ It doesn’t seem like you can use that at all,” he said.

“The fact that [Jane Street is] doing very advanced math ... [and] using all these things which seem so theoretical to me, I thought that was really cool.”

Aarav’s rocketing jump from Year 11 at Pakuranga College to Jane Street’s radar is a reminder that the nation’s public schools, which teach more than nine in 10 Kiwi kids, produce most of the country’s talent.

Aarav studied robotics and advanced maths at the Auckland school.

But he also often had to push his teachers, he said.

He pursued extra studies online through Crimson Global Academy scholarship, and then took to self-learning on YouTube after the course.

He also had to campaign on his own behalf - and prove himself in snap tests - to be allowed to skip ahead years at school.

It’s the same drive that landed him in Hong Kong - albeit with help from his talented older brother.

His older brother Devaansh, a national schoolboy robotics champion at Pakuranga College, found the Jane Street programme and applied for it himself.

Then he convinced his younger brother Aarav to also apply - and even sat up with him past midnight to help and make sure Aarav got his own application in on time.

When the results came back, Devaansh didn’t get accepted - but Aarav did.

Big bro Devaansh “didn’t show one ounce of sadness” and was all class, Aarav said.

“He was just super excited for me.”

During the two-day programme, Jane Street described itself to the 70-odd young university students as the supermarket of the finance world, Aarav said.

Just like how a supermarket buys up farm produce in bulk and brings it to stores where shoppers can find it all in one place and buy just one apple, whenever they want, Jane Street argued it was doing a similar job.

It buys huge volumes of shares and onsells them to smaller traders, collecting a margin on every transaction, but arguing it is taking on the risk and making the process easier for everyone.

Aarav said Jane Street put the students through mostly problem-solving tasks, with games designed to test how they think rather than what they know.

Because he was under 18, Jane Street also flew his dad over, and the family were able to make a holiday of it.

Friends Aarav met at the Hong Kong workshop even skipped the chance to go out to the bars and spent time with him so he didn’t miss out on the fun, he said.

Aarav’s immense curiosity started within his own home early.

At 7, he and the two-years’ older Devaansh taught themselves coding on computers - with help from their data scientist dad.

Later, hearing Devaansh talk maths with dad Saurabh, Aarav thought he wanted to also know this extra language they were speaking in.

At school, he said, class also often got “a little boring” and he was able to cruise through.

But then in Year 8 he sat for and won a scholarship to the online Crimson Global Academy, which covered about 75 per cent of the course cost.

There, he was surrounded by classmates who were “insanely smart”, and they helped push him to work hard.

“That was a very important lesson to learn,” he said about the grit needed to work hard.

It’s helped him ever since, especially when there is a deadline coming.

“Whenever someone gives me a deadline and I really want to do something, I will work all night, all day,” he said.

He called on that ability when - after campaigning to be allowed to skip ahead in school - he was given just four days to prepare for tests proving he had already mastered Level 2 maths and physics. He passed both with excellence.

“I was studying for 10 hours straight ... I just completely forgot to eat.”

When he later had a separate five days to cram for a biology test so he could skip ahead in that subject too, he still kept up the rest of his life - up at 4am for the gym, then school, volleyball training and studying all night.

He said he’s always wanted to be well-rounded and, while many assume his parents must’ve pushed him, the opposite is true.

“It was mainly my thing,” he said about pushing to be allowed to skip ahead in class and leave early for uni.

His parents, including mum Sonal, a mortgage broker, let him choose and backed him when he needed them, he said.

He now thinks he’ll apply for an internship at Jane Street, potentially to train up as a quant trader, though he said jobs at the firm are extremely hard to get.

He said the Hong Kong internship takes around 12 people from the about 20,000 applications it gets swamped with.

Should he miss out, he believes there are many other options from business and hedge funds to research and academia.

As someone racing ahead at just 16 years old, he knows he’s got a head start.

“I’ve always still got a lot of time. I don’t need to do something straight away.”

A Wellington City councillor is urging women to listen to their bodies after falling ill while on holiday with her daughter, leading to the discovery of an “enormous” tumour on one of her ovaries.

It’s been a tough year for first term councillor Andrea Compton – being diagnosed with ovarian cancer, having surgery, and then undergoing six rounds of chemotherapy - all while continuing to work.

Last week, she was told she was NED - no evidence for disease – prompting her to publicly share her health journey and celebrate being in remission.

Ovarian cancer has one of the lowest survival rates of women’s cancers at 42.8% in New Zealand. There are no routine screenings available.

In January, while camping in Hawke’s Bay with her daughter, Compton began to feel ill – but not the usual flu symptoms, she only knew something didn’t feel right.

The next day when her symptoms continued, she went to after hours, where the doctor sent her to the emergency department.

“I was doubled over, I was lying down on the sort of waiting room chairs, like I just felt awful.”

Nearly half of ovarian cancer diagnoses are through emergency presentation according to the latest State of Ovarian Cancer Aotearoa Report.

After scans and blood tests Compton was told she had fibroids – non-cancerous tumours in the uterus - and to wait six months for an ultrasound.

But one of the tests showed her CA125 level, a cancer marker, was elevated.

Compton couldn’t let that go.

She made an appointment straight away with her GP who then sent her to a specialist and had more scans. Compton said she was grateful for private health insurance.

Four weeks after the initial after-hours visit, Compton was told she had late-stage ovarian cancer, which after surgery was later diagnosed as two, stage one tumours.

“My first question was what’s the survival rate? I think that is a very common question to ask.”

But then it was “what’s the plan”.

In New Zealand, one woman is diagnosed with ovarian cancer every day, and one woman dies every two days.

Wellington has no gynaecological surgeon after the last resigned due to burnout in late 2024.

Compton had to fly to Christchurch, one of only two teams in New Zealand, for her surgery. She said there was a struggle to get her health records between the hospitals, due to what she called the broken patient information infrastructure.

Her symptoms worsened between the diagnosis and surgery. Compton said she looked eight months pregnant from bloating, yet she was dropping weight at the same time.

She thought she was going to die from the pain.

“I had two, what I would describe as like flare ups, where just this intense pain all up through like your whole midsection.

“It was just literally the pain of the tumour radiating through the body.”

Compton said the symptoms could have been misinterpreted as something else like irritable bowel syndrome and encouraged others to get checked if their body felt off.

In her major surgery, two tumours were discovered - an “enormous” one on her ovary and another smaller one on her uterus. The pathology said it was stage one cancer, but her oncologist was cautious so treated Compton as though she had stage two.

She then underwent six rounds of chemotherapy, while continuing her job as a Wellington City councillor.

In the six weeks before chemo began Compton felt the healthiest she had in a long time, driving her to push through with her work.

“I genuinely believe it’s because this disease was out of me.

“I honestly felt a million bucks.”

Through the chemo treatment and subsequent fatigue, Compton kept working.

She worked from home frequently due to her immunocompromised health.

“Whilst I couldn’t go to the constituent meetings and the residents’ associations and other things, I had to contribute in other ways, which is why I’ve done things like the project boards and found savings in the Hub2 program.

“But where I’ve been able to do community stuff, that’s been through phone calls and engagement in that way.”

Compton had the option to take a leave of absence but said she personally would’ve felt guilty.

“I chose and I felt still able to continue to contribute to the community.”

At the end of her six treatments, she struggled with low energy but is now raring to go with council after being told she’s in remission.

“I just want the best. This isn’t political for me, this is bringing experience to help them to do things better.”

Compton didn’t need to ask her fellow councillors to not share her diagnosis with the media. She labelled it “a cone of respect” around council, and although they don’t all agree on everything all the time, there is “no hate there”.

“I do wonder if in some ways weirdly it’s kind of brought us together a little bit because we’ve had to be kind of like this cone of silence over us.

“And I have respected that and they have respected me and it’s been great.”

The first councillor Compton told was her Northern Ward colleague and friend Tony Randle.

Randle passed away unexpectedly in August. Compton said they were very close and he constantly checked in on her.

“It was always how are you doing, even while he was abroad. We were emailing about the Harbour Quays and he would be like, how’s the treatment going?

“He was always asking how I was doing, same with councillor Tiefenbacher.”

Councillor Nicola Young attended a wig fitting with Compton, and she said she told Mayor Andrew Little very early on.

During Thursday’s council meeting, Compton was dressed up in a sequined black dress for ‘“Frocktober” – an initiative to raise funds for ovarian cancer research. She publicly shared the news she was in remission.

“I’d had the good result the week before that I was NED, no evidence of disease, that’s a really great milestone.

“And so it just felt like it was the right time to raise awareness and if you have to do that through wearing a sparkly dress, well so be it.”

She said the reaction from her community has been amazing.

“It’s been very overwhelming but quite humbling at the same time.”

Compton’s also had to step away from her beloved netball team of 13 years. She’s itching to get back on the court, saying her position as a “one-handed” goal shoot is “quite a skill”.

She’s also looking forward to spending more time with her daughter.

Compton wanted to thank her family, friends, council members and staff for their respect and support during her treatment.

Proudly wearing her teal ribbon, representing the warriors of ovarian cancer, Compton called for women to listen to their bodies.

She highlighted Amelie Cakebread, an 18-year-old who fought for two years for her diagnosis of ovarian cancer.

“Please listen to your bodies, if something doesn’t feel right, just keep pushing,” said Compton.

“We need more communication and more listening, there’s no screening for ovarian cancer, the best you can get is a pelvic ultrasound and a CA125 blood test.

“In my view, I am not an expert in this field, I think a CA125 should be done at the same time as a smear test.”

She urged women to advocate for themselves.

“Don’t ignore the symptoms, don’t just think it’s IBS, don’t just think you’re a little bit tired. Just keep pushing.

“Women, please, please listen to your bodies.”

Grace Symmans is Wellington-based reporter who covers news in the capital. Grace joined NZME in 2025 as a producer for Wellington Mornings on Newstalk ZB. She can be emailed at grace. symmans@nzme. co. nz.

Act is promising to commit $400 million over four years to retain more doctors in New Zealand, attract them from overseas and incentivise offering more appointments.

Party leader David Seymour told a press conference that the extra $100 million a year represented an increase of about 6%, which he hoped would lead to at least 6% more patients being seen.

In a statement, the party took aim at Labour’s central policy of offering three free GP visits, funded by its capital gains tax, saying it didn’t address workforce capacity.

“Labour’s policy to hand out three taxpayer-funded GP visits each year for the worried well will only make things worse,” Act leader David Seymour said.

“There’s no point promising more free appointments if there aren’t enough doctors to provide them.

“Rather than subsidising demand, Act will increase the supply of appointments by keeping the doctors we’ve got, helping them see more patients, and attracting more from overseas.”

“With 35 per cent of GPs intending to retire within five years and 18 per cent considering moving overseas, we need to make it more attractive for them to stay.

“ACT’s funding will help practices offer competitive remuneration, retain experienced staff, and encourage doctors to remain in practice rather than retire early or move overseas.

Act said its policy could encourage more GPs to work fulltime.

“GPs work an average of 33.9 hours a week, down from 36.4 a decade ago, while nearly one in ten works 19 hours or fewer. Restoring average hours to previous levels would be equivalent to hundreds of additional full-time doctors, without recruiting a single new GP.

“Not every GP can or wants to work more hours. But better funding could help practices offer extra hours, reward additional appointments, and encourage experienced doctors to keep working longer.

The party would also work to attract more qualified doctors from overseas.

“Unlocking New Zealand’s potential means making sure poor health doesn’t hold people back. Combined with ACT’s plans to close the medicines gap with Australia, introduce Pharmacy First, and establish a world-class cancer centre, ACT has the most credible and comprehensive plan to improve healthcare for New Zealanders.”

The funding would be an ongoing $100 million annual boost to general practice, on top of normal capitation increases, totalling $400 million over the first four years.

The General Practice Owners Association welcomed ACT’s commitment to invest an additional $400 million in general practice over four years, saying sustained investment is essential to retaining GPs, attracting new doctors and improving access to primary care.

GenPro Chair Dr Angus Chambers said the commitment recognised the need to strengthen general practice and ensure more New Zealanders could see a GP when they needed one.

“New Zealand’s general practice system is under significant pressure. Patients are struggling to get appointments, practices are facing workforce shortages, and the cost of delivering care continues to rise.

“An additional $100 million a year for general practice is a welcome recognition that we need to invest in the workforce and services that provide the foundation of our health system.”

Chambers said the detail of the funding would be critical to ensuring it delivered meaningful improvements for patients and practices.

“General practice needs sustainable funding that reflects the actual cost of providing care, supports practices to recruit and retain GPs and nurses, and recognises the increasingly complex needs of patients.

‘Overuse of state power’: Documents detail Gloriavale school’s fight to stay open

New Zealand Herald October 17, 2026
