By Jean Edwards of RNZ

The closure of Gloriavale Christian School for student safety reasons would be unlawful, and an overuse of state power on a religious and cultural minority, the governing board says.

The High Court will hear arguments about the future of the West Coast Christian community’s private school on Monday, following the Secretary for Education’s decision to cancel its registration over serious concerns that the school is not a physically and emotionally safe place for students.

Documents released to RNZ under the Official Information Act detail the board’s response to secretary Ellen Macgregor-Reid’s moves to shut the school, after a second failed Education Review Office (ERO) audit in as many years.

In a letter to MacGregor-Reid on 14 November last year, the board said it was deeply concerned that the Ministry of Education’s approach was legally flawed and procedurally unfair, and the school’s closure would be a disproportionate response.

“It is an overuse of state power on a religious and cultural minority,” the letter said. “The school has wholeheartedly committed to doing whatever is asked of it to meet the required standard (if it does not already).

“There is no lack of engagement, passion or goodwill to do what is required. The very significant improvements made to the school over the last two years testify to that - and the work is continuing.

“There are significant flaws in the proposed decision to close the school such that it is unlawful.”

The ministry had not shown any evidence that it had considered the effects of closing the school on Gloriavale children, and members were deeply concerned about schooling outside the community, the board said.

“Parents wish to exercise their rights to educate their children consistently with their religion and values,” the board said. “They regard this as a protected right.

“The school enables them to manifest their religion and enjoy the unique culture of their community, as part of their educational experience. This experience would not be available to them at a state school.

“They are entitled to these rights and the ministry must act consistently with them when making a decision.”

The board said the ministry had also failed to consider the practical effects of closing the school, with the nearest primary school, Lake Brunner School, a 40-minute drive and Greymouth High School a one-hour drive from Gloriavale.

“These are unacceptable distances for children to be travelling back and forth each day, and to do so would not be in the best interests of the children. The ministry would need to put on school buses to enable this transport, but this does not negate the impact of 1-2 hours of travel time daily.”

An on-site satellite school would not seem to address the issues raised and boarding schools were not an option, the board said.

“This would take children away from their families, and their religious and cultural life at the community. Concerns as to discrimination and bullying would be exacerbated by fulltime attendance at the school, and boarding is especially unacceptable to parents, whose children should not be taken away from them through the week without their consent and against their wishes.

“Children being dislocated from their parents, community, culture and religion is unacceptable.

“There is also no evidence provided that community children will be physically and emotionally safer at state schools.”

MacGregor-Reid told school leaders in December that she was cancelling its registration, but the 80-student school has remained open, pending judicial review, as a result of a High Court challenge by the board.

She again confirmed the move in September, after considering the findings of a special ERO review, with the ministry applying to lift interim court orders preventing the school’s closure.

The July review found the school had failed to meet one of the eight registration criteria - to be a physically and emotionally safe place for students - after falling short of three criteria in 2025 and six in 2023.

“Inconsistencies between the school and community child protection policies limit assurance that governance oversight is effective, and that the school is consistently a physically and emotionally safe place for students,” the ERO report said.

“Information was withheld from ERO in relation to provision, monitoring and reporting requirements for health and safety to and by the premises owners.”

The report noted that the teaching council was investigating two allegations of staff misconduct. The school had provided ERO with a letter of suspension for one staff member.

While there had been improvements overall, ERO said it was not confident that the school’s systems were “sufficiently embedded, consistent and reliable to ensure ongoing compliance with the requirements for registration over time”.

Last November, the school board said information relied on by the ministry failed to distinguish between the school and the wider community.

“While it is not accepted that there remain unaddressed issues in the Gloriavale community, the school and the community are not the same. The relevant question for the ministry is whether the school meets the criteria for registration, not whether the wider community does.”

The board said there had been no instances of any “sexualised misbehaviour” at the school and systems were in place to mitigate risk, including a comprehensive child protection policy.

Teachers were trained to recognise, and respond to any concerns or disclosures of abuse.

“The school is a safe, student-centred, externally assured learning environment, where historical patterns of harm are neither present nor possible.”

The ministry was relying on irrelevant evidence, a flawed process, and had failed to take relevant considerations into account, such as the children’s best interests, said the board, which claimed “mixed and evolving” ministry concerns had “created uncertainty about what the actual concerns for physical and emotional safety are, suggesting an underlying agenda”.

“We strongly affirm that Gloriavale Christian School meets the statutory requirements for registration under the Education and Training Act 2020.”

RNZ initially sought documents relating to the ministry’s decision in December 2025, with a response provided in May.

The ministry letters to Gloriavale detailed concerns that the school existed to indoctrinate children, maintain a caste system and grow a workforce, rather than for teaching and learning.

They also outlined concerns over most teenagers being prevented from progressing beyond Year 11, a lack of support for young victims and abusers, and students not being able to use school toilets without fear.

The ministry’s points were rejected by the board.

In October, the ministry released a further 11 documents, after re-assessing its response to RNZ’s request, consisting of letters and supporting information received from the school board between 3 October and 21 December 2025.

“Unfortunately, we have identified that, due to an administrative error while processing your request, some communications that the ministry received from Gloriavale Christian School were omitted when preparing the response. As a result, we have identified a further 11 documents in scope of your request.

“I can confirm that the information contained in these documents was considered in the decision made by the Secretary for Education in December 2025 and apologise for the oversight in our earlier response to your request.”

Gloriavale was contacted for comment.

Act has always campaigned on income tax cuts. What’s the brand cost of abandoning that? – Andrew Ketels

New Zealand Herald October 17, 2026

Act leader David Seymour has called it “immoral” to pay for tax cuts at the moment. Photo / Michael Craig

For the first time in its history, Act won’t go into a general election with a policy of reducing income tax rates. Leader David Seymour has called it “immoral” to pay for tax cuts through additional borrowing and said his party will prioritise tax relief once the Government’s books are back in surplus.

The Association of Consumers and Taxpayers has, over the years, put forward various plans to “flatten” tax rates, so that as workers earn higher salaries, they aren’t disproportionately whacked as they move into higher brackets.

There are two arguments for doing so. One, allowing people to keep more of the next dollar they earn creates an incentive for them to improve themselves and work harder. Two, higher tax rates on higher incomes are driven by envy, and it’s fairer to tax each dollar earned similarly or the same.

The former argument is difficult to land with voters. The latter argument is emphasised because it gets more voter and media cut-through. But for better or worse, New Zealanders don’t see tax in culture war terms.

In 2019, about 18 months after I joined David Seymour’s office, Act began campaigning on a flat tax rate of 17.5% on both personal and company income. Almost immediately, Act’s polling began to improve. But although libertarian-leaning policy purists would have liked to believe this was causation, it was almost certainly correlation.

Even when economic times are good, it’s extraordinarily difficult to get voters to accept that high income earners should not have to pay a higher rate of tax on the upper portion of their incomes.

Even though under a flat tax regime a higher earner will pay more tax in absolute terms, most voters believe it is right and proper that they should be whacked, not only by paying more tax but a higher rate as well.

Your average Kiwi punter is more likely to believe the socialist’s claim that “tax is love” than the libertarian’s that “tax is theft”.

Former New Zealand Herald political editor John Armstrong probably spoke for many people when he said in 2019 that a flat tax was an out-of-touch idea that made it hard for Act to connect with voters.

When Governments do talk about offering tax relief, it is generally targeted at lower- and middle-income earners, because that is where the swing voter resides.

It has long been a source of irritation within Act that the National Party of John Key and Bill English, despite cutting every income tax rate, left the tax system more progressive than it found it. Steven Joyce even boasted that higher-income households were paying a larger share of income tax under National than under Labour, lower-income households a smaller share, and that redistribution across the tax and benefit system was increasing.

If New Zealand’s largest centre-right party is willing to govern on the basis of spreading the wealth around, flattening the tax system is out of the question.

The current National Party would have voters believe that, from the perspective of tax paid, they are and will be better off under their stewardship. But as economist Michael Reddell has pointed out, tax as a percentage of GDP under the current Government, if it is re-elected, will average almost the same as that under the previous Labour Government.

While many New Zealanders are doing it tough and would desperately like to pay less tax, we are still living with Labour’s fiscal decisions and the Government is still living beyond its means. The only path to tax relief is to restrain government spending.

Long-time executive director of the New Zealand Business Roundtable Roger Kerr explained that the only real tax cut is a spending cut. What he meant was that government spending drives taxes. If spending increases today, taxes must increase tomorrow to pay for it. And cutting taxes while the Government is in deficit just moves the tax burden to younger New Zealanders.

The current Government hasn’t gone far enough to bend the spending curve down. The Government is forecast to spend $154.6 billion in 2027, up from $127.6b in 2023. As a proportion of the size of our economy, those numbers are almost identical – with spending in 2027 forecast to be 32.2% of GDP, marginally lower than the 32.3% in 2023.

The deficit is forecast to close eventually, but that will require politicians to continue to make hard choices – something that doesn’t come easily. We need to more quickly and aggressively close the deficit, and then we can talk about tax relief.

The Greens’ claims of austerity are overcooked. On the dictionary definition – Government taking decisions to close a structural deficit – we may be experiencing a very mild form of austerity. But the alternative is ongoing deficits and debt piling up on the next generation.

On the frontline in the war on waste, it has been hard yakka. Seymour – who, as Associate Finance Minister, oversaw a drive to cut spending during the 2025 Budget process – has spoken about his frustrations with National Party ministers who were simply not willing to cut, no matter how poor-quality the spending was.

This term, Act has had more success in stopping new taxes at Budget time and then tried to make its point of differentiation at this election a promise of “no new taxes”, before National made a cynical u-turn and claimed that mantle for itself.

Offering no income tax relief is highly unlikely to hurt Act’s brand or polling. Voters seem to instinctively understand that we can’t afford them right now. With National in the same boat, New Zealanders know there is little prospect of a centre-right Government doing so even if Act did campaign on them.

Andrew Ketels was the Act Party’s chief of staff from 2020 to 2025 and has worked as an adviser to the National Party. He is currently head of government relations for corporate affairs firm Sherson Willis.

Letters: Water infrastructure neglect – but who’s accountable?

New Zealand Herald October 17, 2026

The pollution at Wellington's Moa Pt has been blamed on decades of infrastructure neglect. Photo / RNZ, Samuel Rillstone

Letter of the week: Neglect – but by whose hand?

Wellington Mayor Andrew Little explained that present problems with water reflect decades of neglect of infrastructure.

This is the part I don’t understand. Was nobody given the job of caring for the infrastructure? Was somebody paid to do it but didn’t know how, or just couldn’t be bothered?

One thing I’m certain of is that large salaries were involved. This “decades of neglect” applies all over New Zealand, of course. It’s not good enough. Let’s have some answers.

Susan Grimsdell, Auckland Central.

Reading, writing, maths

What is wrong with Erica Stanford’s initiative in prescribing an hour a day for reading, writing and maths? Chris Hipkins, in the recent leaders’ debate, said all this should be up to a teacher’s initiative.

Many teachers would agree with this, but would also feel that the increasing demands on a teacher throughout the day might see that prescription diminish.

The compulsion to do this stands in the way of other distractions teachers might have, such as sports’ day, school trips and camps, cultural activities, and performing arts. Then there’s teacher-related duties such as assemblies, reporting and assessment.

All these can impinge on a teacher’s time and energy to the detriment of the teacher fulfilling the requirements of a curriculum. Having something prescribed keeps a teacher focused and should not diminish initiative and a creative approach to delivering the very basics of a curriculum.

After all, despite the fact that the jury is still out on the success of Erica Stanford’s initiative, indications of improvements are encouraging. Continued fiddling with what happens in the classroom really needs to stop, especially when there are indications of things starting to go in the right direction.

Bernard Walker, Mt Maunganui.

Domino effect

The story of the butcher (October 16) receiving more than 1000 applications for a meat packer’s job is a sad reflection of the plight of too many of our people living in poverty.

﻿In the Great Depression of the 1930s the then-United Government tried to balance the budget by reducing core public spending, civil servant costs and increasing taxes which only worsened the downturn.

The first Labour Government, elected in a landslide in 1935, and successive thinking Governments from both sides of the house, knew that keeping people in work was, and still is, the first step to improving the economy.

To do this, they have to create jobs – for instance, large public works and housing, etc.

What does not seem to be understood is that fiscal sobriety has a domino effect. While it may help balance the books, as it did in the 1930s, it can worsen the economy. Current indicators confirm that effect.

Reg Dempster, Albany.

Who’s talking to who?

Christopher Luxon has ruled out talking to Quilae Wong to garner votes, so why does he talk to Trump? One is a normal, reasonable person he may need and who is closer to his thinking.

For example - do we support Putin or Zelensky? Doesn’t Luxon keep saying how our values align with Ukraine? I’m confused, but if you can talk to Trump, why not Opportunity?

Both Luxon and Hipkins say they would reluctantly talk to Trump – because you have to. Meanwhile, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori are talking to gangs.

So, let me put the cat amongst the pigeons – if we should talk to Trump, who does deals with Putin just to protect civil process, why shouldn’t we talk to gangs who deal in drugs?

If one is politically acceptable, why not the other?

Double standards? It sure looks like politics is the art of saying one thing to Trump and another to gangs – and saying nothing to Opportunity. That is plain arrogance.

Steve Russell, Hillcrest.

Coalition of Chris and Chris

I imagine most New Zealanders would be very disappointed with Winston Peters’ decision to abstain on the United Nations declaration on pandemic preparedness.

This again shows the weakness of our coalition Government, where the leader of a minor partner is able to make decisions on our behalf.

Maybe Chris and Chris could have a chat about a grand coalition. Cut out all the minor parties and work together on long-term plans for our future.

Linda McGrogan, Taupō.

Complex social issue

The knee-jerk criticism of Te Pāti Māori and Green representatives meeting the Mongrel Mob shows the deterioration of political discussion in New Zealand.

The National Party Prime Minister from 1975-1984, Robert Muldoon, famously met gangs and offered gang members work schemes in an effort to re-integrate them back into society. Muldoon was no liberal on law and order, but even he recognised gangs were a complex social problem that the state could not just arrest its way out of.

More recently, in 2021, Act Party MP Nicole McKee met with a representative of the Mongrel Mob. Thankfully, she was not subject to the same knee-jerk criticism as Te Pāti Māori and the Greens have been.

Sadly, patched gangs have been a feature of New Zealand life since the 1950s. Rather than engaging in melodramatic criticism, it would be better for MPs across Parliament to work together to tackle long-term drivers of criminality and gang recruitment, such as poverty, family violence, social exclusion and alcohol and drug abuse.

Cameron Walker, Howick.

Promises and platitudes: The art of political discourse – Editorial

New Zealand Herald October 17, 2026

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia gave new meaning to the term "brief" when she left her first news briefing this week after four questions. Photo / Getty Images

Another week in the theatre of leaders’ debates; a trail of policy promises and platitudes to analyse and decode.

But one of the most salient observations this week came from Bianca O’Keefe, an independent Waitākere candidate, who had her hoardings vandalised with swastikas and profanities. O’Keefe paid for them by working multiple minimum-wage side hustles.

She said it hasn’t put her off politics, despite having to pull down four signs and start all over again. As dispiriting as this was, it had to do with a deeper, more troubling malaise.

“What we are seeing across the country on both sides of the divide is the fact we are losing the ability to talk with each other, to evaluate ideas, thoughts, and outcomes.”

There will always be heat and name-calling in politics, and there will always, sadly, be rogue acts of vandalism that do nothing to advance the conversation or debate in election campaigns.

What contributes to this is sloganeering and cliches – and it comes from the very top.

O’Keefe’s comments highlight what is indeed lacking in national and political discourse.

Take another grander political theatre, the White House, where this week the freshly minted press secretary for US President Donald Trump, Katie Zacharia, addressed the press corps. She gave new meaning to the term “brief” and left after four questions. It later emerged that her credentials as a lawyer were being questioned. There is no record of her being called to the bar in the United States.

The US Campaign for Accountability said Zacharia had described herself during television appearances as a lawyer and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.

Yesterday, the the White House confirmed press secretary Zacharia had been fired after less than week in the job. “Maybe it’s not for her,” Trump told reporters

Words, and how we use them, are important. They can diminish something worthwhile to nothing. And what is lost in the not-hearing of a well-constructed argument?

It was George Orwell who in 1946 wrote: “Political language is designed to make lies sound truthful and murder respectable, and to give an appearance of solidity in pure wind.”

What this tells us is that we are not unusual – some of our current crop of politicians are not exactly dazzling exemplars of higher thought or intellectual banter.

When they use words designed to denigrate whoever is in their line of fire, it not only suggests they aren’t capable of phrasing their beliefs in more sophisticated or specific ways, but they encourage the same in their constituents by reducing someone who isn’t like them to a boorish, childish buzzword. Worse, it may incite an act of physical violence or vandalism.

Which brings us back to Bianca O’Keefe and her lament at the level of understanding and communication.

And if nothing else, it reveals we desperately need new cliches.

An 18-year-old Rotorua air cadet is running the Auckland Marathon in full uniform next month to raise money and awareness for veterans.

John Paul College student Luke Wilmoth told the Rotorua Daily Post he joined the 29 Squadron Rotorua Air Cadets when he was 15 and had spoken to veterans at ceremonial activities.

This exposed him to the “sombre side” and “truly what happens” when serving in the Defence Force, he said.

“That’s kind of motivated me to try and help out where possible because I know that there are a lot of veterans and their families that struggle as a result of service.”

Wilmoth said his late grandfather was involved in World War II and “quite affected by it”.

“He was lucky enough to survive, but obviously there were still scars.”

Wilmoth said his run was inspired by Major James Poole, a Royal Marine who ran the London Marathon this year in full dress uniform.

Wilmoth is running the November 1 race to raise money for the Royal New Zealand Returned and Services’ Association (RSA), which supports veterans.

“Because leaving the military doesn’t leave behind the mental scars and injuries formed as a result of service,” he said.

“That’s why I’m running 42km on the 1st of November to raise money and awareness for our veterans.”

The money would be shared around nationally “where it’s needed most”.

Wilmoth has dedicated at least seven hours a week to training, including running and going to the gym.

He also ran the Rotorua Marathon this year.

Wilmoth joined the 29 Squadron Rotorua Air Cadets after a friend did and encouraged him to check it out.

The New Zealand Cadet Forces is a voluntary military-style training organisation for young people aged 13 and over.

29 Squadron is part of the Air Wing of Cadet Forces and is Rotorua’s civilian Air Training Corps.

Wilmoth said it was a four-year training programme, on which he learned basic drill movements, navigation and first aid in the first years.

As the programme progressed, “you’re starting to teach lessons or lead squads and have some responsibilities”.

“Also in cadets, you do a lot of community stuff, so we’re always down at the Sir Howard Morrison Centre and the World War I Memorial for, like, Anzac Days and Armistice Days and Battle of Britain.”

The cadets also went camping, gliding and power flying.

“Power flying is when you’re flying a power[ed] plane, and then gliding’s the one where they tow you up and you use the wind currents on the mountains to go up and down.

“I’ve been lucky enough to do both. It is really fun.”

The cadets have a weekly parade night for learning and teaching.

Wilmoth hopes to transfer to a unit in Auckland next year, when he plans to study sport and human performance at the University of Auckland.

Wilmoth, who is an Australian and New Zealand citizen, said he wanted to join the New Zealand or Australian Defence Force and help youth at some point in his career.

Donations can be made via his Instagram page, luke_wilmoth, or directly to the RSA.

Megan Wilson is a health and general news reporter for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post. She has been a journalist since 2021.

Fordson E27N crawler: Waikato collector Roger Benton preserves rare machinery history

New Zealand Herald October 17, 2026

After driving his first tractor at 4 years old, 80 years on, Roger Benton is still collecting and driving them. Photo / Catherine Fry

Around 80 years have passed since Roger Benton first sat on his father’s Fordson N as a 4-year-old and, according to family stories, decided to drive it through the gate his father had just opened.

“I would have kept driving from then onwards, steering them when someone was feeding out, and building up to using them to work on the farm,” Benton said.

Benton has lived on a farm all his life, first on family farms, then owning his own dairy farms from 1971 to the early 2000s.

His current farm in Tauwhare is leased out, and he keeps a few acres back for growing steers.

Benton collects mainly Fordson and County pre-1985 machinery.

He has 24 tractors (including other brands), two bulldozers and three County crawlers.

While he admits he isn’t great at the bodywork side of things, he is more of a mechanical engineer and thinks nothing of swapping engines in and out and looking after the mechanical side of his machines.

After driving a Fordson E27N with a Perkins P6 engine as a teenager, Benton developed a liking for this classic engine.

He has a 1949 Fordson E27N crawler, complete with a factory-installed Perkins P6 engine.

“I bought it pre-Covid from a deceased estate in Levin, so I don’t know too much about its history.”

The crawler is a County CFT (County Full Track) built on a Fordson E27N skid unit.

“It has a 4.73 litre Perkins P6 diesel engine with around 50hp.

“It has three forward gears and one reverse.

“There were two first and second gear ratios available, and this one has the slow version.”

The crawler would have carried out discing, ploughing and general cultivation in areas that were too wet for a tractor to work.

A bulldozer blade attachment was available, and the crawler has a three-point linkage system.

Benton has hitched it to a trailer plough and ploughed with it.

“There’s a belt pulley on the side so with a belt fitted, the crawler could run as a stationary engine for threshing mills, cow sheds, water irrigation and similar tasks.”

Benton said his crawler would have been expensive in its day.

He said, compared with what was available pre-World War II, it was advanced technology, as wars create innovation through necessity.

Benton is a member of the Waikato Vintage Machinery Club, where he is an active participant in their social outings.

Camille Cottin walked away from a hit series. Then came an offer to film with George Clooney

Sydney Morning Herald October 18, 2026

The in-demand actor also gets frank on France’s handling of #MeToo: “It’s very slow here.”

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Camille Cottin knows her job is ridiculous. “It can be easily despised and mocked,” she admits of show business, before listing the reasons why: “Money. Superficiality. Frivolity. Narcissism. Egocentrism.”

That sums it up, but Cottin knows better than most why her industry matters. She is the star of Call My Agent!, the brains and sass behind the lead character Andréa in the French series about actors and their long-suffering lackeys. It appeared on Netflix at the precise time in the pandemic when everyone needed eccentric people to laugh at. And recently it returned, as a film, to cheer us up all over again.

We meet in – where else? – Paris for a coffee down a cobbled side street just by the Opera. The 47-year-old is bright-eyed, with a calm, collected presence and wearing a blue denim skirt and shirt.

Call My Agent! was watched by four million people an episode in France before it went to Netflix, racked up millions of streams and appeared in Top Tens all over the world. If Normal People provided the sex for those stuck at home during the pandemic, and I May Destroy You brought the grit, Call My Agent! was like tourism – giving us a chance to gawp at Paris without having to watch Emily in Paris.

Then, after four series of cameos from stars including Monica Bellucci (playing a version of herself who cannot find a boyfriend) and Isabelle Huppert as a stressed workaholic, Call My Agent! stopped.

Why was it a success? “It’s like a concert,” Cottin says. “You dream of backstage, and this gets to the private lives of actors. At first, French TV channels turned it down. They thought it would be niche. But I’ve been to Argentina, Greece, Brazil, England, India – everybody knows it.

“It laughs at the absurdness of actors, but loves them too. An agent never turns their phone off. If an actor calls at 3am, they have to answer. And it’s for nothing! Just for cinema! It’s not the White House. Or a hospital. You’re not saving lives, but nevertheless you live with the job with the same intensity, and there is something quite funny about that.”

It had become so popular that Sigourney Weaver asked to appear (and there was a less successful British spin-off that Cottin hasn’t seen), but it was time for a change. “You don’t want to disappoint people, and season four was fine, but everyone was disorientated, so we decided to stop,” Cottin says.

Did she think the show was over for good? “Yes and I wanted it to be done, too. I just wanted to do something else.”

Which Cottin did, going on to become a star worthy of cameos herself in the underrated kidnap drama Stillwater with Matt Damon (2021) and House of Gucci (2021), alongside Lady Gaga. She joins Marion Cotillard and Léa Seydoux as the most in-demand French stars in Hollywood.

Yet five years after calling it quits, she has returned as Andréa in the film. What changed? First, the original writer, Fanny Herrero, is back after missing out on series four. Second, Andréa is a director now, rather than an agent, which makes the role a new challenge.

Oh, and George Clooney is in it, which after Damon and Pitt means Cottin has completed the Ocean’s set. “I still need Julia Roberts,” she says, smiling. Clooney is in fine form – sending himself up to such an extent that he rips apart his own 2014 film The Monuments Men. He even sends up his father. “You know, he wrote that part,” Cottin says. Such is the power of Call My Agent!, a show that has made actors finally realise that honesty and humour are the path to respect.

Cottin was born to Gilles, an artist, and Edith, who wrote stories, in the suburbs of Paris in 1978, then moved to west London as a teenager because her stepfather had a job there in finance. What is the biggest difference between London and Paris? “It was 30 years ago. I don’t remember much.”

Her first job, back in France, was as an English teacher, but all she wanted was to act, taking jobs in fringe theatre and landing small roles in TV and film, always hoping for more.

Then, in 2013, came the TV show Connasse. What is its best translation? “It’s hard.” Is it rude? “Very rude.” Is there an English word that suits? “C---?” Right. Anyway, Connasse was a hit, which led to Call My Agent!

Cottin has risen in an entertainment industry that has changed. A couple of decades ago, most of the films about films, or TV, would focus on the glamour – some decadence, sure, but the lives would be aspirational. Now, though, self-referential TV shows tackle recent malaises that have tarnished showbiz, from overwrought diversity quotas to #MeToo scandals.

Call My Agent! faced the latter head-on. One TV episode had Juliette Binoche refusing to go on a yacht in Cannes with a powerful bad man, while in the film, when an actor drops out of her film, someone suggests to Andréa that she cast Gérard Depardieu who, last year, was convicted of sexual assault.

“We have our issues with Depardieu,” Cottin says, sighing. “Our president said that he was representing France, so we were all shocked.”

In 2023, after the accusations against Depardieu surfaced, President Macron said in an interview that the actor “makes France proud”, before slightly softening his stance.

There is a preconception abroad that the French can be blasé about #MeToo. Is that fair? “It’s very slow here,” Cottin says, nodding. She mentions the 54-year-old French actress Judith Godrèche, who has said that when she was 14 she began a relationship with the director Benoît Jacquot — who was 39. “How come everyone thought it was normal? Because it was cinema! Why did everyone find it glamorous? So, it is changing. But justice is very slow.”

We move to a lighter note — after all, Call My Agent! is a comedy and Cottin the breakout star of the show, effortlessly cool in her portrayal of an agent who loves her job a little too much. Its success is one reason the British version, Ten Percent in 2022, was a bomb – we had all spent a year watching the superior original.

Cottin, though, has also been part of a remake that did not last. In 2019, she took on the Phoebe Waller-Bridge role and turned Fleabag French. The show was called Mouche and, as with the remake of Call My Agent!, everyone had seen the original so it was cancelled.

“Our remake was basically the same,” Cottin says. “But, obviously, Phoebe had lived with that character and it was so personal that it was a bit crazy to try to do it again. But I met Phoebe, so I’m so happy.” No regrets, then? “No. You learn. It’s not the kind of accident that kills you.”

Another reason Cottin is back in Call My Agent! is that her husband said she should be at home more. She tells me this not with resentment, but with a sense of the practicality and juggling that people often forget celebrities have like the rest of us – and sounds like precisely the sort of insider plot that made Call My Agent! stand out.

Cottin is married to Benjamin, an architect, and has two children, Léon, 16, and Anna, 11. When Léon was born, she gave up her career in the theatre because otherwise Benjamin would be alone with the baby every night, and she struggled to make ends meet before Call My Agent!

“That changed my life,” she admits. “But, then, I started doing things abroad and my husband said, ‘You’re away too much, your family needs you.’ So now I’m trying to do stuff in Paris.” Stuff like Call My Agent!, a forthcoming film version of Les Misérables and this year’s breakout French comedy Just an Illusion.

“I just turned down a director I really like, but my daughter is starting a new school and I want to be there. He understood. He said, ‘The moment from when your children need you to the moment they don’t want you is so fast.’” She smiles. “But it’s hard because time goes by quickly and you’re scared, because it’s hard to do this job if you don’t do it 100 per cent.”

Call My Agent! The Movie is on Netflix now.

September 11 to Qantas grounding: ‘White-knuckle ride’ for man behind Sydney’s new airport

Sydney Morning Herald October 18, 2026

Simon Hickey has faced plenty of challenges overseeing the birth of the nation’s first major airport in half a century.

Three months after Australia was plunged into lockdown to thwart the spread of COVID-19, Simon Hickey took the reins overseeing construction of the nation’s first major airport in half a century. Navigating the unknowns of a pandemic was quickly followed by floods in western Sydney, bushfires and locust and mouse plagues.

Through sheer coincidence, the Western Sydney International Airport chief executive has often found himself at the centre of crises.

Twenty-five years ago, he was in his office in New York’s landmark MetLife Building working for Bovis Lend Lease when a colleague rushed in to tell him the World Trade Centre was on fire. “If you stepped outside my office, you could just look down and see the World Trade Centre,” he recalls.

“There was so much smoke, and then there was a flash, which was clearly the second plane going in. We turned on CNN, and it looked like a small plane. And then they slowed it down, so you could see what was going on, and it was clearly a passenger airplane. We realised at that point that there was a terrorist attack. That was the only thing that would cause that.”

The next day in a near-deserted Manhattan, Hickey – then the Australian company’s most senior executive in the Americas – visited the site of what became known as Ground Zero. “[It was] a moment in time when the world changed,” he says.

In the chaotic days that followed the September 11 terrorist attacks, Hickey played a pivotal role after Bovis Lend Lease was awarded a contract for the rescue mission. “It did change me in a way. It makes you a little introspective … about what you want to do in your life,” he says.

Those days in 2001 were the start of other consequential moments for Hickey.

A decade later, he was involved in arguably one of the most controversial decisions in Australia’s aviation history while serving as a senior Qantas executive. The grounding of Qantas’ entire aircraft fleet to break an industrial dispute in 2011 was, as he describes, a “monumental moment” and one he believes to this day was the right call. “I was on the executive committee that considered it, and I supported it,” he recalls.

After steering Qantas’ frequent flyer business, Hickey went on to become head of its international and freight operations. “It was a white-knuckle ride. We had to turn around an international business. It’s very different from growing a business from scratch,” he explains.

These experiences have influenced the man who has overseen the complexities of building a major new international airport and enticing airlines to fly passengers there when it opens to passengers on October 25.

Hickey, 61, concedes there was a “level of scepticism” when he was at Qantas that an international airport on Sydney’s western fringe would open a decade later. He certainly did not think he would be the person leading it. “You don’t know what’s in the future,” he laughs.

Having taken the reins at the Commonwealth-owned airport corporation during the early months of the pandemic in 2020, Hickey oversaw one of the largest earthmoving projects in Australia’s history as farmland was flattened for what was to become Western Sydney Airport. “We moved 27.5 million cubic metres of dirt. From the highest to the lowest point was the equivalent of a 12-storey building, and at one stage at the site we had the largest number of earthmoving pieces of equipment in the world,” he recalls.

The major build was happening at the same time as work was shutting down due to the pandemic. And as the focus turned to constructing the runway and terminal, Hickey and his team faced two years when western Sydney was struck by one-in-100 year floods. “In a building project that’s exactly what you don’t want to see. We got excellent at working in those conditions, and kept on moving forward,” he says.

“We had two major plagues that came through after that. We had a mouse plague and there was a locust plague. The problem with that is they eat your cables. We’ve had bushfires up to the boundary.”

The first passenger flight from Western Sydney International (Nancy-Bird Walton) Airport on October 25 fires the starter’s gun on competition with Kingsford Smith Airport at Mascot. The fledgling rival’s trump cards are its curfew-free status and federal government ownership.

Yet, the privately owned incumbent has shown every intention of doing its utmost to retain its vice-like grip on aviation in the Sydney basin.

Hickey’s rival is Sydney Airport chief executive Scott Charlton, who earned a reputation as a dealmaker from his long tenure expanding Transurban into a toll-road powerhouse. He left Transurban in late 2023 for the role steering Australia’s largest airport.

Sydney Airport is now embarking on its largest expansion since the city hosted the 2000 Olympics by merging its two domestic terminals. Charlton says the goal is for it to become more efficient and exploit the benefits of its location about eight kilometres from the CBD.

Yet, there is little doubt that it is partly a response to the arrival of a competitor at Luddenham, more than 50 kilometres away by road.

“We want to compete for every passenger,” Charlton says, adding that Kingsford Smith spars with Melbourne, Brisbane and Auckland airports for air traffic.

The silver-haired Texan, who counts one of his first jobs as designing laser-guidance systems for smart bombs, says he was impressed by the new airport when he visited for a sneak peek several years ago, and concedes that the new rival’s advantage is its curfew-free status.

“All great cities have two or three big airports, and we think that keeps the centre of aviation clearly in Sydney and NSW. It makes us sharper and more focused,” he says. “We’d rather share a bigger pie than have a smaller pie. Long term, it’s good for both of us.”

As a new chapter starts, one of the flow-on effects will be a cut to the number of aircraft granted exemptions to land at Sydney Airport during an overnight curfew. From November 1, up to 74 freight flights a week that have been permitted to fly over Botany Bay to land at Sydney Airport during the 11pm to 6am curfew will be forced to use the new airport.

Flight Centre founder and managing director Graham Turner says the two airports are likely to have different priorities in the short term: Sydney Airport in managing high demand at peak times and its rival in convincing airlines to fly there.

“It’s got a big catchment area, and it’s a growth area, western Sydney,” he says. “It’s a very positive sign that we have a major secondary airport in a place like Sydney. I’ll be surprised if it’s not a reasonable success.”

For Hickey, overseeing the construction and opening of the new airport is a career pinnacle. “To my mind, this is the most impactful piece of infrastructure that Sydney has seen since we built the Harbour Bridge. This is a lasting legacy for generations,” he says.

The next test has only begun for Hickey and his across-town airport rival.

The best hotels in Europe with five-star vibes at three-star prices

Sydney Morning Herald October 18, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Is there any greater holiday pleasure than that self-congratulatory thrill on arriving at your hotel to find it is pinch-me marvellous?

Marvellousness is to be expected if you’re staying at a five-star grande dame. But winkling out something that’s cheap and lovely – that’s the real buzz.

But how to find such a place? The star rating system is of little help. Many of Europe’s hotels are lumped into the three-star category, which is dominated by budget chains and dreary B&Bs. Yet it is also home to some ineffably charming small stays – sustainability passion projects and ancestral homes turned boutique boltholes. Often, the very things that prevent these small hotels from winning more stars is what keeps them special: their intimate scale; their refusal to install a lift in a Renaissance palazzo.

Three stars (the good ones) are for the great romantics. For people who don’t like golf or the gym, who value what a star-rating system cannot measure: character, beauty, warmth – those qualities that make them unforgettable. Here are some of the loveliest in Europe.

Sign up for the Traveller Deals newsletter

Get exclusive travel deals delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up now.

The quintessential Mallorcan hideaway: a dreamy, ochre-stone agriturismo in native gardens, a few kilometres from the sandy coves of the south-east coast. Inside is cool and high-beamed. There are 12 rooms and suites, some with green-shuttered windows, others with private terraces. In the morning, breakfast comes courtesy of the vegetable garden, served on the sun-dappled terrace beneath the pines. Doubles from $160 a night.

Imagine Vivienne Westwood let loose in a colonial Cuban casa and you’ll have some idea of Chic&Basic Habana Hoose, in Barcelona’s El Born neighbourhood. It’s Scottish meets punk meets Cuba – young and hip and chic, though hardly basic. Rooms are bonkers-bold and fabulous, bathrooms dark and inviting, beds large and well-dressed. There’s a restaurant too. Doubles from $135 a night.

This handsome hacienda, bougainvillea clambering all over its lemon and white facade, still feels like a grand family home, though it took a 10-year restoration from neglected olive farmhouse to get there. There are inviting spaces indoors and out – cane chairs in a shady corner, dining tables in the courtyard, squishy sofas beside a fireplace, books, paintings, heirlooms and antique beds in the 14 rooms and casitas. Gardens are glorious: paths through towering oleander, arbours strewn with cushions, a mosaic-tiled pool. The kitchen serves simple, seasonal dishes beautifully cooked. Seville and Jerez de la Frontera aren’t far, but it’s tempting not to leave at all. Doubles from $476 a night.

It’s easy to forget that Marbs, with all its glitzy five-star resorts, is in Spain’s most fiery, passionate region of Andalusia. Hotel Claude is a reminder of where you are – it’s a classic 17th-century Andalusian house, once home to Eugenie, Empress of France, with a colonnaded Moorish courtyard at its heart, a peaceful roof terrace, and galleried upper floors leading to seven rooms and suites, decorated with contemporary furnishings and irreverent art. Doubles from $333 a night.

Tucked in a quiet bay on the island’s west coast is Hotel Bahia, with a beach and the brightest aquamarine sea right at the foot of the steps down from the terrace. This unfussy, sandy-toes kind of place has simple rooms and a laid-back restaurant that serves excellent fish and paella. Doubles from $180, including breakfast.

An eclectic mix of modern and historic come together at AdAstra, a characterful 16-room hotel set within a family-owned mansion with expansive gardens in the groovy Oltrarno neighbourhood. Design is bold and beautifully curated: mid-century flea market finds offset frescoed ceilings and antique chandeliers, and books and fireplaces give it the feel of a new-generation aristo’s apartment. Ineffably romantic in a wholly original way. Doubles from $224 a night.

Superstars have been taking dips in Como’s green-blue waters since the Golden Age of Hollywood, Italian nobility far longer, and its waterside villas tend to be five-star fancy. So three-star Casa Olea is quite the find – a 19th-century rectory turned eco hotel, completely solar-powered, with six sophisticated, contemporary rooms, a saltwater pool and a garden overlooking the lake, plus a bird hide in the neighbouring woodland for spotting bee-eaters, golden orioles and turtles. Doubles from $299 a night.

Youthful spirit in the Eternal City? Whatever next? Converted from an early 1900s apartment block in Rome’s boho Monti neighbourhood, whippersnapper Condominio Monti is refreshingly modern – velvet headboards, bold wallpapers, art deco lighting – designed by two young locals. Breakfast is served on the rooftop, and there’s a proper Roman restaurant on the ground floor. Doubles from $156 a night.

The ceilings steal the show at Palazzo Vannoni, in the old heart of Levanto on the Italian Riviera. The seaside town is just outside the Cinque Terre, making it a good base for exploring the candy-coloured coast on foot or by car. Levanto has its own smattering of pink and yellow houses, churches and castles, piazzas and restaurants – plus the only sandy beach on this stretch of coast. Doubles from $258 a night.

Back in the 1920s, the owner of this mountain refuge eschewed the trad chalet detailing in favour of clean-lined modernism, and today Hotel Brio cuts a sharp silhouette against the pine-forested slopes. Rooms in Briol are alpine-adorable – lots of hefty scrubbed pine and white linen, windows opening onto truly uplifting views, and air so clean you’ll break into song. In recent years they’ve added a treehouse suite, plus a few family apartments in the forest below the hotel. Doubles from $221 per person half-board.

The regal rooms of Relais Monastero Santa Teresa are scattered across two palazzi and a medieval monastery in Nardo, down in Italy’s hot heel. This once-grand little city has a many-layered history apparent in its art and architecture – Roman, Norman, Byzantine, Renaissance, Baroque – and a stay at this splendid albergo diffuso (“scattered hotel”) literally immerses you in its past and present glories. Vaulted ceilings, ornate gateways, cloisters and colonnades – deeply romantic and completely unique. Doubles from $169 a night.

Take a morning train or drive out from Paris and you can be in Honfleur in time for lunch – which, on the Normandy coast, means oysters and a bottle of white. Tucked away in the medieval streets behind Honfleur’s impossibly quaint harbour is 12-bedroom La Maison de Lucie, a beautiful house that’s furnished with antiques, warm colours and art all over the oak-panelled walls. Some rooms have terraces, others terrific views through shuttered windows that let in the light that drew Monet and Turner to this spot. Doubles from $265 a night.

All the trademarks of Provence are found at family-run Les Florets: a sun-dappled stone terrace set with wrought-iron chairs; views over the painterly Vaucluse landscapes and forested slopes of the Dentelles, surrounding villages of absurd prettiness. The pool is swisher than you might expect, the restaurant smart but jolly, and the wine list 350 vintages long. Doubles from $124 a night.

A 1920s three-star hotel with a three-Michelin-starred restaurant. Chateau Richeux looks out across Mont-Saint-Michel Bay and is part of the Roellinger family’s Maisons de Bricourt estate, where Hugo Roellinger’s Le Coquillage is the main attraction, but rooms upstairs in the chateau are exquisite too: warm-hued, wood-panelled, with deep modern beds and antique French furniture. Doubles from $400 a night.

Over the Cap from Antibes, the more down-to-earth Juan-Les-Pins is home to Hotel Le Sud, a Riviera three-star gem of a hotel. Inside, it’s all-white simplicity with citrus zings of colour and bamboo furniture; outside, there’s a delicious little courtyard garden and deckchairs around a pool shaded by palms and pine trees. Settle in with Francois Sagan’s 1954 Bonjour Tristesse, set right here. Doubles from $130 a night.

“The Hideaway” is right at home in the hip enclave between Belleville and the Canal Saint-Martin. Interiors are beautiful, en-vogue-eclectic, mixing up jewel-coloured fabrics, brocantes and modern finishes. The former apartment block has 36 rooms upstairs and, in what was a sweet shop, a vibrant salon on the ground floor, with reception staff on hand 24/7 for insider tips on Paris. Doubles from $233 a night.

Your classic Loire Renaissance fairy tale: turreted on top, redly damasked within, with the kind of soul-stirring grounds that are de rigueur round here. Less de rigueur is the price: rooms start from around $188. There’s a formal restaurant and, in the delightful kitchen garden, a tomato bar. Ah, oui – they are very proud of their tomatoes. Come in September for the Tomato Festival, not to be confused with Spain’s fruit-flinging La Tomatina. In the Loire, that kind of behaviour will have you chucked out on your ear. Doubles from $177 a night.

Unapologetically flowery, as the name suggests, La Roseraie has the most magical gardens – lawns and trees, pool and pergola rose walk – stretching down to the Vezere river, flowing serenely and greenly through the Dordogne (you can take canoes out). The rooms and suites are equally floral, dressed up French country style. White tablecloths in the restaurant, naturally – but it welcomes children too. Doubles from $160 a night.

You don’t have to surf to stay here – many come for the astounding location, cantilevered over the most glorious, deserted sandy beach on Portugal’s Atlantic coast, with sea views to stir the soul. But if you ever wanted to try it, this is the spot. Noah’s instructors teach all levels and ages from six up, on a lagoon or west-coast breakers, both surfing and paddleboarding. There’s also Pilates, yoga, hiking, a long pool, driftwood-chic restaurant and roof terrace hosting barbecues and sundowners. Beach houses (sleeping up to three) from $312 a night, including breakfast.

All the romance of Sintra is encapsulated in this historic townhouse, with its white-icing balconies, intricate carvings and pastel exterior of rose and sea-blue. Homely charm runs throughout, from garden to living rooms with fireplaces and vintage furniture. Breakfast is served in-house at sunny Cafe Saudade. Doubles from $139 a night.

It took 25 years to rebuild the abandoned village of Aldeia da Pedralva, down in the south-west corner of the Algarve. Sensitively restored, retaining plenty of rustic charm, it is now an offline retreat of 26 gorgeous one- to three-bedroom stone cottages – whitewashed and terracotta-roofed, doors painted blue and yellow and red – along with a restaurant in the village square and a swimming pool. It’s a year-round kind of place for outdoor types – go horse riding, dolphin watching, kayaking, sailing, surfing, cycling and hiking the Algarve’s coast paths and rugged interior. Cottages from $122 a night.

This former 19th-century farmhouse, daubed with the primary blues and yellows of Portuguese pottery, is set on its own 365-hectare estate along the Costa Vicentina in Portugal’s south-west corner. There are 18 rooms and suites spread across five houses and cottages with shady terraces. Chill by the pool, with views of the Atlantic, or find your own beach along the estate’s own 2.9 kilometres of coastline. Doubles from $241 a night.

The Dalai Lama, Edward VIII and Brazil’s Emperor Pedro II have all been put up at the Grande. Despite its illustrious guests, old-fashioned opulence and silver service, this fin-de-siecle hotel remains a three-star steal. While its 90-odd rooms have been updated since 1880, they remain grandma-pleasing in pastels and florals, while marble bathrooms retain an art deco air. Doubles from $88 a night.

Folegandros gets overshadowed by its superstar neighbour, Santorini – precisely why thoughtful travellers love this island, which still feels wild and undiscovered. Clifftop eyrie Anemomilos has, over the past three decades, elevated simple Greek chic to an art form. Stylish but unpretentious, it has large individual suites with terraces, a delightful pool, cocktail bar and all-day restaurant dishing up locally sourced salads, fish and mezze – all with sensational views, shared with precious few others, over the Aegean. Suites from $410 a night.

Stone, wood and natural materials create the earthy aesthetic of Nostos, an understatedly stylish, unbelievably good-value boutique hotel on rugged Serifos. Owners Harrys and Bianca, a Greek-Swiss couple, brought in leading architects and designers to breathe fresh life into Harrys’s grandfather’s property in Livadi and create a 17-room mindful modern retreat. There’s no pool, but Livadakia beach is a five-minute walk away and the knockout Psili Ammos a short scooter ride over the headland. Doubles from $118 a night.

For most of the past century, Andros was an exclusive enclave for holidaying shipping magnates. Luckily for us, one of them recently built a superb hotel where anyone can stay and experience this enchanting Cycladic island. Onar, the passion project of Mateo Pantzopoulos, is a collection of low-slung contemporary suites and villas, some with private pools, stacked on the hillside above the otherwise deserted Ahla beach in the island’s north-east – a region riven with secret coves and sensational hiking trails. Suites from $431 a night, including breakfast.

If sustainability, authenticity and wellbeing are the new luxury, then Eumelia has it in spades. This agriturismo is set on a regenerative farm that encompasses olive groves, orchards and vineyards, and the produce is made into natural wines, oils, and farm-to-fork dishes. Cooking classes are also on offer, along with yoga. Five barn-like houses of raw timber and concrete have living rooms with fireplaces for winter stays, full kitchens, private gardens and verandahs overlooking the Peloponnese mountainscapes – glorious hiking and biking territory. Houses (sleeping up to four) from $400; two-night minimum stay.

A trio of abandoned 200-year-old cottages were sensitively restored to form the five-suite Merchant’s House in Old Perithia, Corfu’s oldest village. Interiors are appropriately traditional, though not without mod cons (air-conditioning, TV, Wi-Fi, high-quality bed linen) and each suite has an outdoor seating area. A stay in this hinterland hideaway, in what was until fairly recently a ghost town, gives an insight into a side of Corfu most don’t witness. Doubles from $190 a night, including breakfast.

The Telegraph, London

The WNBA is shattering records. Is women’s sport in Australia falling behind?

Sydney Morning Herald October 18, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

No gift articles left

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Article gifting is here

Give anyone free access to subscriber-only stories when you subscribe.

The sound is deafening.

It’s July 10 and Bell Centre stadium in Montreal is packed, with 20,996 fans on their feet screaming as the Toronto Tempo and Dallas Wings take to the court against a backdrop of indigo strobe lights and rock music.

The crowd shattered the WNBA’s regular-season attendance record for a single game, an extraordinary statistic given Montreal doesn’t even have its own WNBA team.

It didn’t take long for an avalanche of posts on social media.

“Tough day for the ‘No-one watches women’s sports’ crowd,” one user cheekily proclaimed alongside footage of the roaring crowd.

The records didn’t stop there. Last week the WNBA announced the first round of the play-offs was the most-watched yet, with an average of 1.3 million viewers tuning in across the network over 10 days. Meanwhile, an analysis from Sports Business Journal found the WNBA drew a league-high record of 3.79 million fans to games in 2026.

The WNBA’s skyrocketing popularity is the accumulation of what many people in women’s sports spaces have been dreaming about for decades.

The league’s record-breaking attendance, sold-out stadiums, in-demand merchandise, fan activations and superstar players have set the benchmark for what marketing in women’s sports can do.

But what about here in Australia?

Dr Kasey Symons, a lecturer in sports media at Deakin University, says Australia has fallen behind the United States when it comes to creativity and innovation for marketing in women’s sports.

“I want to be generous to where we are in our sporting landscape in terms of resources, revenue, and support, but we are undoubtedly behind,” she said.

“It’s not enough any more just to say, ‘One day we’ll get there’. ‘One day’ is now, and we can take some examples from other sports to see what they’re doing.”

We’ve contacted athletes, player agents, content creators, academics and marketing experts to ask which women’s sports in Australia are thriving in today’s marketing landscape. More importantly – which ones need to catch up?

Not many have had a closer look at the WNBA’s expansion than Australia’s most-decorated basketballer, Lauren Jackson. Over more than a decade in the American league, Jackson won two championships, was crowned MVP three times and was a seven-time WNBA All-Star.

Now, as chief strategy and partnerships officer in Australia’s WNBL (in which she also played, winning seven championships), Jackson has the task of trying to emulate domestically some of that success she’s been privy to abroad.

“There are so many moments that are contributing to us being here right now and in a position where we are starting to grow – we are getting eyeballs,” Jackson said of the WNBL.

“We’re able to start making a little bit of noise around the game and the global women’s basketball movement is happening, and it’s real. There’s a lot of investment going into it. For us, it’s about trying to capitalise on that, trying to grow with it, and [to] stay globally relevant.”

Jackson said the way the WNBA is now marketing its players – where individual stars have become household names – has been a big contributor to its success.

“When I first went into the WNBA, they made us not be ourselves, we weren’t being marketed as ourselves, it was more what they thought society wanted to see,” she said. “Whereas, I think what’s happened in the last 10 years or so is that you start to see way more authenticity. The athletes are stepping into their own power, and it’s resonating with society.”

Symons has a theory about why the US has been able to produce these cult-like figures, noting American sporting culture allows “individual personalities to shine and be themselves”.

“I think in Australian sports we still have a bit of that tall-poppy syndrome, where individualism is a bit less celebrated, and we do like athletes to stay more humble.”

Symons also praised the multipurpose marketing campaign implemented by the WNBA for fans across a diverse demographic, highlighting the impact of New York Liberty’s famous mascot, Ellie the Elephant – who has dedicated fan pages and had appeared in Vogue.

The WNBA also attracts investors such as Serena Williams (part-owner of the Tempo), Tom Brady (who has a stake in the Las Vegas Aces), Magic Johnson (part owner of the Los Angeles Sparks) and Karlie Kloss, who is an investor in the group that owns the Liberty.

The WNBL has recently introduced private ownership and Jackson believes will help propel opportunities in, and visibility of, the league.

Netball remains one of the most interesting women’s sports in this conversation. It attracts a largely female fan base and has mammoth participation numbers in grassroots levels. While total attendance numbers during the Super Netball league have increased this year, the sport is still battling for attention.

Alexa Prinno is a Perth-based presenter and content creator of Your Netball Bestie – a media platform with a combined 120,000 followers.

From a marketing perspective, Prinno believes netball is falling behind other sports and is eager to see more branding, media visibility and sponsorship opportunities to transform netballers into household names.

“I’d say from a fan perspective, yes, I would say netball is behind, from what I’ve seen there’s no denying that,” she told this masthead.

Netball Australia recently announced Priceline Pharmacy as a partner, and Prinno believes the sport should capitalise more on its growing female fanbase.

“Marketing research shows approximately 80 per cent of all household purchasing decisions are made by the women in the household, and yet, for some reason, a lot of big brands still really aim for male-dominated sports,” she said.

“We are looking at females as second-tier decision-makers when they are actually the main decision-makers for purchases. All brands who want to make money should pivot to a predominantly female audience, which is exactly what netball brings.”

Prinno wants Super Netball to draw on inspiration from the WNBA and see more Australian netballers become “the face of the sport”.

“We see other sports really lean into platforming their superstars, and then we kind of associate the superstar face and name with the sport,” she said.

“I don’t know anything about [the] WNBA, but I do know Caitlin Clark, and I’m interested in watching her play because of the branding and the platform that she has.”

Clark is the highest-profile player in the WNBA, and considered one of America’s most marketable athletes.

Australians love to tune in for the biggest moments on the international stage, proven in the commercial success of the Matildas, Diamonds and the women’s cricket team.

However, when we look to our domestic leagues – the AFLW, NRLW and the BBL – attention and attendance is generally less.

“We see women’s sports sort of explode in a relatively short period of time and start to professionalise, and so when you factor in the emergence of the WBBL, the NRLW, AFLW, [and] Super Netball, there’s now literally 15-odd leagues competing for the interest of 25 million people,” said senior lecturer in sports management at Deakin University, Dr Hunter Fujak.

So how do those leagues attract and maintain their fan bases?

Former AFLW player Aliesha Newman, who designed the league’s pride ball this year – wants marketing for women’s sports to be a year-long commitment, not just, for example, at the start of an AFLW season, which is much shorter than a men’s campaign.

“The promotion for the AFL is non-stop, so I’d love for there to be promotion for AFLW during the whole year, not just leading up to it,” she said.

There’s also the importance of tapping into, and understanding, the audience and, more significantly, what they want to spend their money on.

Newman said AFLW does a great job of integrating the LGBTQ community through Pride Round, but wants to see more opportunities for merchandise and branding.

Sports agent Bruce Kaider has an impressive client list, which includes basketballers Jackson and Ezi Magbegor (Australia’s highest-paid player in the WNBA) as well as Matildas stars Alanna Kennedy and Mackenzie Arnold.

It means he’s had a perfect view of both the WNBA’s expansion, and the surge in Matildas fans following the 2023 Women’s World Cup in Australia and New Zealand.

He noted that it’s not just the personalities in the WNBA and the Matildas’ squad that have made them so easy to market, but the standard of the sports they play.

“No matter what happens, you’ve still got to be able to have the best players performing to higher standards, and the competition still needs to be a very, very high level,” Kaider said. “That still becomes a really, really important part of this because, as a sports fan, you want to watch the best.”

With so many of Australia’s best athletes leaving these shores to play overseas in more competitive leagues, it creates talent deficit in domestic competitions. Of the 26 players called up for the Matildas matches in October, only two played in the A-League Women’s competition.

Author of The Matilda Effect, Fiona Crawford, said the professionalisation of international leagues has pulled players – and fans – their way. While some domestic leagues – including the AFLW, NRLW and A-League Women – are still semi-professional and seasons are sometimes half the length of men’s leagues in the same code, the availability of players to media, fans and brands, is far reduced.

She also said being seen as an addition to men’s leagues means they aren’t capitalising on the increasingly successful models being utilised overseas.

“What’s occurring in other sports, [and] teams around the world is they recognise they are playing the same sport and that’s where the similarity with existing men’s sports models start and finish. Instead, these other approaches are reimagining the model to cater for players and fans alike because the content, needs and audience are completely different,” Crawford said.

“I think there’s a lot we can learn from them, not least starting with recognising that women’s sport is a completely different product and investing the time and energy to figure out what that could look like, and then properly backing it.”

Art dealer who sold forged Warhols sentenced to nearly four years in prison

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 20:22:43 GMT

Leslie Roberts, 62, who created fraudulent invoices and authentication documents, also ordered to repay $2.6m

A Miami art dealer who admitted to selling forged Andy Warhol artwork has been sentenced to nearly four years in prison.

Leslie Roberts, 62, created fraudulent invoices and authentication documents, as well as counterfeit stamps to deceive buyers, the US justice department said in a statement issued on Thursday.

The US district judge Roy Altman sentenced Roberts to three years and 10 months in federal prison on 2 October. The Associated Press reported that Altman also ordered Roberts to repay $2.6m stolen through his scheme centering on artwork falsely attributed to the leader of the pop art movement.

Roberts sold the fakes in question through his Miami art gallery, claiming he acquired the artwork from the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, according to the justice department. He provided fraudulent invoices that appeared to have been issued by the organization before pleading guilty in June to conspiring to commit wire fraud.

He also enlisted Carlos Rodriguez Melendez to pose as an employee of a New York-based auction company and falsely authenticate the work. The accomplice also pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

A statement from the southern district of Florida’s US attorney, Jason Reding Quiñones, said it was important to prosecute Roberts “because art fraud undermines confidence in the legitimate art market and victimizes buyers who rely on the authenticity of the works they purchase”.

Roberts “exploited the trust that collectors place in art dealers and the authenticity of the works they purchase”, Reding Quiñones said.

Reding Quiñones said Roberts’ prison sentence “sends a clear message: fraud is fraud, whether it happens on Wall Street or in an art gallery. Those who profit through deception will be held accountable.”

Others have also been convicted in recent months of selling fake Warhol work.

In April, a father and daughter in New Jersey, Erwin Bankowski and Karolina Bankowska, admitted to commissioning an artist in Poland to create at least 200 Warhol, Banksy and Pablo Picasso fakes and ultimately defrauding buyers of at least $2m.

The pair pleaded guilty to running a years-long counterfeiting scheme in which they tricked galleries and auction houses into buying the forgeries. When sentenced, they could face up to 20 years’ imprisonment as well as at least $1.9m in restitution, the US justice department said in a statement.

Champions Cup roundup: La Rochelle beat Lions after emotional tribute to Andrews

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 19:32:34 GMT

Lions lock Hyron Andrews, 31, found dead on Friday

Connacht 45-36 Saracens; Sale 27-47 Glasgow

The Johannesburg-based Lions put up a gritty fight on an emotional Champions Cup debut but came up short 31-14 at La Rochelle as both sides paid tribute to the South African lock Hyron Andrews, who died suddenly at the team’s hotel in western France.

The whole stadium observed a minute’s silence while Andrews’s No 5 shirt was laid on the pitch before kick-off. La Rochelle’s three South African players presented a jersey to their visitors in memory of the player, who died on Friday at Lions’ hotel on the nearby Ile de Ré.

A source close to the investigation said that Andrews, who was 31, was found in cardiac arrest in a shower cubicle that was locked from the inside.

Andrews’s death came exactly 10 years after Munster coach Anthony Foley died in his hotel room ahead of their match at Racing 92. Those two teams had already planned a commemoration when they play in Cork later on Saturday.

The wingers Tevita Ofa and Davit Niniashvili were on the scoresheet in the first half for hosts La Rochelle, who led 19-14 as Lions replied through Henco van Wyk and Morné Brandon. Second-half scores from Australia hooker Silatolu Latu and Fijian winger Avakuki Niusalelekitoga earned La Rochelle a bonus point.

In the other game in Pool 2, Cian Prendergast and Ciaran Frawley scored two tries apiece as Connacht defeated Saracens 45-36 in a thriller. Saracens made the better start and opened up a 12-0 lead through tries from Sione Vaenuku and Noah Caluori but the Irish side came storming back.

Three tries in 12 minutes from Prendergast, Cathal Forde and Shamus Hurley-Langton put them in front, but the latter was sent to the sin-bin just before half-time and Nick Tompkins capitalised to make it 19-19 at the break.

It remained nip and tuck as Prendergast went over for his second only for Rotimi Segun to find a swift reply. Frawley was next to cross before Vaenuku grabbed his second but tries from Caolin Blade and Frawley’s second helped Connacht open up a 14-point gap.

That was reduced to nine when Elliot Daly scored Saracens’ sixth try following a yellow card for Prendergast but Owen Farrell missed the conversion to deny them a bonus point.

Glasgow Warriors extended their unbeaten start to the new season by pulling away to claim an impressive 47-27 win at Sale in Pool 1. Glasgow’s winning score looked convincing, but they secured victory in the final 20 minutes after Rekeiti Ma’asi-White had temporarily reduced Sale’s deficit to four.

The hosts had made all the running in the early stages and were 12 points up inside the first 10 minutes thanks to tries from Ben Curry and Arron Reed. The visitors hit back through a penalty try and further efforts from Kyle Steyn and Jamie Dobie to carve out a 21-15 lead at the interval.

The game looked in the balance until late tries from Rory Darge, Ollie Smith and debutant Tavi Tuipulotu helped Glasgow pull away and wrap up a bonus-point win. Glasgow host Pau in their next Champions Cup encounter while Sale travel to Leinster for a tricky test in mid-December.

Also in Pool 1, Leinster produced a fine second-half display as the Irish side recorded a bonus-point 48-23 win against Clermont at the Stade Marcel-Michelin.

Tadhg Furlong and Dan Sheehan both scored tries for Leinster in the opening period, but the visitors trailed 16-15 at the interval after a Joris Jurand try and 11 points from Harry Plummer’s boot. Sam Prendergast crossed for Leinster moments after the half-time break and they took full control when Clermont collapsed a scrum which handed the visitors a penalty try and led to Nohem Ez Zahouany being sent to the sin-bin.

Leinster quickly took advantage of their numerical superiority as Sheehan touched down for his second try of the afternoon. Mathys Belaubre crossed for Clermont’s second try of the day, Jack Conan quickly responded with a converted score that gave Leinster a 20-point advantage when the penalty expired.

Tommy O’Brien’s 76th-minute try then added gloss to the score as the Irish side wrapped up an impressive victory on French soil.

In Pool 3, the Stormers ran in seven tries in a 49-12 thumping of Bristol in their Champions Cup opener. The home side were on top from the start in Cape Town, with Seabelo Senatla scoring their first try in the seventh minute before Leolin Zas added a second eight minutes later.

Joe Owen broke away down the wing for a solo try for Bristol in the 22nd minute but Jonny Roche restored Stormers’ advantage before the half-hour mark. JJ Kotze was shown a 20-minute red card for head-to-head contact before the break, while a yellow card for Zas – resulting in a disallowed try – gave the Bears a significant numerical advantage that they took advantage of through a first try for the club from Sol Moody.

However, Roche then scored his second and the final 10 minutes was a horror show for Bristol as they conceded three more tries. First, Warrick Gelant crossed, then Andre-Hugo Venter got in on the act before Vas ended an eventful game with his second – with all seven tries converted by Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu. Munster host Racing 92 in a late kick-off in the same pool.

In Pool 4, the Bulls beat Stade Français 21-6. Bath are hosting Montpellier in an 8pm BST kick-off in the other match in that group.
