‘Sometimes it’s not perfect, but it works’: film-maker Charles Burnett on his chronicling of Black working-class life

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 13:00:32 GMT

A restored version of his 1983 film My Brother’s Wedding, set in South Central LA, brings Burnett’s vision to a new audience

Charles Burnett had a dilemma. He had agreed to attend the wedding of a co-worker, but the wedding was scheduled for the same day and time as a funeral for a childhood friend.

Initially, the film-maker – a landmark chronicler of Black working-class lives – decided he’d go to the funeral. But when he tried to break the news to the co-worker, she was so dejected that he couldn’t go through with it. He tried asking the bride to change the wedding – which was “ridiculous to think of trying to do”, he says decades later – but that didn’t work either. He decided he’d go to both events.

But when the day came, he got trapped at the wedding. He “suffered through that” and, in the process, missed the funeral.

This dilemma is at the heart of My Brother’s Wedding, Burnett’s tragicomic 1983 film. Like Burnett, character Pierce Mundy has committed to going to a wedding when a childhood friend suddenly dies. Like Burnett, Pierce feels an obligation to be at both places, though the wedding and funeral were scheduled for the same time. Like Burnett, Pierce even, unsuccessfully, tries to change the wedding.

“The idea was the fact that if you want to be someone’s brother’s keeper, you have to have principles and you have to be mature enough to make decisions and say, yes or no,” Burnett says. “You may have good thoughts and be a decent person, but you have to have more than that. If you’re going to be responsible for someone, you have to have a certain amount of maturity. It means making just decisions, proper decisions in your life.”

My Brother’s Wedding was beset with production problems that limited the film’s release. The main actor disappeared from set after demanding more pay (when Burnett tracked the actor down, he had reinvented himself as a pastor).

In post-production, a German broadcaster asked Burnett for a finished cut of the film. He rushed through a rough cut, which the production company accepted as the final cut against his wishes. That longer, unfinished version of the film was shown to mixed reviews at the New Directors/NewFilms festival in New York City in 1983, and was essentially impossible to view for many years.

“It would have been better just to say, start all over again,” Burnett said. “The days were gone by that time. Rather than re-edit the film, I had to make terms with the material I had. That’s what film-making is about. You run into all these problems, and in each one, you have a whole set of different problems. Sometimes it’s not perfect, but it works, it works.”

At 82, Burnett, once called “the nation’s least-known great film-maker” by the New York Times, is enjoying a resurgence of interest in and celebration of his career. In 2025, his 1978 debut film Killer of Sheep, considered a masterpiece, was restored, introducing the director and his oeuvre to newer audiences. And this year, after several decades, My Brother’s Wedding, the director’s sophomore film, was digitally restored and remastered by Milestone Films, the largest Black-owned film distributor in the US, UCLA Film & Television Archive, the Berkeley Art Museum & Pacific Film Archive, and Kino Lorber.

Burnett supervised the restoration of My Brother’s Keeper in consultation with Maya S Cade, president of Milestone Films, and Jillian Borders, head of preservation at the UCLA Film & Television Archive. The restored film has enjoyed sold-out screenings at New York’s Film Forum, is being shown at theatres across the country and is available to stream on the Criterion Channel. The film is also slated to be screened across the United Kingdom and Europe later this year.

Cade said that the restorations of both films “feel like resurrections”. Both Burnett’s debut and sophomore films are, decades after their initial release, able to be presented as originally intended. “We’re trying to use the tools available to ensure that Charles’s vision lasts not only our lifetimes, but many other lifetimes to come,” Cade said. “The goal of restoration is to use every tool in our arsenal to make the song that you may be familiar with, if you will, sing anew.”

Cade, who also runs Black Film Archive, an online database of Black films made between 1898 and 1999, has been Burnett’s archivist for more than one and a half years. Recently, while sorting through his materials, she uncovered never-before-seen images made on the set of My Brother’s Keeper. The images, printed here, are raw and intimate. They’re testaments, Cade said, to the number of people required to make a film and “its own kind of archival repair”.

They are also ways for the non-professional actors and everyday people who participated in the making of the film to be honored. For Burnett, the restorations and the images allow him to reminisce about his experiences with old friends, many of whom are now dead. It’s both a painful and joyous experience for the auteur. “It’s nice to see them again,” he said. “I do appreciate what they’ve done because most of the independent films I made were done with non-actors, and I’m always so guilty about not having the money to pay them. But I’m glad [about] the restoration because I’m sure they see it and they can see it again in a positive way. It looks good and it’s their story.”

Burnett wrote, directed and produced My Brother’s Wedding on location in south central Los Angeles, where he grew up. His realism frankly depicts Black life in LA, using non-professional actors who, like the director, are firmly rooted in a time and place. In his original treatment for the film, Burnett wrote that “the story communicates to all persons.”

Making the film allowed Burnett to explore his feelings about class differences that he saw and experienced while growing up in Watts, a neighborhood in south LA. In the film, Pierce’s brother, Wendell, is engaged to Sonia, an upper-middle-class woman whose “sweetness”, Pierce thinks, is “about as fake as a $3 bill”.

In one scene, Wendell and Sonia’s families share dinner together. Sonia’s family’s wealth is on display – “signifying”, Pierce calls it, elsewhere in the film – from their fine wine to a maid who serves the family dinner. Pierce, who “has a romantic view of the ‘have-nots’”, is over it.

He lists various jobs he’s held, from driving a cement truck, working as a brakeman at the railroad and driving explosives and “all sorts of dangerous materials”. Pierce’s mother says that she wishes her sons were a doctor and lawyer, like Sonia’s parents’ children, instead. The scene culminates in a fiery exchange between Pierce, Wendell and Sonia.

“When we were growing up in LA, there was this class difference. We had this romantic notion about the poor and the middle class,” Burnett says. He said that class limited the opportunities available to lower-income people in his community.

Burnett, who was born in Vicksburg, Mississippi, said there was a “porch life”, when he was growing up, where people talked and told stories about their lives in the south. Like him, most of his neighbors were southerners – from Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas and Arkansas – who moved to California.

“My grandmother and mother and them would always be talking about their experiences in Mississippi,” he said. “They were from Natchez and Vicksburg … It was this vision of the south. It was so mystical, in a way, because of the way they told it and their relationships with people … It was like this story of this place that had this magical quality about it.”

In his films, Burnett maintains this culture of storytelling, and an intrinsic understanding of the importance of the mundane, translating it to the screen. The characters in My Brother’s Wedding are just people. They have wants and desires; they are not caricatures of good or evil, even if they are in conflict with each other. The film’s humor is found in the simple moments, much like it is in real life.

Much of the film follows Pierce as he lives his life. Burnett’s decision to focus on a narrative about a young Black man and his experiences in south central LA was revolutionary. Pierce isn’t a larger-than-life character from a Blaxploitation film, nor is he a caricature. He is just a young man with a difficult decision.

Burnett was a central figure in the LA Rebellion film movement, in which several Black film-makers, including Julie Dash, Haile Gerima and others, rejected Hollywood norms and instead prioritized realism and a focus on Black life. “The whole idea was telling stories about Black experience,” Burnett said. The directors were pushing back against racist films that shaped American cinema, like DW Griffith’s 1915 film The Birth of a Nation, which led to a resurgence of the Ku Klux Klan and anti-Black violence. “[In the] LA Rebellion, we’re responding to the negative images of Hollywood, particularly Birth of a Nation and things like that, that really destroy who we are … We were fighting against those negative images and Blackface and things like that.”

It’s worth considering how Burnett’s career might have developed differently had his sophomore film received the distribution it deserved. His first film inspired generations of artists, such as Ava DuVernay, Sean Baker, Yasiin Bey and Barry Jenkins. Though his career was not allowed to flourish as it should have, in many ways, Burnett is responsible for generations of film-makers, though he speaks about himself and his career with a humbleness that doesn’t hint at the weight of his impact. Arthur Jafa and Dash, both of whom would go on to shape cinema in their own right, first met while working as assistants on My Brother’s Wedding. Jafa was first assistant camera, on his first-ever film set, while Dash was first assistant director. Years ago, while he was casting for a professional acting crew, Burnett said that he ran into many older Black actors. When they walked into the room, he asked, “Where have you been?”

“It’s a dumb question to ask, because you know where they’ve been,” he said. “Not given an opportunity to express themselves [even though they] are so talented. That was one of the most difficult experiences, realizing this wasted talent.”

But, in some cases, their stories are preserved in the archives. They’re in photos, like the ones from the set of My Brother’s Wedding, or in other documents Cade has found in Burnett’s archive.

Burnett was always focused on telling stories, on being a director – he eschewed any notion that he himself was or should be a brand. And yet, he subconsciously created an archive, allowing himself and others to step back in time and appreciate the largely under-sung work he and other Black artists did for American cinema.

Move over, pervert glasses – the latest toxic trend is robogroping

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 13:00:31 GMT

Whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and women

You may be familiar with rule 34 of the internet, which states that if something exists or can be imagined, there will almost certainly be online porn of it. Now let me introduce my rule 35: whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and women.

See, for example, Meta’s “pervert glasses”. As anyone could have foreseen, putting a tiny camera and microphone into smartglasses would immediately lead to people using them to record and harass women. Lo and behold, that is exactly what happened. So-called manfluencers have filmed themselves trying to flirt with women in public spaces and then uploaded the footage to TikTok. The women in these videos are often not aware they’ve been recorded until their identities are shared online and they are harassed by strangers. And what’s Meta doing about this? It’s instituted a few bans and made some privacy updates, but doesn’t seem to have an appetite to properly solve the problem. Indeed, at the Meta Connect 2026 keynote, Mark Zuckerberg did not feel the need to apologize to the women whose lives have been upended by his technology.

Then there is the Flock license plate tracking system, which has been abused by an extraordinary number of law enforcement officers to track the locations of their exes or other women they are sexually interested in. And, of course, there are the AI image generators, which have been used to create deepfake pornography of women and girls. According to a 2023 report, “deepfake pornography made up 98 per cent of all deepfake videos online, and 99 per cent depicted women”.

Now, there’s a new toxic tech trend to worry about: livestreamed robogroping. Police in Cologne, Germany, are currently investigating an incident in which a humanoid robot controlled by two teenage males touched a 16-year-old girl’s buttocks and made sexually suggestive gestures toward her. Footage of the groping robot, which was wearing human clothes and a fake mustache, was reportedly livestreamed by the two males online.

The robot in question has now been confiscated by the local police, who seem a little befuddled by the whole thing. “We have not been aware of this phenomenon so far,” a police spokesperson told the Associated Press, adding it was “new territory for us”.

It may be new territory but I can guarantee you that this won’t be the last time we hear about an incident like this. Getting your hands on an AI-powered humanoid robot is still a lot more expensive than buying a pair of smartglasses, but the technology is rapidly becoming a lot more accessible. Earlier this year, a school in New York made headlines after announcing its new teaching assistant would be a humanoid robot called Sally, made by a company that makes realistic sex dolls. Outrage over the announcement forced the school district to halt its plans, but it’s only a matter of time before we see humanoid robots in schools. Indeed, in a report published last year, Bank of America predicted that, as costs go down, we will see mass adoption of humanoid robots from 2035 onwards. By 2060, they expect there to be 3bn humanoid robots, which will replace 20% of the workforce in the industrial sector and 50% of the workforce in the service sector.

As the industry develops, expect corporations to ensure that their profit-maximizing robots have more legal protections than the humans they may harm. This week in Philadelphia, for example, a woman was arrested after allegedly blocking the path of one of the annoying Uber delivery robots that are now ubiquitous in the city. (The fact the police intervened is absolutely wild to me as a Philadelphia resident, considering they rarely seem interested in doing their jobs.) A growing body of case law has found that police officers are not under any legal obligation to protect citizens who are not in their custody. Yet they seem surprisingly keen on protecting robots.

Our brave new world, everyone! I’m afraid pervert glasses are just a small glimpse of what’s to come. By 2060, robogroping may be as commonplace as catcalling is today.

Braden Eric Peters, who goes by the nom-de-influencer Clavicular, shot to fame for smashing his face with a hammer in order to beautify himself. Bonesmashing, as it’s called, is part of a toxic trend called looksmaxxing, which involves people (largely young men) going to extremes to increase their “sexual market value”. When not bonesmashing, Peters gets into regular trouble with the law. Most lately, he was charged with rape and drug offenses in Massachusetts last month; his attorneys have denied the allegations. Nevertheless, it seems that there are people out there willing to pay $7,500 for a week at Camp Looksmax, a new venture in which Peters coaches attendees on confidence and dating.

“If more women put the same energy into their marriages and into finding a spouse that they do into their careers, you would see society have a lot more babies because, ultimately, that’s what led to the downfall of Rome – when women stopped having babies, and you started putting energy elsewhere,” Stephen Miller’s influential wife said on Fox News this week. Someone buy the Millers a history book please.

Smith, 25, and her husband, 28, have four kids called Slim Easy, Rumble Honey, Whimsy Lou and Fawnie Golden. Speaking on the Aspire podcast recently, Smith said she didn’t think she could handle having another kid. Sounds sensible to me, but I’m not sure Katie Miller’s going to approve of that decision.

“The damage caused to women by these types of misdiagnosis can be very long lasting in terms of trusting doctors and their own self-esteem,” the lead author of the UK-based study said.

Reem Asaad Awad was killed when an Israeli airstrike hit her home. Her young daughter, Maryam Ahmed Ghanem, was pulled out of the burning building. Maryam’s father was reportedly killed earlier in the ongoing genocide, and it’s unclear whether she has surviving family or will become one of Gaza’s many WCNSFs: wounded child, no surviving family.

The bestselling author said last July that royalties from her book would be used to support direct action group Palestine Action, which has been proscribed as a terrorist organization in the UK, despite the fact that it has never killed anyone or attempted to do so. Rooney has now said she can no longer sell her work in the UK and can’t visit because she risks imprisonment. A round of applause, please, for the brave British government for arresting thousands of people, many of whom are pensioners, for their Palestine Action support and protecting us from dangerous people like Rooney. Meanwhile, the British Museum is rolling out the red carpet for Igor Tulchinsky, a billionaire who reportedly funded an illegal Israeli settlement in the West Bank.

Twenty-three-year-old Najmeh Amini has been sentenced to death on charges of “sab ol-nabi” (insulting the prophet). Death sentences for blasphemy are relatively rare, but rights groups have warned that Iranian authorities are increasingly using capital punishment to quash dissent.

Oh, dear! She didn’t even get her 15 minutes of fame; her disastrous first press briefing only lasted 14 minutes. Maybe Trump should replace her with a humanoid robot.

If you desperately need a palate cleanser now, I recommend the Guardian’s week in wildlife photographs. I particularly enjoyed the photo of the black crested gibbon and its thousand-yard stare, which pretty much mirrors my expression all week. Hope you ape-preciate it.

‘We’re not playing games’: Parents launch playground protests to fight school field sell-off

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 13:00:31 GMT

School looking to sell piece of open land beloved by people in Devon town to fund refurbishments

On Saturdays throughout autumn, residents of Totnes have met at a field on the banks of the River Dart to play ballgames, fly kites or simply sit on the grass and chat.

But it hasn’t just been about having fun – this has been a “play protest” aimed at trying to save a beloved piece of open land in the historic Devon market town.

The local comprehensive, King Edward VI Community College (KEVICC), has been given the go-ahead by the UK government to sell the 1.5-hectare plot – Lower Field – and it is likely houses will be built on it.

School leaders say they desperately need funds to revamp neglected buildings but campaigners claim the sell-off is an example of land that has been used by communities for decades being whisked away – a modern “enclosure” of public space.

“It’s devastating,” said Becca Robinson, who uses the field for women’s and girls’ fitness classes. “I’m trying to get women and girls to be more active and to get outdoors. The great thing about the field is it’s an open space, so it feels safe. It really worries me that, if we lost it, fewer women and girls will exercise.

“It’s also a spot people go just to do their own thing rather than take part in structured sport. You can just make an ad hoc decision to go and play a game or just to sit and read.”

Earlier this year, the anti-poverty charity Trussell published research revealing almost half of UK residents (45%) had lost access to at least one community space – such as a park, social club, library or post office – since 2023.

Danielle McIlven, who has been organising games of rounders on the field, attended the school and said Lower Field had been part of her life for years. “It’s about the unstructured play that can take place there. In the summer you see swarms of teenagers playing there or heading down to the river.”

Anna Ali, the organiser of a women’s football “kickabout” and a member of the campaign group Friends of Lower Field, said the town had a reputation for being middle class and affluent. “But there is quite a lot of hidden impoverishment. Public green spaces are vital. I was speaking to a woman who brings her grandchildren here. They can’t afford to join sports clubs, so kicking a ball around on the field is a lifeline.”

Lewis Winks, a leading member of the Right to Roam group, said Lower Field had been shared by the school and the wider Totnes community since it was gifted by the Elmhirst family, known for progressive farming, forestry and educational projects on the nearby Dartington Estate, about a century ago.

A key issue the Friends group is digging into is the details of the Elmhirst gift – and whether it may have been legally given to the community or permanently protected for community use.

Winks said: “Lower Field is a vital place for young people and families to play, exercise and spend time together. Losing it would undermine the town’s vitality and wellbeing.”

The Friends group wants Education South West, the trust the school is part of, to explore whether the field could be sold to the community. Winks said: “We are asking for a realistic window to raise the money. A community purchase could help fund improvements at KEVICC while safeguarding the field for its pupils and the wider community.”

But it is a race against time. The land is expected to be put on the market in January, giving little time to raise funds. Campaigners also highlight that measures under the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 aimed at giving communities greater influence over the places and assets that matter to them are unlikely to come into force in time. “We’re falling through the gap regarding a right to buy,” Winks said.

Matthew Shanks, chief executive of Education South West, said it understood how important the site was to the Totnes community and wanted to have an open and constructive conversation with people.

He said money raised would support significant refurbishment and modernisation across the school estate, including improvements to buildings and facilities. Shanks said the school would retain playing fields which would remain available for public use.

School principal Alan Salt said he understood the future of the field mattered hugely to the community. “We want to be open and transparent about what is proposed.” The trust and school have organised an open meeting to discuss the field.

Salt argued that selling it made sound financial sense. There had been little capital investment in the school for six years and it had “temporary” classrooms more than half a century old.

“So we’ve got a really acute set of challenges within a very difficult national context,” he said. “At the end of the day, we are a comprehensive school trying to get the best for the students in a really difficult national picture.”

Kartal battles past Ostapenko in Wuhan to secure spot in first WTA 1000 final

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 12:26:53 GMT

The 24-year-old becomes new British No 1

Biggest final of career after six months out with injury

Sonay Kartal’s dream comeback continues as the Briton beat Jelena Ostapenko in straight sets on Saturday to advance to the biggest final of her career at the Wuhan Open. Kartal was behind in both sets and fought off six set points to claim a 7-6 (9), 7-6 (5) win over the former French Open champion in her second tour-level tournament back after injury.

The 24-year-old, who started this week ranked world No 170 due to her recent inactivity, becomes the lowest-ranked player to reach a WTA 1000 final since the format began in 2009. The victory means Kartal is guaranteed to jump into the world’s top 50 in the WTA rankings next week, overtaking Katie Boulter to become the British No 1.

“That was probably one of the toughest matches I’ve played in,” Kartal said. “At times [Ostapenko] is unplayable and sometimes you have to ride that wave. Mentally, this is one of the best performances I’ve had.”

Kartal clawed back a double break in the opening set and rode her luck on serve before forcing a marathon tie-break, which she edged 11-9 after saving two set points. She also had to dig deep in the second set, recovering another break and saving two more set points on serve at 6-5, forcing a second tie-break that she took to complete the win.

It extends a remarkable series of wins against the former Olympic champion Belinda Bencic, two-time slam finalist Jasmine Paolini and the world No 6, Elina Svitolina.

Kartal made her breakthrough by reaching the fourth round of last year’s Wimbledon, but her career stalled after sustaining a back injury that kept her out of action for six months. She showed positive signs by winning two matches on her return at the China Open this month.

From little acorns … to his 1,000th article for the Guardian country diary

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 12:00:30 GMT

As Mark Cocker approaches a landmark for the world’s oldest column in an English-language newspaper, he is still inspired by powerful encounters with nature

In the autumn of 1987, Mark Cocker sat in a field near Norwich and watched a jay burying acorns for the long winter ahead. He described the scene in his first country diary for the Guardian. Thirty-nine years on, some of those jay-planted acorns will be mature oaks now, and Cocker is completing his 1,000th diary for the world’s oldest column in an English-language newspaper.

In his next diary, he will reflect on the changing birdlife around Flint Clough, in the Peak District, where he first marvelled at rare birds aged 12 after devouring bird books in his bedroom. As a boy, he would find cuckoo, golden plover, ring ouzel and twite, a once-common bird which is now virtually extinct in England.

On his latest visit a few weeks ago, he saw raptors he would have only dreamed of as a boy, “a whole slew of buzzards, two peregrines, two marsh harriers – the first I’ve ever seen in Derbyshire – and several red kites”.

The Guardian country diary began in 1904 with the nature-loving dispatches of Thomas Coward, a retired textile bleacher from Cheshire. Today there is a diverse roster of about 30 diarists spread from Cornwall to the Cairngorms who include farmers, scientists, conservationists, a vicar, a thatcher and a forager, as well as writer-naturalists such as Cocker, who pens a fortnightly dispatch, usually from his local patch in Derbyshire.

Despite honing his skills by working as a warden at Holkham national nature reserve in north Norfolk, while also becoming the first member of his family to attend university, where he studied English, Cocker says it took him 10 years to master the deceptively difficult craft of the diary – a compelling story about rural life in just 360 words.

“You need quite a long apprenticeship to get it right because it’s so short,” he said. “It’s like a haiku. You’ve got to awaken the subject from its dormancy and get straight into the theme. And then the best diaries link it to something else.

“You have a single shaft of light and, if you can, you excavate its relationship to the other parts. You have to often imply or adumbrate rather than specify. And it’s that connection between the part and the whole, the moment and the universal, which is the trick of the diary.”

For Cocker, who earlier this month published The Nature of Seeing, a collection of recent diaries alongside new essays exploring how we might experience nature more fully, the close observation required for appreciating nature is a discipline that benefits all writing. He points to the surprising number of literary greats who have also kindled a passion for wildlife, from Margaret Atwood to Vladimir Nabokov.

Before he began writing, Cocker worked as a refuse collector, a road sweeper, a potato picker and, as a penniless student, posed nude for the local art college.

His big break came after a conservationist friend wrote to the Guardian to complain about the surfeit of inconsequential diaries about cricket matches. “She said: ‘The Guardian needs to get its boots and hat and coat on, and get out into the wild,’” remembered Cocker.

Cocker did that, writing early columns on chiffchaffs, silver-studded blue butterflies and sparrowhawks, before becoming a regular when the legendary Lakeland diarist Enid Wilson fell ill. Between them, Wilson and Cocker have covered a span of 76 years.

Cocker shrugs off his own skills as a naturalist, which he says would be completely normal in another culture or era. In The Nature of Seeing, he writes about Inuit fishers who navigated home through the fog by recognising the subtly different patterns of snow bunting songs which corresponded to particular sections of the (invisible) coastline. “That is the level of attention to the living world which we’ve lost and need to recapture,” he said.

He never steps outside with a preordained list of subjects to write about but seeks powerful encounters. “I have to feel the article viscerally. I have to feel that it moved me. That’s really where the experience begins and ends. If it doesn’t engage you personally, if you aren’t affected by it, the diary is a cheat.”

After Phil Gates retired recently following nearly 40 years on the diary, Cocker is now the longest-serving diarist.

The country diary editor, Paul Fleckney, said: “Mark is a gift to the diary. What you get from him is hyper-detailed knowledge with one eye on the bigger picture, and all written with such persuasion. Beneath it is a deep, deep love for the natural world, but also a rare kind of indefatigability. It’s as if all he wants to do is open people’s eyes and ears to the wonders around us, and it is infectious.”

In a time of climate and biodiversity crises, as overconsumption imperils humanity, Cocker is convinced that, for all its modesty, the country diary’s time has come.

“Meaning has been poured on to the diary because it is a repository now for a sense of the impending crisis which assails all life,” he said. “We’re now recognising that the intensifying nature of capitalism, the rise of the right, migration, climate change, drought, starvation, overpopulation – everything is to do with one meta-story, and that is our relationship with the rest of life. The diary’s become a valuable philosophical place for big ideas to be shared.”

Mark’s new book, The Nature of Seeing, is out now, published by Jonathan Cape

‘If AI were asked to make miso, it would taste like this’: the best (and worst) supermarket miso, tasted and rated

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 12:00:30 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

We ran supermarket pastes through the ‘soup test’ to find out which ones have an authentic flavour and which are nothing like the real thing

The best supermarket kimchi

Miso is a simple product that’s traditionally made by fermenting pulses (usually soya beans) with salt and koji, typically a grain (rice or barley, and more recently oats, say) inoculated with Aspergillus oryzae mould. Bar one fabulous exception, however, our supermarkets seem to have flipped the “you get what you pay for” adage on its head when it comes to miso: the least authentic and most processed products in this test were also some of the most expensive, even though they’re little more than synthetic imitations cut with thickeners, colourants, acidulants and preservatives.

I asked my friend Jono Hope from Slow Sauce, a miso and shoyu brewery in Scotland, for advice, and he told me not to taste it straight from the jar; its intense, salty flavour would ruin my palate. Instead, he advised mixing a teaspoon with warm water, then drinking it – “the soup test”.

★★★★★

A glossy, burnt sienna paste with a granular texture and rich, floral, sweet and earthy aroma. Soup test: fresh, sweet on the nose, with a salty, fruity flavour. Made simply.

★★★★★

A very smooth, sienna-coloured caramel paste with a velvety texture and yeasty, umami aroma. The soup is mild and very sweet, with notes of barley. Great Taste two-star winner in 2024. A perfectly simple recipe formula (34% soya beans, rice, 11.9% salt) and incredible value.

★★★★★

A coarse yellow paste with a sweet and fruity aroma. Soup test: a soft, sweet lactic aroma and a clean taste. Made with Scottish oat koji, flamingo peas and sea salt, all magnified through the slow fermentation. Sweet, young, funky and alive – and this week’s best splurge.

★★★★☆

A shiny, dark chocolate brown paste with an unfathomably rich and mature soy sauce aroma. Soup test: a sweet, subtle aroma, and a deep, meaty, mushroom flavour with an underlying sour twang. Made from brown rice koji.

★★★☆☆

A matt, umber-violet paste with a smooth texture and deep, rich and floral aroma. Soup test: a sweet, fruity scent and a rich but mildly astringent taste. Made to a simple formula. Great Taste one star in 2025.

★★★☆☆

A glossy, yellow paste with a super-smooth texture and a deep, smoky, fishy aroma. Soup test: a smoked bonito and fruity, sweet sake lees aroma, perfect for instant miso soups and noodles. An ultra-processed recipe, though, including MSG, bonito, disodium inosinate and disodium guanylate.

★★☆☆☆

Thin, glossy, caramel-coloured paste with the aroma of ethanol, acetic acid and soy sauce. Soup test: mild, sweet and simple in flavour. Made with 53% miso cut with water, alcohol and yeast extract.

★☆☆☆☆

A thin, glossy, brown sugar-coloured paste with a sour but rounded umami aroma. Soup test: an acidic aroma and intensely salty taste with rich umami notes in the background. It’s 55% miso paste cut with salt, sugar, acidity regulators and preservatives.

★☆☆☆☆

A thin, ochre paste with an acidic umami aroma. Soup test: sour-forward with a rounded, earthy flavour. Made with 45% miso paste cut with cornflour, acidity regulator and preservative potassium sorbate.

☆☆☆☆☆

A thin, shiny, yellow paste with an odd sour but still umami aroma. Soup test: unexpectedly sour. If AI were asked to make miso, I expect it would taste like this synthetic impression of miso that’s nothing like the real thing. Contains citric acid, colour (plain caramel) and potassium sorbate.

From 3,000 feathers to pet portraits, Rolls-Royce rides high on custom craze

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 12:00:29 GMT

In our second in a series on high-end UK manufacturing, we visit the artisans producing rich clients’ bespoke luxury cars

‘Our town is making jeans again’: meet the firm reviving jobs and skills in Wales

They are the plaything of kings, presidents and A-listers, with Rolls-Royce enthusiasts ranging from the Sultan of Brunei to Rowan Atkinson, from King Charles III to Kermit the frog.

And at the carmaker’s factory in Goodwood, West Sussex, special requests from customers get more indulgent every year. An interior lined with 3,000 iridescent feathers, or a built-in champagne cooler, or a car built in homage to its owners’ dog, have all become part of the job.

Even with a fast-growing team of artisans and engineers, the company is stretched, and soon it will nearly double the size of its factory as part of a £300m investment by its owner, BMW, which it said at the time of the announcement was part of “securing our future here in the UK”.

Behind much of the demand is a new kind of client, who is younger than ever and with a fortune built in technology, says Julian Jenkins, Rolls-Royce’s director of sales and brand. The average buyer is now just 43 – down from 56 in 2010. “Never has there been so much wealth created so quickly at such a young age,” he says.

Bespoke, high-value customisation is becoming an increasingly valuable pillar of UK manufacturing, which still makes up about 9% of the UK economy despite the years of deindustrialisation that Andy Burnham has vowed to reverse. This week, the wider sector helped drive a surprise expansion of GDP in August, after growing 0.8% month on month.

On a tour of the Goodwood factory, an inner door panel is emblazoned with a bitcoin symbol, hinting at changing tastes. “The industries – cryptocurrency, AI and tech – are where we see some of these young entrepreneurs finding their way very quickly to Rolls-Royce,” Jenkins says. “They are very specific about what they want.”

Another car, built for a wealthy American couple, was devoted to their Labrador, Bailey. The dog’s face was pieced together on a rear panel using more than 180 individual slivers of wood, which was a four-month project, with paw prints engraved in the doors for good measure. Clients nowadays, Jenkins says, “are creating something in their image”.

Four models make up the current Rolls-Royce range: the Phantom, starting at £441,000, the nearly three-tonne Cullinan SUV, from £345,000, the Spectre electric car, from £333,000, and the cheaper Ghost, from £290,000.

But the average Rolls-Royce sells for about £500,000, up from about £300,000 a decade ago, driven largely by customisation work. A heavily personalised car can cost 25% more than the standard price, and seven-figure sums are “not unusual”, a spokesperson says.

“The limits are set by the client,” Jenkins says. “We’ve seen some extremely complex and intricate commissions, and some of those can take multiple years. With that, there is value that comes as a consequence.”

It is a vision Rolls-Royce’s founders could scarcely have imagined for a company that staked its early reputation on reliability. The business dates back to 1904, when Charles Rolls, an aristocrat and racing driver, met Henry Royce, an engineer, at the Midland Hotel in Manchester, and agreed to sell every car the latter could build.

By 1907, Autocar magazine called the Silver Ghost, an early model, the “best car in the world” after completing the gruelling Scottish Reliability Trial without a single mechanical fault. Now, Rolls-Royce has its own entry in the Collins dictionary, as a byword for “anything considered to be the very best of its kind”. Its longest-running model, the Phantom, celebrated its centenary last year.

An expansion into aero engines during the world wars made it a manufacturing powerhouse, but later financial collapse forced the government of the time to nationalise the company in 1971. The car business was split off and sold to the engineering firm Vickers. Rolls-Royce, the FTSE 100 aerospace giant, still shares the same logo.

In 1998, BMW bought the right to put the Rolls-Royce name on cars, and in 2003 opened the Goodwood factory, promising to triple annual production from about 2,000 cars a year. Two decades later it succeeded, when output peaked at 6,032 cars, falling back to 5,664 last year.

Would the Rolls-Royce engineers whose Merlin engines powered the second world war Spitfire have guessed the company name would end up in German hands?

“Rolls-Royce motorcars is very much a British company at heart,” says Chris Brownridge, its chief executive. However, he admits it benefits from “synergies” with BMW, such as “battery technology research and development, access to wind-tunnels and other major facilities”.

The expansion at Goodwood comes as carmakers are under significant strain from Chinese competition, soaring industrial energy costs and US tariffs. Jaguar Land Rover recently said it would cut 4,000 jobs, while Volkswagen, which owns Rolls-Royce’s arch rival Bentley, is cutting 100,000 jobs by 2030.

Shrinking demand in China, a key export market for luxury goods, has “obviously been significant”, Jenkins admits, pointing to Rolls-Royce clients “who made their wealth through the [Chinese] property market … which has been adversely affected.”

Electrification has been part of that story, too. Rolls-Royce’s first electric vehicle, the Spectre, launched in 2022, alongside a pledge from the company to sell only EVs by the end of the decade. The model sold briskly at first but deliveries nearly halved in 2025, and earlier this year Rolls-Royce scrapped its 2030 target.

Jenkins says the company is “not immune to the shifts that have happened, and some of the resistance that we’ve seen [to EVs]”. A revamped version, the Spectre Series Two, recently launched with a longer range and more power.

The latest factory upgrade, Jenkins says, is less about pumping out more cars, but rather about meeting the “ever more complex” demands of clients. Every car is made to order and assembled at Goodwood, where 2,500 people work across a production line with 45 stations. A single car can take up to 600 hours to build, passing through more than 100 pairs of hands.

Those include 14 artisans finishing personalised vehicles. Artists hand-paint designs on bodywork and inner panels, while embroiderers are on hand to make the ceilings of cars look like the night sky. A standard sky contains up to 1,600 fibre-optic stars and takes around nine hours to thread by hand, while the most elaborate commissions can take two full days.

A trio of innovation specialists work on novel techniques. One dragon design used a method borrowed from fine furniture called sand shading, in which each individual scale is burned at the edges in a hot pan to create a shadow effect across the creature’s body.

Andrew Hopkins, a lead craftsperson, studied furniture making before joining Goodwood when it opened in 2003. Does he ever think a request is a bit much? “Whether you like it personally, you don’t really take it into account,” he says. “You learn quite fast not to be the taste police.”

But who is paying for it? Well-documented owners include Tyson Fury, David Beckham and members of the Kardashian family. Kylie Jenner had her Rolls-Royce Cullinan finished with a pink interior and a plaque reading “Stormi’s Mom” in honour of her daughter.

Despite its slowdown, many of the youngest, tech-rich buyers are still coming from China. Jenkins was recently in Beijing, opening a new dealership and presenting a car to a 26-year-old woman who had “fallen in love” with a custom design.

“They are individuals that are very much on the way up in terms of their wealth creation,” he says, “but doing so at an incredible pace.”

Is the growing concentration of wealth among fewer and younger people a good thing for society? Whatever the answer, it has certainly helped Rolls-Royce. “It’s a fact, isn’t it?” says Jenkins.

England stunned as Tonga tonking leaves Rugby League World Cup hopes in shreds

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 11:35:53 GMT

Pool B + C: England 12-30 Tonga

England Women thump Wales 70-6

The Rugby League World Cup began with a sense of mission improbable for England, but after one game, it already represents something more like mission impossible.

The talk pre-tournament from Brian McDermott had been about being different. Going against the grain of how the national team has played against the world’s best and falling short; having a creative spark that would be significant in crucial moments. For all the talk of change, the most important thing of all remained the same in Perth on Saturday: the result.

Whoever lost this game was always going to be a victim of the farcical format this reduced World Cup has in place. The six nations from Groups B and C will be put into a combined league table with the top two joining the winners and runners-up of Group A in the semi-finals.

This defeat, arguably of England’s own making given their profligacy in attack and critical disciplinary lapses, means they are now relying on favours elsewhere. England need Tonga to beat Samoa on 1 November while they pile on the points against Papua New Guinea and France to stand any chance.

The most plausible outcome, though, is that England are heading home in a fortnight and it would be the first time they have not made at least the final four. A damning indictment on the English game, at a time when its administrators are once again stalling over a deal to sanction much-needed NRL investment.

This contest could have been different. For half an hour England were excellent, pushing Tonga on to the back foot with intuitive and entertaining second-phase rugby. But when they found themselves in Tonga territory, just like in last year’s Ashes, England did not have the creative capability to find a decisive play.

That meant Tonga could absorb a lot of what England threw their way and responded with Stefano Utoikamanu’s try somewhat against the run of play. The outstanding Isaiya Katoa converted the try and added two penalties to put Tonga ahead by 10 at half-time. Harsh? Perhaps. But this is international rugby: where the margins are fine.

“We opened them up in that first 20 and found ourselves in good positions, but we had some scrappy finishes,” McDermott said. “It was too erratic. Our gameplan doesn’t need to change, we just need to be patient.

“It was a really good contest and I thought we stood toe to toe with them for nearly all the game. They’re a big, strong team and they’ve got some tremendous players. There’s tonnes of positives to take. There’s one or two glaring things that we need to get rid of, such as losing possession, but we’ll be chasing the good stuff.”

However, the format means patience will be in short supply. In contrast, Tonga remain in control of their own destiny. Roared on by a passionate Mate Ma’a fanbase, they won the crucial moments and showed greater composure on their opponents’ line. AJ Brimson’s early second-half try looked as though it had swung momentum back England’s way, but penalties relieved the pressure for Tonga and they took advantage.

England Brimson; Young, Savala, Farnworth, Eckersley; Williams, Smith; King, O’Neill, Thompson, Nsemba, Pearce-Paul, Radley. Interchange Currie, Litten, Havard, Walters. Tries Brimson, Young. Goals Savala 2.

Tonga Hopoate; Watene-Zelezniak, Koula, Toia, Fifita; Fainu, Katoa; Fonua-Blake, Foketi, Taumalolo, Olakau’atu, Wong, Frizell. Interchange Lolohea, Utoikamanu, Vaimauga, Halasima. Tries Utoikamanu, Olakau'atu 2, Koula. Goals Katoa 7.

Referee G Sutton (Aus).

Katoa’s clever kick caught England out and allowed Haumole Olakau’atu the space to score. Three minutes later, Tonga struck a devastating blow as Tui Lolohea cut the English defence open with the boot, Toluta’u Koula reacting fastest. England were in big trouble.

They threatened a grandstand finale when Dom Young finished a slick move in the corner, but with 10 minutes left, Tonga re-established control through Olaka’atu’s second and another wonderful move in the final moments meant Koula claim his second late on.

Some of England’s problems, as McDermott admitted, were indeed of their own making. With time, they can be cleaned up. But here is the thing: England don’t have time. It might have already run out.

Meanwhile, England’s women warmed up for next Saturday’s game against the reigning world champions, Australia, with an eye-catching 70-6 win over Wales in their opening match.

All eyes are on the English to see whether they can provide a competitive challenge to the all-conquering Jillaroos when they meet in Perth next Saturday to decide who wins Group A. Australia beat Samoa 40-0 on Friday.

Anna Davies and the debutant Connie Boyd scored hat-tricks for England, with Izzy Rowe scoring twice and finishing with a points haul of 26.

The power of AI is worrying senior Labour figures – as is the fear of ‘falling behind the public’

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 11:33:20 GMT

Westminster appears to be waking up to warnings over AI safety, with concerns over its use by extremist groups and bad actors

“I have this sense that, within a few months, AI is going to be all anyone is talking about,” said one cabinet minister, with an ominous stare.

It was Labour conference, with everyone from ministers to activists jubilant at Andy Burnham’s takeover and a bounce in the polls after the change of leader.

But a number of senior Labour figures were privately starting to name the power of AI as the thing worrying them most, alongside the immediate pressures on the cost of living and fragile economy.

One cabinet minister – with a brief unrelated to technology – told the Guardian that dangerous, out-of-control AI was the issue keeping them up at night, fretting about the threat to humanity. It was “not killer robots” causing the worry, they explained, but the idea of a huge amount of concentrated, super-intelligent power potentially ending up in the hands of bad actors.

Another expressed concern that the government was “falling behind the public” in terms of dealing with worries about AI safety – and that it needed to catch up fast.

In his conference speech, Ed Miliband was the most strident about the “daunting” dangers of AI, making the case that politicians could not and would not allow the profits of tech companies “to come at the expense of our children or indeed humanity”.

And it has not taken long for these alarm bells to ring even louder, with the last seven days looking like the week Westminster fully woke up to the warnings.

A flurry of activity started on Monday with Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister, stating it was “likely, if not inevitable” that rogue agents would hack the British state, and saying the UK was looking to strengthen its forthcoming cybersecurity legislation.

It was the main topic of discussion at cabinet on Tuesday, and that was followed by the MI5 chief Ken McCallum warning AI was “supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders”. He said the biggest threat was extremist groups using the technology to unleash bioweapons – toxins used to cause death and disease.

Liam Byrne, the chair of the business, innovation, science and trade committee, said the change of government from Keir Starmer to Burnham was partly behind the increased focus on protecting the UK from AI threats but more still had to be done. “The reality is that the Starmer administration was much too close to the big tech companies,” Byrne said. “And Burnham is not, frankly, so there has been a change of posture. Those things, plus the security services issuing their warning, that is what has changed the weather on this.”

One senior Labour government figure agreed that Burnham’s government was taking AI safety warnings more seriously. “I do feel there has been a shift. Under the last lot, too many of them had drunk the tech-bro Kool-Aid,” he said.

Byrne’s committee held an evidence session this week with civil service leaders in charge of AI security and executives from the key companies – Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind and Meta – with a split between them about whether government testing of new models should be mandatory.

He said his committee was “lighting up” the issue, particularly in terms of working with the US to regulate and monitor new models. It had been reported that Donald Trump’s administration had asked AI companies not to share their latest models with the UK’s cutting-edge AI Security Institute for testing, though Narayan confirmed this week that they had managed to retain cooperation.

But Byrne said the government now needed to seize the moment and take the lead on new regulation, particularly if Trump’s Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections to the Democrats.

“I think the government is still caught in a dilemma between how to keep model access, given a capricious US president, and the safeguards that the industry itself now says are essential. It’s make-your-mind-up time, I would say,” Byrne said.

“The companies want to cooperate … It’s not in their commercial interest to issue models which are lethal. Now they too have got to navigate the White House. So I just think this is a moment when the government has actually got to do what is right for the country because Congress is about to change the dynamics on this in the US.”

The UK’s upcoming G20 presidency will be the key moment to push for international action to rein in AI. Geoffrey Irving, the former chief scientist at AISI who spoke at this week’s parliamentary hearing, believes Whitehall concerns are justified. OpenAI and Anthropic’s technology has already shown its hacking capabilities but their models are released with safety guardrails in place that at least mitigate against the threat of malicious behaviour.

after newsletter promotion

However, so-called open source AI models are freely available and can be adapted. Typically, they caught up with the paid-for models such as OpenAI’s within less than a year, said Irving, although they could cause disruption already.

“It’s very likely that open source models are already powerful enough to do serious damage,” Irving told the Guardian, adding that he expected open source technology to reach the capabilities of OpenAI and Anthropic products “soon”. Safety guardrails “either don’t exist or can be trivially removed” from open source models, he added.

The business committee heard this week that AI-enabled bioweapons could become the next serious threat to manifest itself, in the wake of cybersecurity, as models become more powerful and therefore capable of designing novel bio-harms – although experts suggest there is a gap between designing dangerous pathogens and weaponising them.

Concerns over cybersecurity and bioweapons can escalate rapidly to fears about AI wiping out humanity in a variety of scenarios – a concern that is widespread within the AI community, and is shared by Irving.

However, some experts argue that the government should focus on immediate risks from AI. Prof Elena Simperl, a co-director of the Institute for Artificial Intelligence at King’s College London, said the existential risk argument had “no evidence” and was a “theory” rather than a credible threat.

“There are bigger, more immediate risks that AI technology is posing now and are actually evidenced, like hacking and signs that AI can be as addictive as social media,” Simperl said.

In the absence of international AI regulation, there are some in Whitehall worried about whether the UK is doing enough preparation to defend against AI warfare and attacks.

Defence sources said there was concern about the cancellation last year of the AI programme at the government’s Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (Dstl), based at Porton Down, with worries that this was shortsighted given the need for cutting-edge research on advancing the nation’s capabilities and defending against its risks.

This was countered by an MoD spokesperson who said AI was “transforming defence from industry to the battlefield and will play a decisive role in how we fight and defend” and that it must be “integrated across all workstreams, rather than a standalone programme”. They pointed to a £400m investment in AI-focused capabilities over the next four years to “prepare the UK for the future of warfare”.

Others in Whitehall have the opposite concern: that worries about safety could become too dominant – and end up holding back the government’s adoption of tools that could be transformative for productivity and solving longstanding problems in public services, from medical care to reducing waiting lists.

The former cabinet secretary Gus O’Donnell told the Guardian that ministers needed to be as aware of “the risk of being left behind” when it came to AI as being aware of the need for guardrails.

Launching a Global Government Forum report on AI with the tech firm Cognizant, O’Donnell told the Guardian: “There is a big need to get it better and to really push on. I’m really optimistic, but the challenge for us, obviously, is managing the risks along the way, making sure that we don’t make mistakes, which reduce people’s trust, which means that that sets us back.”

Fake Linda and me: the Agatha Christie-worthy mystery of the fraudster who stole my byline

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 11:00:30 GMT

How a string of bizarre events led writer Linda Geddes to don her sleuthing cap and dig into a world of shadowy impersonators

It started with an entirely ordinary interaction on LinkedIn. Someone had tagged me in a post, saying how much they’d enjoyed contributing to a New York Post article I’d written about “chronoworking”. As the author of a book about circadian rhythms, it was exactly the sort of subject I might write about. Except I’d never heard of this person, let alone interviewed them.

I clicked on the link and my stomach dropped. There, above an article about people who organise their working lives around their biological clocks, was my name: Linda Geddes.

It was the latest in a string of increasingly bizarre events that had begun three weeks earlier, when a friend who works as an editor at the scientific journal Nature texted to ask whether I’d been pitching stories to one of her colleagues. I hadn’t.

It turned out that someone had been approaching Nature editors using my name and an email address that wasn’t mine, referencing articles I’d previously written to make their pitches more convincing. Worse, the journal had recently encountered another impersonator posing as Caroline Williams, a former colleague of mine. That person had convinced an editor at Science to commission and publish an article under Caroline’s name, receiving about $1,000 for it.

Further digging revealed that Fake Linda had also pitched a story to Science, unsuccessfully. Then, last week, an editor at Nature Medicine contacted me to ask whether I’d been pitching to them and Nature Health as well.

I donned my sleuthing cap and discovered a potential link between Fake Linda and Fake Caroline. Entering my impersonator’s email address into Outlook. com’s account recovery system revealed a partially obscured Gmail recovery address. An editor at Science had independently discovered the same address pattern associated with Fake Caroline’s email.

As someone whose livelihood depends on the reputation I’ve spent decades building, I find this deeply unsettling. Someone is potentially making money by passing themselves off as me, while putting my professional credibility at risk. Apart from one interview conducted by email, the quotes in the New York Post article were lifted from previously published features, without attribution. Many of Fake Linda’s pitches also bear the hallmarks of AI-assisted writing. Even unsuccessful pitches could damage relationships with editors.

The New York Post has since removed the article, conducted an internal review and referred the matter to the appropriate authorities, a spokesperson said.

What I find particularly baffling is the motive. Freelance science journalism is hardly a lucrative profession, and is quite niche. My best guess is that a struggling freelancer is impersonating more established peers to boost their earnings, perhaps using AI to make the process more efficient. But how would they receive payment without revealing their identity?

Other possibilities have crossed my mind. Could it be a PR professional trying to secure coverage for a client, or someone testing how easily publishers can be fooled? Perhaps it is someone with a personal grudge. But as Caroline put it: “Why us? We’re nice!”

Dr Simon Miller, the director of policy, strategy and communications at the UK fraud prevention service Cifas, is equally bemused. “Ordinarily, if you’re seeking to defraud, you’re seeking to do it at scale, in a relatively light-touch way, using mechanised, industrialised processes,” he said. “This is tantalisingly unusual. It’s almost the stuff of Agatha Christie, but with 21st-century technology.”

Journalists are far from the only people finding their names attached to work they didn’t produce. In April, Prof Eric Topol, of the Scripps Institute in California, discovered his name on a scientific paper he knew nothing about. Four of his five supposed co-authors were similarly unaware of the paper, while the fifth could not be identified. Within hours of Topol flagging the incident on X, the journal’s website had disappeared.

Topol, who is a bestselling author, said he has discovered at least 12 books on Amazon with his name on that he didn’t write, including several cookbooks. “I don’t even know how to cook,” he said. Particularly upsetting was when a patient told him he’d read his supposed memoir. “They said: ‘I was reading it, and a lot of those things don’t seem to be accurate.’ That’s how I found out about it.”

Dr Leslie McIntosh, a vice-president of research integrity and security at Digital Science, said someone might add a respected name to a scientific paper without permission to make the work appear more credible. Fraudsters also sometimes added respected researchers as editors to make bogus journals appear legitimate and attract publication fees.

Even more nightmarish would be someone deliberately publishing misleading information under someone else’s name to damage their reputation. “If their name ended up on a retracted paper, they would then have to explain that retraction,” she said.

Employers are encountering yet another form of impersonation. Jamie Collier, a researcher at Google Threat Intelligence, said criminals had used stolen personal information to secure remote jobs under other people’s names, sometimes without the victim’s knowledge.

Generative AI is making such deception easier, “mainly by stripping away the usual tell-tale red flags that hiring managers relied on to spot fraud,” Collier said. Large language models can generate convincing CVs, tailored cover letters and fabricated evidence of professional experience.

“Real-time video filters and voice-cloning tools are the next step. While live deepfakes are still relatively nascent … threat actors are already testing them to bypass quick video screenings and mask regional accents,” Collier said.

The Society of Authors and the Writers’ Guild of Great Britain have warned of increasingly sophisticated scams involving people impersonating literary agents and publishers, in an attempt to get writers to part with money or sign away their rights.

The Society of Authors’ chief executive, Anna Ganley, said she personally received between five and 10 scam emails a day, supposedly from book festivals, literary agents, publishers and others. Some writers had lost thousands of pounds after responding to genuine-sounding offers. “It’s incredibly difficult for writers, because you are often looking for opportunities to market your books,” she said.

Unlike those scams, Fake Linda’s activities seem like a lot of work for relatively small financial gain. But the latest technology could make such impersonations easier. Miller said: “AI is allowing criminals to create sophisticated impersonations at unprecedented speed and scale.”

Or multiple impersonations. I’ve since identified a third science journalist, Sara Novak, with a potential link to Fake Linda and Fake Caroline. Fake Sara apparently pitched a story to Chemical and Engineering News in August, which was declined. When Real Sara shared her impersonator’s email address with me, I discovered it links to the same masked recovery address.

The consequences extend beyond those being impersonated. “The risk for journals and publishers is huge,” said Dr Ben Johnson, the chief editor at Nature Health, who turned down a pitch by Fake Linda. “People trust the Nature brand as a source of evidence-based quality information. If an AI-generated story from a fake journalist is submitted then I will likely spend hours editing it from AI slop into Nature prose, including all the fake quotes from people never interviewed.”

All of this raises uncomfortable questions about how you can be sure you know who you’re dealing with when communicating online. When I emailed the New York Post about my impersonator, it agreed to help rectify the situation, then asked: “I see that you’re emailing me from a Guardian email address. Is there any other info you can provide to verify who you are?”

After discovering that Science had inadvertently published a news story by Fake Caroline, its managing news editor, John Travis, said his team had started running all pitches and drafts through AI detectors, “though they are not perfect”. “We also require Zoom calls for any new writers,” he said.

The experience has also put editors at Nature on higher alert. “Sadly, for early career freelancers, this makes me less likely to commission news stories from journalists that I haven’t worked with before,” Johnson said. “I will also have to try to find the time to have a call with new freelancers before they write, to check they are who they say they are.”

Even video calls are no guarantee of identity. Google Threat Intelligence recently documented North Korea-linked hackers using real-time deepfakes to lure executives into Zoom calls with trusted peers. “They faked video and audio glitches to get the target to download a ‘troubleshooting tool’ that wiped out their credentials and wallets,” Collier said.

Miller advises independently checking unexpected approaches through an established email address or telephone number. McIntosh advocates several layers of verification, like the multiple identity checks at airports. “You have to have multiple ways to ensure and triangulate that you’re speaking to the person you think you’re speaking to,” she said.

For people whose identities have been hijacked, Miller advises warning professional networks and monitoring for further impersonation attempts.

There may also be legal remedies. Rupert Earle, senior counsel at the London law firm Bates Wells, said that under UK law, impersonating someone to secure paid work could constitute fraud. Victims could also have civil claims for “passing off” – misleading people into believing that work or services come from an established person or business – or false attribution, if work they didn’t create was published under their name.

However, identifying the perpetrator and taking legal action can be difficult, particularly when the publications are overseas and the impersonator’s location is unknown. Despite uncovering several clues linking Fake Linda and Fake Caroline, we still don’t know who is behind the accounts.

But the hunt for Fake Linda continues. I’ll be reporting the incident to the UK’s Report Fraud service. I’ve also sent a cease-and-desist email to my impersonator, demanding they stop.

For such a prolific writer, they’ve gone surprisingly quiet.

All the president’s women: a familiar downward trajectory on Trump’s team

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 09:00:28 GMT

Half of the women on Trump’s team have been replaced by men, while men facing misconduct allegations remain

Donald Trump is not, by any measure, a feminist. He has said so himself. But the president has often pointed to his hiring and promoting of women in an attempt to stave off criticism of both his policies and personal conduct over the years.

During his second term, however, there is one common characteristic among most of those who have departed the Trump administration.

In the space of just a few months, half of his eight high-level female officials have either resigned or been fired. All have been replaced by men. Several other women in his administration have also departed, whether voluntarily or involuntarily.

On Friday, Trump was forced to deny reports that he was considering replacing Susie Wiles, his White House chief of staff, and the first woman to do the job. “She’s gonna be here for a long time,” he claimed.

Numerous top male officials, meanwhile, from Trump’s defense secretary Pete Hegseth, who has on multiple occasions courted global condemnation, to the widely ridiculed FBI director Kash Patel, have survived intense scrutiny and repeated calls for their resignation – and yet remain in post.

The latest female casualty was White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, who was fired on Friday just five days into the role. After a rocky start to her tenure, sparked by a widely panned first White House press briefing on Tuesday, she had also faced questions over her legal credentials after admitting she did not pass the bar exam. The ensuing semantics battle over whether or not she is a lawyer, or an attorney, placed her in a pickle – even with the rightwing cable network Fox News.

Zacharia had taken over from Karoline Leavitt, who said in August that she had chosen to resign from the role after 20 months so she could spend more time with her young family.

In terms of firings, the first domino to fall was former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem, who was the face of Trump’s mass deportation campaign until she was unceremoniously sacked on 5 March. Her tenure was plagued by controversy, in large part amid national uproar over federal immigration enforcement operations that killed two US citizens in Minneapolis (one of whom Noem called a “domestic terrorist”, with no evidence), and coincided with a sharp decline in national support for Trump’s immigration agenda.

Her suggestion at a congressional hearing in March that Trump had known about her decision to approve a contract for a $220m ad campaign to encourage immigrants to “self-deport” – which prominently featured Noem on horseback – reportedly left Trump “pissed” and appeared to be the straw that broke the camel’s back. There had also been scrutiny of general leadership failures under Noem, as well as questions the influence of her adviser, Corey Lewandowski, who also left his role when she was ousted.

Noem was repurposed as special envoy to the so-called “Shield of the Americas” coalition and, after that arrangement expired last month, is now serving in a vaguely defined advisory role. She was succeeded as DHS secretary by Markwayne Mullin.

Next fell former attorney general and Trump loyalist Pam Bondi, who was pushed out in April after a turbulent 14 months that saw the president increasingly frustrated over her mishandling of the Department of Justice’s long-awaited release of the Epstein files. The Epstein issue became a huge political liability for Trump and infuriated his Maga base, and he also felt that Bondi had failed to sufficiently prosecute his political enemies.

Bondi revealed a month after she was ousted that she had been diagnosed with thyroid cancer. Her deputy, Todd Blanche, assumed the role in August.

It’s worth noting that commerce secretary Howard Lutnick faced public scrutiny after details emerged surrounding his past ties to Jeffrey Epstein and visits to his private island emerged. By contrast, the White House supported him after Democrats called for his resignation.

Also in April, former labor secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer stepped down after a Department of Labor inspector general investigation led to a series of allegations of misconduct, including having an affair with a subordinate and drinking alcohol on the job. She was replaced by Keith Sonderling.

Kash Patel has also been alleged to have been intoxicated or absent on the job. He has denied these allegations, and remains FBI director.

A month later, in May, Tulsi Gabbard resigned from her position as Trump’s national intelligence director.

While she officially cited her husband’s rare cancer diagnosis, Gabbard was reportedly forced out after a tumultuous stint in which she was largely sidelined as Trump launched attacks on Venezuela and Iran. She had previously testified to Congress that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon.

Gabbard was replaced on an acting basis by Bill Pulte, a Trump loyalist with no previous experience in the intelligence sphere, and eventually by Jay Clayton.

Earlier this week, the Trump administration asked longtime Trump ally Kimberly Guilfoyle to step down from her position as US ambassador to Greece after weeks of reports that she sought payment from a Trump donor in exchange for access to administration officials.

The only senior male official to have been somewhat punished by Trump since his return to office is Mike Waltz. The then-national security adviser was fired in May last year after inadvertently adding a journalist to a Signal group chat in which Hegseth disclosed secret war plans.

Waltz had been on thin ice with Trump for a while, and the president was reportedly annoyed by Waltz’s hawkish stance on Iran. Signalgate merely sealed his fate.

But he didn’t disappear to some obscure advisory role; Waltz was nominated to the position of US ambassador to the United Nations. Hegseth, meanwhile, was allowed to ride out the controversy and – several controversies later, including allegations of war crimes – remains in post.

Democrats have highlighted the double standard that Trump only seems to fire women in his administration – even those who are ultra-loyal to him, and decidedly less incompetent than some of their male colleagues.

“If you’re a man in the Trump administration, it seems that they reward misconduct,” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the Democratic congresswoman, observed in April.

“I wouldn’t say I’m a feminist,” Trump said in a 2018 interview. “I mean, I think that would be, maybe, going too far. I’m for women. I’m for men. I’m for everyone.”

But not everyone gets to stick around.

The hill I will die on: Cinemas have been getting away with lies. Films should begin on time

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 09:00:27 GMT

If cinemas must run 20 minutes of adverts before a feature, they could at least be honest about it. Or, I have a better solution …

Do you remember the last time you were lied to? I certainly do. I was tricked by the North Finchley Vue, which sold me and my boyfriend tickets to a 7.15pm showing of The Odyssey. Guess what was playing at 7.15pm? A car advert. Ten minutes later, it was a trailer for the horror film Werwulf. Then there was an advert for Vue – as if I wasn’t already there. The film was half an hour late to its own showing when it finally started at 7.45pm.

I am sick and tired of cinemas getting away with such treachery. I don’t want to follow in the footsteps of my friend, who knows that the ads at her local run for 22 minutes so slinks in at just the right time. I shouldn’t have to do mental maths because I am being lied to by cinemas. We are all the victims of their predatory time-wasting system.

If you went to see a play and the ticket said the show started at 7.30pm, you’d rightly be annoyed if after 20 minutes the performance still hadn’t started. Yet when it comes to watching movies, we’ve collectively accepted that it’s fine for them to start later than advertised. Which also means we all put up with people coming in late, shining their phone torches and bumping into you because they tried to show up when the film actually starts.

Now that almost a third of wide releases run over two hours and pre-show advertising and trailers last for 20-30 minutes, something’s gotta give. I say films should start on time. I know a better moviegoing experience is possible. I grew up in Canada, where our cinemas played their films at the ticketed time and the ads started earlier. When my family showed up 10 minutes late to The Fellowship of the Ring, we missed the entire opening sequence explaining the history of the rings of power. We deserved that!

A brave senator in Connecticut tried to tackle this injustice in 2025 with a bill that would “require the disclosure of accurate movie start times in advertisements and listings”. However, it was watered down to a mere “working group” after pushback from cinema operators. They warned they’d lose vital revenue if advertisers pulled back because people started skipping the pre-show entirely. Erin Brockovich wouldn’t have given in so easily.

How can we succeed where the Connecticut senator failed? Simple: we also get rid of assigned seating. Say goodbye to paying £26 for an Ultra Lux recliner if you want the best view. It’s a flat fee no matter where you sit. Welcome to the Hunger Games of cinema seating.

If you want a “good” seat for a film, you have to earn it by showing up early. Exactly like when I was young, the ads and trailers will play before the start time so the film can begin promptly. Arrive on time, after the trailers, and you might be stuck in the front row, but that’s on you for avoiding the ads.

I’m just a cinephile, standing in front of a movie theatre, asking it to respect me and my time. Why is that so hard?

Jeffrey Ingold is a freelance journalist covering LGBTQ+ issues, music and culture
