French schoolchildren have been treated like enemies to be crushed – for telling the truth

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 04:00:20 GMT

To protest against shameful conditions in schools is entirely legitimate. The government’s response is not

As a secondary school pupil in 1994, I took part in protests against a reform that would have allowed French employers to pay young people below the minimum wage. Our campaign was successful, but if we had had to face the terrifying police response unleashed on student protesters in France over recent weeks, I would have stayed at home.

A 14-year-old boy, Eden, suffered a fractured jaw and had teeth knocked out after a police teargas grenade struck him in the face. Sixteen-year-old Maël lost the sight in one eye allegedly after being struck by a shot from an LBD, a form of rubber-bullet launcher. Evan, 15, had his hand blown off in an explosion involving a police stun grenade. And in Dunkirk, a police SUV is alleged to have driven repeatedly at groups of secondary school pupils, as an officer could be heard saying: “Come closer, we’ll smash their fucking faces in.” Accounts from children left terrified by brutal treatment in police custody describe traumatic experiences with severe psychological and physical consequences.

France, the self-styled home of human rights, is now attracting the kind of international legal scrutiny you would expect if this were an authoritarian regime gone mad. The human rights organisation Ligue des droits de l’Homme has condemned the alarming “brutalisation of young people”, and the threat to their freedom of expression.

A UN special rapporteur has called on the French authorities to respect the physical safety of protesters. The UN human rights office says it is following incidents surrounding the protests in France “with concern”. Amnesty International has called for the suspension of rubber-bullet launchers at school protests, condemned the disproportionate use of force and reminded the authorities of their duty to protect children. The Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, whose activism increasingly encompasses struggles against oppression and state violence, travelled to France this week to support school pupils.

It is often argued that France is broke, and that crippling debt levels make the student demand for €10bn of investment to improve their learning conditions a non-starter. But even in our difficult fiscal position, public spending is a political choice: to reduce debt you can cut public spending or you can raise revenue.

Economists Élise Huillery and Romane Paris have come up with a credible proposal for investing an additional €11.8bn a year in education, funded through tax reform targeting large inheritances, raising €12.7bn in 2026 and increasing taxes only for the wealthiest 1% of heirs. This would make money available to raise teachers’ pay, improve support for pupils, student grants and housing, and expand university places.

But the debate about public spending does not invalidate the legitimate grievances of pupils, teachers and parents, which are not new. Nor does it justify a vicious law and order response. Learning conditions in some of the most disadvantaged schools have been deteriorating to shockingly poor levels for a long time. I highlighted school conditions in France in the Guardian three years ago, arguing then that the state education system was among the most unequal in the developed world. The lack of resources assigned to such basic things as teaching vacancies has been glaringly apparent for years, with jobs in some districts sometimes left unfilled for months.

More than 20m teaching hours were lost in state secondary schools in 2024-25, equivalent to almost one in 10 lessons. More than 15m of those hours were lost because no replacement teachers were provided. Schools in designated priority education areas, which serve disadvantaged communities, have been particularly affected, according to France’s National Audit Office.

In Seine-Saint-Denis, the poorest part of mainland France, two-thirds of school doctor posts were vacant in 2023. As early as 2022, the Créteil education authority reported a shortfall of 60 school nurses and 20 social workers, with 90% of the unfilled posts in Seine-Saint-Denis. In 2025, 49 suicides were recorded among staff in the national education system. While these deaths cannot all be attributed to work, it is hard to avoid thinking of the severe deterioration in working conditions across the sector.

Then there are the schools that are physically falling apart: water that is unsafe to drink because of bacterial contamination, pupils reporting rats and cockroaches, filthy toilets, and in one case, a septic tank that overflows when it rains. There are power cuts, missing furniture and some classrooms are so poorly insulated that temperatures fall below 14C in winter and hit 40C during heatwaves.

In Mayotte, where protests began, a secondary school built for 900 pupils is accommodating 2,300. The protests then spread to mainland France through a school in Créteil that began the academic year short of 13 teachers and other staff, as well as a deputy headteacher.

Another issue at the core of pupils’ anger is Parcoursup, the system through which school leavers apply for higher education. Seen as discriminatory, it has left 126,000 applicants – many from disadvantaged backgrounds – without a place this year.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

Rather than deal with this crisis as justified social protest based on legitimate demands, the government has invoked a doctrine set out in its Operational Guide to Urban Violence. It has treated school pupils as internal enemies to be neutralised. This sets up a coercive response, disregarding the possibility of resolving the conflict through constructive measures.

By 8 October, 6,877 people had been taken into police custody, about 80% of them children. On 1 October alone, police made 1,949 arrests, exceeding the highest single-day total recorded since 1961, says the historian Éric Anceau. According to the Syndicat de la magistrature, a French judges’ leftwing union, the numbers reflect a clear determination to crush the movement. So overwhelming has the police deployment been that teachers and parents have had to form human chains to protect children.

The police operations are also driven by a focus on arrests, which encourages forceful confrontations and fuels the escalation. This in turn draws more people into rioting. About 700 police officers and a number of teachers have been injured since the start of the unrest.

The sociologist Olivier Fillieule points out that policing protests requires an assessment of risk. If the swift break-up a blockade exposes teenagers to serious injury, you have to consider alternatives. Temporarily accepting a degree of disorder when immediate intervention risks creating more of it should remain a guiding principle of policing protests, Filleule says, noting that the French authorities know how to apply restraint when farmers stage blockades.

Yet while the police have opened internal investigations into 36 allegations of officer violence, the interior minister Laurent Nuñez said he had given the forces “no instructions to exercise restraint”. This is a shameful and contemptuous way to respond to young people’s healthy expression of dissent. Such violence towards citizens has no place in a democracy.

Rokhaya Diallo is a French journalist, film-maker, activist and Guardian Europe columnist

Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 04:00:20 GMT

Whether it was youngsters proving their skills or state sabotage, Europe’s most hacked country was left with a mountain of waste after food began cooking in freezers

Shortly before midnight last Sunday, the digital thermostats controlling hundreds of supermarket cold aisles across France began to flicker and rise.

In a “bizarre and unprecedented” cyber-attack, hackers had remotely overridden the temperature settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F).

Over the next four to six hours, the food inside first defrosted, then slowly began to cook.

Shop staff arriving early to restock shelves reported catching a blast of hot air, like opening an oven, when they went to fill freezers. One Normandy supermarket reported a number of its freezers had been pushed to 80C (176F). In certain stores, the extreme temperature rise had sparked fires triggering sprinklers and water damage.

“It was a catastrophe,” said one worker at the large Intermarché supermarket in the south-west suburb of Issy-les-Moulineaux in Paris. “They pushed the freezers here up to 62C. Everything had to be thrown away. It was such a waste.”

After removing tons of spoiled food, staff at the store worked until almost midnight on Monday to reorder and restock shelves. “Thankfully, we were able to get things almost back to normal the same day,” another shop worker added. “But we had to clear out everything in the freezers.”

If shop managers first assumed it was an isolated failure, it soon became clear up to 700 stores – including those from the Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains along with a number of smaller independent shops – had been victims of a cyber-attack.

Dominique Schelcher, the president of Coopérative U, said 80 of its 2,000 supermarkets had been targeted. “This is a completely unprecedented, unexpected, and extremely serious attack. In my entire professional career, I’ve never seen anything like it,” the shocked executive told French radio.

The Paris public prosecutor’s office immediately opened an investigation into the latest in a series of cyber-attacks that have made France the most hacked country in Europe.

Gérôme Billois, a partner in the cybersecurity and technology company Wavestone, said the hack had the hallmarks of political sabotage.

“The two most feasible scenarios are either it was a group of youngsters or activists who wanted to blow up a few freezers to prove what they could do, or it was a destabilising attack, what we call sabotage, by internal or external state actors,” he said.

“As for the attack’s signature, the most likely scenario is still a destabilisation attack – one designed to convey the message to populations that they are not safe, to convey the impression that the government is falling apart, and ultimately to instil fear.

“Currently there are two international actors known for doing this sort of thing: Iran and Russia.”

The hackers had pirated the controllers supplied by the Danish company Danfoss that controls the freezers and fridges. Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. Initial investigations suggest the hackers disabled alarm systems before tampering with the thermostats, or extended the defrost programme by several hours to avoid triggering alarms.

Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” that customers install updates or replace obsolete unsupported systems. The affected refrigeration units were “running outdated firmware”, it said. In the days following the first wave of attacks, France’s cyber-attack alert centre ANSSI confirmed supermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted.

Marta Rybczyńska, a cybersecurity specialist and researcher, said she had found previous security warnings about old supermarket freezers running out-of-date software and newer models not having firmware updated.

“Some of these freezers hadn’t been supported by the manufacturers for several years and there were notices saying they should be replaced. Other freezers were newer but the software hadn’t been updated,” Rybczyńska said.

“The hackers found these weaknesses and used them.”

She added: “Many of the freezers appear to have been running with a default password. The hackers were able to modify or turn off the alerts so the shops only realised when the first person arrived in the morning and saw the damage that had been done.”

The most recent French cyber-attack mirrors a similar incident in the US in August when connected fridges and freezers at a dozen military commissaries – on-base food stores – went into unscheduled defrost cycles overnight causing massive food loss.

France is the most heavily pirated country in Europe by the volume of records exposed by hackers, according to the cybersecurity and risk management company Upguard.

In the last three years, hackers have breached France’s health system, France Travail, the government-run jobseekers agency, the National Agency for Identity Documents (ANTS) and most of the big mobile phone companies. This summer, the economy and finance ministry lost the personal and fiscal records of 678,000 taxpayers to a series of cyber-attacks.

Billois says France has fallen behind in addressing cybersecurity and has still not adopted the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act (2024) that introduced mandatory security for internet-connected devices.

“It’s a text that’s not political and that everyone agrees on but is delayed because there’s always more urgent legislation or there are quibbles about amendments, and this has been a disaster,” he said.

In the UK, the cyber security and resilience (network and information systems) bill to tackle cyber threats, is wending a similarly tortuous way through parliament. However, it fails to directly cover the food industry.

Supermarket boss Schelcher was quick to shift the blame for the attack on to unnamed refrigeration contractors who maintain the cold aisle equipment. “Our supermarkets are not customers of Danfoss,” he told RTL radio.

As yet, no individual or group has claimed responsibility for the supermarket cyber-attack; Paris prosecutors have instructed detectives from its anti-cybercrime unit but Billois says finding the hackers will take time.

“It’s possible they’ll be identified eventually, but it could take weeks if not months to be certain because hackers know how to hide their tracks,” Billois said.

Rybczyńska added: “Whether it’s possible to trace the hackers depends on their level of capability; if it’s a handful of youngsters, it’s easier because they probably won’t have thought to remove traces. If they are professionals it’s more complicated and will take longer. If they’re in a foreign country, it’ll be extremely difficult.”

The total cost of the cyber-attack has yet to be calculated but Thierry Cotillard, the CEO of Intermarché, said losses could run to “tens of millions of euros”, which store companies say is unlikely to be covered by their insurance.

“It’s a bizarre story,” Billois added. “There’s a shared responsibility between the supermarkets, the refrigeration companies who are sub-contractors and who maintain the material, and the software company. We cannot say who is to blame except, of course, the hackers.

“But in the end it comes down to freezers connected to the internet without being adequately secured. And that must be a wake-up call to everyone.”

Women just want to work out in peace. Why all the thigh-rubbing lechery?

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 04:00:20 GMT

On Saturday Night Live last week, comedian Shane Gillis made a pathetic ‘joke’ about the clothes women wear to the gym. It was puerile – but also pernicious

I’ve spent the morning doing Shane Gillis’s work: checking out women in the gym. If you’ve avoided Gillis thus far, apologies for enlightening you – he’s a “comedian” who recently told a “joke” on Saturday Night Live that began: “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dressed like whores now.”

Well, reporting for duty from the weight room, here’s the clothing tally: eight women in leggings and T-shirts; six in T-shirts and trackie bottoms; five in shorts and vest tops; one in a crop top and leggings. It’s not exactly the Folies Bergère – there’s not much, I would have thought, to cause Gillis to blush. But maybe I’m wrong – how undressed, exactly, constitutes whorish? Is a glimpse of a female forearm a distracting provocation? Should we pull up our socks to avoid inflaming male passions with our slutty ankles when we’re doing step-ups?

There’s a long, grim history of women trying to do physical activity in appropriate clothes and not being allowed, or feeling able to. We might not be sweating in floor-length dresses and corsets like early Olympian women, but bros are still complaining about girls doing squats in shorts in their eyeline, staring, propositioning and commenting (the #gymcreep hashtag is a veritable rogues’ gallery of them). Even Gillis’s language isn’t, unfortunately, exceptional: after his monologue, fitness writer Mikala Jamison shared a message on her Substack from a man she considered a friend, saying a gym had “whores everywhere”.

Thigh-rubbing lechery around women’s workout gear, however jokey, is gross and infuriating, but it’s more pernicious than that. Women get alienated from sport and fitness when they’re not allowed to feel comfortable in their bodies and clothes: research by the England hockey player Tess Howard found that many girls were put off sport because of clothing requirements and concerns around sexualisation, while Women in Sport found more than 1 million girls in the UK “fall out of love” with sport in their teenage years. Women are less active than men, with 38% still not doing 150 minutes of exercise a week. When girls and women are deprived of, or never allowed to develop, a sense of ease and enjoyment around having a body in public, this is the result.

I say “enjoyment” specifically because that’s something I think gets left aside in making the inarguable, entirely correct, case that what women wear to work out for comfort, practicality or ease of movement, is nobody’s business but their own. But what about pleasure? Gyms are many things – a refuge, a third space, a repository of crimes against music – but they’re also a place to enjoy your body, including how it looks.

I know, because going to the gym made me feel good about (bits of) mine for the first time since puberty. I was the one in the crop top this morning, flaunting my stretchmarks, hernia and distended belly button, yes, but also the results of two years’ hard work. I’m proud I can lift a wardrobe now, but I’m also proud to look a bit pumped. It gives me confidence: enough to walk into strange weight rooms full of men wherever I happen to be and do my thing. Those experiences in turn have shown me that most gym-goers of both sexes aren’t remotely interested in what anyone else is doing, or wearing – they’re working on (maybe admiring!) themselves.

But I’m 51, and my experience of the gym isn’t the same as it is for younger women. Sport England research published this summer found 19% of women aged 16-34 felt uncomfortable or unsafe in fitness centres because of the possibility of harassment or intimidation; 86% reported experiencing physical, verbal, non-verbal or online harassment or intimidation in a fitness or leisure centre in the last three years. This kind of comment feeds the fear, and emboldens aggressors, making it not just unfunny, but depressing and enraging. Everyone should be able to enjoy moving their body unmolested, that’s a given. But dammit, we should also get to enjoy wearing short shorts, second-skin leggings and spaghetti-strap tops. To look safely and happily in a gym mirror and find ourselves, yeah, a bit fit.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

Five Great Reads: cocaine nation, a 28-year walk home, and Americans give their verdict on Trump

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 22:03:56 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Miles Herbert

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and happy weekend to you all.

We have reads for you today from all over the world. So sit back, ease into the weekend and be transported by mysteries in Cuba, mountains in Colombia and midterms in the US – just to name a few.

Enjoy.

Cocaine seizures in Europe have increased more than fivefold in the past 10 years. A host of drug cartels have taken root as the continent’s “insatiable appetite” for cocaine grows. One man, Jos Leijdekkers, has successfully turned Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco state, according to intelligence sources. A Guardian investigation, which drew on dozens of interviews with intelligence and police officers across two continents, has revealed the murderous cost of the drug trade.

‘It is state capture by a criminal network on a scale never seen’: Leijdekkers is Europe’s pre-eminent cocaine baron. The Dutchman is credited with importing volumes “vast enough to repeatedly crash Europe’s cocaine market”. He is also comfortable with deadly violence. It is reported that high-ranking police officers are among at least 14 people killed in Sierra Leone on Leijdekkers’ orders. The cocaine kingpin is also the son-in-law of Julius Maada Bio – the president of Sierra Leone. Sources say Leijdekkers’ empire was at one time generating a $150m (£113m) monthly profit – greater than the cost of running the entire country. In 2025, the Netherlands sent a request to extradite Leijdekkers – one of Europe’s most wanted men. But Sierra Leone denied even knowing who he was.

Notable quote: “We’ve had cocaine disputes before, but nothing like this. We’ve entered a new era.” – European police source

How long will it take to read: just over nine minutes.

Further reading: As drug cartels take root in Europe, what is state capture and why does it matter?

Come 3 November, millions of Americans will head to the polls and cast their vote in the midterm elections. The stakes are high, with the results predicted to have a huge impact on Donald Trump’s last two years in office. Voters are set to decide whether they trust the president’s Maga allies to keep control of Congress, or return Democrats to the majority. With the cost-of-living continuing to hurt households, and the US-Israel war on Iran unpopular with many across the political spectrum, Democrats have a shot at taking back control of the House of Representatives and the Senate – potentially giving them the power to block Trump’s authoritarian agenda. What really matters to Americans? When the Guardian asked readers what issue mattered most to them and if they were optimistic about the future of America, common themes emerged. Most voters were concerned about the state of the economy. Justin Daniels from Michigan said: “I don’t understand why so many CEOs are saying companies are making record profits while people have to have two and three jobs.” Morgan from California saw a discrepancy between ordinary citizens and Donald Trump: “He is benefiting from his office, increasing his income [by] billions of dollars, while Americans are suffering with high gas prices and food prices and so forth.” Another theme was the Trump administration’s assault on migrants. Scott from Georgia told the Guardian: “I feel like [ICE] right now is having the largest, most powerful negative impact on people in this country. And it’s very blatant, and I feel like stopping that would be a good touchstone for how we all move forward.” How long will it take to read: less than six minutes. Giving US readers plenty of time to register to vote. Further reading: Everything you need to know about the US midterms in one place.

How far would you be willing to walk home? More than a kilometre and I am probably calling a cab. But Karl Bushby has walked more than 36,000 miles (58,000km) since he left his home in Hull back in 1998. After bush-bashing through deserts, surviving kidnappers and being held at gunpoint, Bushby says “some things are worth dying for”. But why walk? What is Bushby running from?

An overwhelming sense of his own mortality: A keen distance runner, Bushby would suffer from anxiety attacks if he went a day without running. Poor mental health pushed him to finally lace up his hiking boots and walk across the world. But his biggest driver was death. “I took death seriously. You’re dying, you’ve got one life, and what are you going to do with it? That really resonated with me,” Bushby said.

Notable quote: “I always say 99.999% of the people I met represented the very best of humanity. Every country has been the same.”

How long will it take to read: 11 minutes. But don’t worry, Bushby’s trek may be coming to a screen near you. German film-maker Werner Herzog is making a documentary about the journey.

Further reading: Are there places on Earth where humans haven’t been?

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

It’s a mystery that has haunted American intelligence services for the last decade. Dozens of CIA officers have been afflicted by the strange and debilitating symptoms often referred to as Havana Syndrome (official documents refer to it as anomalous health incidents). This read asks: is it just hysteria, or is there something more nefarious behind the unexplained phenomenon?

Is Russia behind Havana Syndrome? A new book by two CBS journalists asserts that Russia was behind at least some of the documented episodes of the strange illness. The theory posits Russian intelligence found a way to wound or intimidate covert US operatives using a previously unknown weapon that delivers sonic or pulsed microwave energy. The book also suggests that parts of the US government and intelligence community covered up the evidence. But others, like Douglas Fields, a cellular neuroscientist and author of several books about the brain, claim that theories of an energy weapon should be taken no more seriously than sightings of the Loch Ness monster.

How long will it take to read: a bit under 10 minutes.

Further reading: What the experts say about Havana Syndrome.

Sarah Collard, Indigenous affairs correspondent for Guardian Australia, spoke to four young men who have lodged civil proceedings alleging historical sexual abuse by staff and fellow detainees at youth detention centres in Canberra. They give eerily similar accounts, despite their experiences being separated by years and occurring at different centres. They allege they were not believed, were dismissed or had no way of disclosing their abuse at the time.

Notable quote: “It seemed to be a bit of a protect-the-perpetrators club there … The few that did [speak up] were shunned out.” – Kirsten Nasser, from the legal firm Maliganis Edwards Johnson, a solicitor specialising in cases alleging institutional abuse.

How long will it take to read: just over five minutes.

Further reading: Sarah Collard talks to the First Nations children’s commissioner.

The Guardian view on the banks: too big to fail cannot mean too big to tax

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 16:52:37 GMT

Financiers owe their windfalls and bonuses to higher interest rates. Britain should reclaim more for the public and resist City lobbying

John Healey is planning to tax British banks, the Guardian revealed, in the forthcoming budget. It’s about time for the chancellor to act. Banks have been raking it in. The campaign group Positive Money reported this summer that Britain’s four biggest banks made £29bn in the first half of this year, up a fifth on 2025. These windfalls owe more to higher interest rates than better products or services. Households and businesses pay more to borrow. Meanwhile, the Bank of England pays the banks tens of billions in interest on their reserves, with the Treasury footing the bill.

The chancellor is said to favour restoring the bank surcharge from 3% to 8%, which could raise around £2bn a year. This would recover a very modest share of the sector’s bonanza. Louis XIV’s finance minister, Jean-Baptiste Colbert, said that “the art of taxation consists in so plucking the goose as to obtain the largest possible amount of feathers with the smallest possible amount of hissing”. Britain’s banks have plenty of feathers. That hasn’t stopped them hissing. The banks say that they already face higher taxes than other companies, that they won’t be able to lend as much, and that their profits won’t last.

But banks aren’t taxed on their windfall gains, and what levies they face are less than those paid by oil and gas companies. The Bank of England said banks spent £7.7bn on dividends and buying back shares in the first quarter of 2026 without affecting lending. Higher taxes might mean trimming shareholder payouts. There’s nothing to suggest productive lending must take the hit. Over the past five years Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds and NatWest – which control the majority of UK personal and business accounts – made profits of £200bn. Positive Money says that households lost out on £44bn in deposit interest in 2025. Some of this paid for banking services. But that does not explain why the sum is five times the equivalent average figure for 2009-21.

The chancellor could be more radical. The precedent here is not a socialist one. Margaret Thatcher taxed banks’ windfalls in 1981. A comparable 2.5% levy on today’s interest-free deposits would, a paper by the New Economics Foundation and Positive Money suggests, raise more than £11bn. In August, Positive Money suggested looking at Spain’s success in levying a windfall tax on banks’ net income above €800m. It says that such a windfall tax – levied at the same rate as that paid by fossil fuel companies on a comparable tax base – would bring in £19bn from the UK arms of the big four banks. That would pay for a universal and comprehensive adult social care system.

Banks need to be both public utilities and good corporate citizens. Yet the sector is paying the highest bankers’ bonuses since the 2008 global financial crisis. “Most financial sector activity,” concluded a paper published in The Manchester School journal this month, “is simply negative for overall economic performance.” Politicians should stop mistaking finance lobbyists’ demands for a growth strategy. Their job is to curb a finance sector so large that it risks crises and weaker growth. Taxpayers rescued the banks after they helped crash the economy 18 years ago. Public protection carries public obligations. As Sir Philip Augar, the author and former banker, told the BBC: “Banks can’t be too big to fail and too big to tax.”

The Guardian view on Winnie-the-Pooh: now we are 100

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 16:52:01 GMT

He may have been eclipsed by the more progressive Paddington of late, but AA Milne’s creation is not just a Silly Old Bear

“Pooh, promise you won’t forget about me, ever. Not even when I’m a hundred,” Christopher Robin implores his bear in the final chapter of AA Milne’s The House at Pooh Corner. This week Winnie-the-Pooh himself turned 100, and he certainly hasn’t been forgotten. Birthday celebrations have included a week of special programmes, introduced by the queen, on Radio 4; a collection of Royal Mail stamps; and a Google doodle.

Not bad for “a bear of very little brain” who appeared in four slim books. Winnie-the-Pooh, illustrated by EH Shepard, was published on 14 October 1926 and had sold 150,000 copies in the US by the end of the year.

Despite his success, the honey-loving bear was resented by both Milne and his son Christopher Robin Milne, the first for eclipsing his work as a playwright and comic writer, the latter for stealing his childhood. And he was too sugary for some. “It is that word ‘hummy,’” Dorothy Parker wrote waspishly under her pseudonym Constant Reader, “that makes the first place … at which Tonstant Weader fwowed up”. PG Wodehouse and Evelyn Waugh were equally sniffy. But generations of children disagreed. Winnie-the-Pooh was voted No 7 in the BBC Big Read poll in 2003.

Pooh’s position as Britain’s favourite bear is under threat from a younger ursine model. Separated by 32 years and one day, Michael Bond’s A Bear Called Paddington was published on 13 October 1958. These two polite and accident-prone bears differ in more than a taste for honey or marmalade.

Both stories were created in the aftermath of war: Winnie-the-Pooh was Milne’s escape from the horrors of the Somme; Paddington was inspired by evacuees in the second world war. Pooh was based on a toy from Harrods, Paddington on a solitary teddy that Bond found in a toyshop on Christmas Eve. The Hundred Acre Wood is a sheltered rural idyll; Paddington arrives at a bustling postwar London station. Both are beloved at Buckingham Palace, but it was the bear from Peru who was invited to tea for the platinum jublee of Queen Elizabeth II.

Thanks to three hit films and now an award-winning musical, Paddington has shaken off his slightly fusty image to become an emblem of modern Britain. Where Paddington is progressive, Pooh seems stuck in a posher past.

Aside from being one of the world’s biggest merchandising franchises, Winnie-the-Pooh’s cultural afterlife has been bumpier. Screen adaptations have been mixed, from Disney’s 1966 animation, which EH Shepard declared “a complete travesty”, to the indie slasher horror Winnie the Pooh: Blood and Honey, made after Milne’s US copyright expired in 2022. Pooh has become an unlikely symbol of political dissent in China after President Xi was visually likened to him in 2013, with protesters in Hong Kong picking up the comparison in 2019.

According to a Canadian medical journal, each character represents a form of neurodivergence or mental health disorder: Tigger stands for ADHD, Piglet for anxiety, Eeyore for depression and so on. The article may not have been entirely serious, but the author Matt Haig has described Winnie-the-Pooh as “the ultimate self-help book”. Pooh is not just a “silly old bear”. In our speeded-up age, where children spend more time on screens than outdoors, Milne’s world of freedom and innocence remains deeply comforting, for “in that enchanted place on the top of the forest a little boy and his Bear will always be playing”.

The appeal of eating a loved one’s ashes

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 16:32:40 GMT

Readers respond to an article by Rachael Stirling

I would like to reassure Rachael Stirling (‘I didn’t expect to be portrayed as a cannibal’: Rachael Stirling on eating her mother Diana Rigg’s ashes, 11 October) that, far from grimacing or feeling disgust over her admission of eating a few grains of her mother’s ashes, I was deeply moved. My best friend’s beloved mother died last year and I immediately sent the quote to her, as I knew it would resonate with her.

As your review of Stirling’s book entitled All About My Mother states, she eats a grain of her mother’s ashes so that she is “cloaked in her, shielded and shrouded by her. I am her. My mother is my superpower. She always was.”

These words perfectly encapsulate how my friend feels about her own mother, and how so many of us feel about the person from whose body we came. Emily Hall Llanbadarn Fawr, Ceredigion

I was interested to read Rachael Stirling’s article as I have long been familiar with the practice of drinking the ashes of the deceased. Kenneth Good’s book Into the Heart: An Amazonian Love Story describes his anthropological study of the Yanomami people in the Amazon, where, after cremation, all the ashes are mixed into a drink made of sweet, ripe plantain and consumed – with an accompanying feast – by the close family, friends and others who wish to show their respect. I find that the practice has a certain appeal and can fully sympathise with Rachael’s use of her mother’s ashes. Pauline Lowe Bryn Y Maen, Colwyn Bay

I don’t expect to be the only one writing to reassure Rachael Stirling – I did it too! A tiny bit of my mum’s ashes in 1990, and of my partner’s in 2020. It’s a way of keeping them part of you. And I don’t see how it counts as cannibalism, which is defined as eating human flesh. Fiona Collins Corwen, Denbighshire

Kitchen utensils with family stories to tell

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 16:32:31 GMT

Guardian readers reflect and reminisce about the cooking equipment that has been significant in their families

Among the wedding presents from 1963 that I still use (Letters, 9 October) are Denby ovenware, a complete set of Prestige kitchen utensils, a Victorinox paring knife we bought with money given to us for bedsheets, and smoked-glass wine and sherry glasses from a friend of my parents. When a grandchild noticed that we had rather a lot of flower vases, we had to confess that when asked what we would like as a present, we were so embarrassed that we always said “a flower vase”, knowing that it could come in at any price. It was a vintage year, 1963. Prue Baker Brighton

I inherited my mother’s potato masher, bought just after the war. As a newly married housewife setting up home with everything in short supply and rationing continuing, she told me that she was delighted to see the masher for sale and bought two – one for her sister. It was flimsy – a thin circular metal holed base with three wires attached, which were twisted to form the stem, and a wooden handle painted blue. History and memories in a utensil. Sue Rawson Scarborough, North Yorkshire

For Christmas 1944, I gave my mother a breadboard fashioned from a slab of elm – probably an offcut from a coffin board. In spite of decades of mockery about its imperfection – I have to confess that it is a far-from-regular octagon – she used it for many years before passing it back to me. It is still in daily use. Martin Knight Hovingham, North Yorkshire

My elder daughter has insisted I leave her my bag of clothes pegs – they largely consist of very worn spring-loaded ones which belonged to my mother. I suspect that many of them date from late 1930s. Joy Stephenson High Peak, Derbyshire

Premier League action, Champions Day and Dubois v Wardley II – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 15:59:20 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

The Wallabies are chasing a first Bledisloe Cup win over the All Blacks in Sydney in more than half a decade, a galling 12-match losing streak against their trans-Tasman rivals highlighting the disparity between the sides. The Wallabies last beat their fierce rivals in 2020, ironically under the coaching of the now All Blacks mentor, Dave Rennie. Last Saturday’s 50-19 drubbing in Auckland illustrates the task facing Les Kiss’s chastened side. The Kangaroos’ thrilling Rugby League World Cup win over New Zealand on Thursday night might serve as inspiration, however. Follow the action with our live blog.

Tom Bassam rises early to set the tone for the day’s action and ease football followers into the weekend. Saturday brings five Premier League clashes: Everton v Chelsea, Fulham v Hull, Brentford v Liverpool, Manchester City v Ipswich and Newcastle v Aston Villa. There will also be updates and breaking news from across the Championship – where the day’s big game is Swansea v West Ham – the Scottish Premiership and European leagues, featuring Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Inter. Why not join the conversation by emailing your thoughts to matchday. live@theguardian. com?

Another stellar cast assembles for British Champions Day, with Gstaad front and centre in the Queen Elizabeth II Stakes. Having been second best to Bow Echo for so long, Gstaad flourished at the Curragh in the Irish Guineas and can shine again at Ascot. In the Champion Stakes, Calandagan seeks to defend his crown. No horse has been able to better Kalpana in the last two running of the Fillies and Mares Stakes and it is hard to envisage anything stopping her hat-trick bid. Australia made good use of the reversing ball in the fourth innings in Durban, with a similar wicket expected at St George’s Park for the second Test. ‘Tough to watch, impossible to ignore’: reviewers on NAZA documentary

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 15:42:46 GMT

Film interviewing military insiders about mass killing of civilians in Gaza wins widespread praise around the world

Critics around the world have hailed the award-winning documentary NAZA as a “brilliant and harrowing” film that is “impossible to ignore”.

NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, was released in UK cinemas this week and will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.

The investigative documentary, which contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders speaking anonymously on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night, has received widespread praise.

In a five-star review, the Financial Times’s Danny Leigh says that as a piece of cinema, “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. The Times calls the film “hugely provocative and a disturbing account” of Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, and the Irish Times brands NAZA an “essential record of engineered nightmare”. In a four-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw says the “anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus”.

British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film” that outlines the “restrained, meticulous, bone-chilling depiction of the progressive erasure of Gaza”. The magazine says the film “feels destined to become an enduring historical document, one which will and should be seen by generations to come”.

Time Out magazine says NAZA “puts together a restrained, intelligent, articulate, precise and utterly damning case against Israel’s actions in Gaza and their ongoing actions through the region. As a work of cinema, it is exemplary. As a work of journalism, it is inarguable. As a document, it is an indictment.”

The New York Times makes the film a “critic’s choice” and calls NAZA a “haunting” documentary that is “tough to watch, and impossible to ignore”. The Los Angeles Times says NAZA is a “stone-cold frightening” film that “burns the conscience”. And in New York magazine, it is described as “one of the most important films of our time”.

The Hollywood Reporter praises NAZA as a “sober and thoroughly documented bombshell of an exposé” that “leaves one with a deadening feeling, as if humanity may have lost all hope”. The Toronto Star says “NAZA is heartbreaking but essential viewing, questioning the systems that cause and quantify civilian death in modern warfare”.

The Spanish outlet El Mundo hailed NAZA as “the film of our time, a superb, electrifying, and devastating documentary about the systematic model of annihilation of the Palestinian people” that ultimately “points the finger at us. At night, in silence.”

The French newspaper Le Monde says the film “has the effect of an uppercut that leaves the viewer stunned”, while the Danish culture magazine Soundvenue calls NAZA a “soul-crushing testimony to the genocide in Gaza” that is an “example of how the world increasingly seems like a dystopia”.

The United Arab Emirates’ state-owned newspaper the National calls NAZA a “sickeningly tough film to watch”, and an editorial in the Israeli-outlet Haaretz says the film is “trying to force Israelis to confront what they already know: that Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza has left a black stain”.

When the film opened in Italy last month, it topped the charts. The Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera says NAZA lasts “only 80 minutes, but no more is needed: the ‘scientific’ coldness with which the interviewees reconstruct how they are destroying Gaza is something unforgettable”.

The film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.

Various organisations, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was received a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize.

Calling the shots: what NAZA says about perpetrator cinema

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 07:00:53 GMT

The documentary detailing Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza is the latest film to give a voice to those who carry out atrocities – confronting viewers with some of the most difficult questions of all

Are we still talking about the banality of evil? When that overworked phrase was first used by philosopher Hannah Arendt, it described the blank persona of Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann. Now, in NAZA, anonymised members of Israeli intelligence discuss their remote execution of the assault on Gaza. The comparison to Hitler’s Germany, while understandably controversial, is made by a subject themselves. If they are banal, it is a modern, oddly familiar kind. These are articulate, middle-class millennials. They say they are leftwing and non-racist. Put differently, they could be Guardian readers.

And yes, one remarks, they have been conducting a genocide.

The work of directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor is shattering. But we have been shattered before by the firsthand accounts of people who carry out atrocities – sometimes called perpetrator cinema. In 2013, director Joshua Oppenheimer released The Act of Killing, an astonishing film involving members of 1960s right-wing Indonesian death squads. It was lavishly acclaimed. Since then, it has only kept feeling painfully relevant.

Before that, documentary wild card Errol Morris made Standard Operating Procedure, interviewing US soldiers who abused Iraqis at the notorious Abu Ghraib jail. Edging into drama, you might even include Jonathan Glazer’s The Zone of Interest, where the commandant of Auschwitz lives happily with his wife and children. (Glazer is an executive producer of NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian.)

Questions gnaw through them all. To begin: who is it that commits crimes against humanity? The answer can feel inconclusive. NAZA is filled with Tel Aviv high-fliers, some citing as justification the horrific attacks of October 7. But the American troops of Standard Operating Procedure are ordinary grunts in the “war on terror”. Meanwhile, in The Act of Killing, ageing street thugs recreate their murders of trade unionists and teachers as the action movies they imagine them being. Flamboyance blooms in the abyss.

In every case, what we see won’t leave our heads, even as we flail for an adequate response. The late critic Roger Ebert famously called movies “empathy machines”. But these films short circuit the machinery. How can we empathise with people who seem to show no remorse?

For some, NAZA presents a bigger problem than that. The Israeli government has floated stripping Abraham and Szor of their citizenship, among other threats. But even for audiences far from the Middle East, the film is hard to deal with. We may feel anguished just as we are reminded how safe our anguish is. We might even think about that most unfriendly word: complicity.

But perpetrator cinema is about more than complicity. It is about the attempt to fathom the perpetrator. Discussing NAZA on the Jewish Currents podcast, Oppenheimer spoke to that task. “To understand a crime as a human activity, we have to look at the human beings who undertake that activity.”

Or do we understand mass murderers enough through what they do? In 2013, The Act of Killing also met pungent criticism. One influential figure in British documentary publicly called it a “snuff film”. (Oppenheimer next made The Look of Silence, about the victims.) And NAZA has faced pre-emptive criticism from Palestinians, including poet Mosab Abu Toha, arguing that the last three years in Gaza have already been documented by Gazans. “It’s all there,” he posted on social media. “So what will this film add?”

In this reading, NAZA is accused of privileging the perpetrator – giving literal voice to those for who the best platform, perhaps, would be a trial at the Hague. And yet another question is both obvious and uncomfortable. What’s in it for them anyway?

In this year’s documentary Killing Anna, former Syrian army officers were catfished into discussing civilian massacres by an academic posing as a loyalist of Bashar al-Assad. But most perpetrators are wholly aware they are being recorded. As such, we might expect a sobbing confessional. Not quite.

The torturers of Standard Operating Procedure came close now and then, but only amid a lot of evasion. As further ethical complication, they were also paid for their interviews. With The Act of Killing, though, Oppenheimer found a still more disturbing truth – his butchers were gleefully unrepentant. (They also believed that, as an American, he would approve of garrotting leftists.) And in NAZA, Yuval Abraham has said some of his interviewees spoke from “the opposite of shame”. That word complicity comes up again. Should a film-maker be doing this?

The thing is, though, lack of shame has a price. “War crimes are defined by the winners,” an Indonesian gangster says in The Act of Killing. “I’m a winner, so I can make my own definition.” In these films, that definition changes hands. Brilliantly, Oppenheimer did it by granting his subjects the freedom to reveal their nightmare psyches. In NAZA, journalism of the highest quality draws out a guilty plea with a seemingly howling lack of conscience.

Palestinian accounts of the assault on Gaza have been wrongly ignored. The response, to this Israeli version, of the Netanyahu government is telling. Aside from menacing the directors, a mimicking rebuttal, Naza: The Real Story was recently launched, desperately trying to reclaim control of the story.

And a director’s “complicity” is often indispensable. In 2017, the scalding Adriana’s Pact saw Chilean documentary maker Lissette Orozco interview her aunt, rumoured to have worked for the secret police of dictator Augusto Pinochet. When it turned out she had, the aunt’s berserk response to what she saw as a family betrayal was crucial to the story. Now the exposures of NAZA come from interviewees who would presumably never have talked to Abraham and Szor were they not Israeli too.

But more than that – the fact they are is also proof that Israelis can still say no to this Israel. Vital as they are elsewhere, the real power of these films is in the societies they portray. Official Indonesian history echoed the gangsters’ tales of bravely ridding the country of communists. Oppenheimer made the film available free there. Now NAZA confronts the belief that atrocities are only ever down to far-right “bad apples”. In perpetrator cinema, a common thread is directing us to unseen hierarchies – the politicians and generals whose lies to their own people are now laid bare.

Put like that, hope almost glimmers. Still. These films advise caution. Hollywood movies are delivery systems for catharsis. Here, it is elusive. Near the end of The Act of Killing, the most naggingly sympathetic of the subjects starts to retch, as if his body is trying to expel his own past. But nothing comes up. And now we watch NAZA, and know what has happened in Gaza still happens today.

No, what hope perpetrator cinema gives us is specific. Appearing with Oppenheimer on the Jewish Currents pod, Palestinian film-maker Rami Younis recalled meeting a giant of his country’s cinema, director Hany Abu-Assad, whose movies had been accused of humanising Israeli police. “What do you think happens when you keep demonising your enemy?” Abu-Assad said. “What happens to you?”

Usually “humanising” implies a soft focus. But NAZA and The Act of Killing remind us being human involves being capable of evil. They also offer the chance to fight back. The perpetrator of genocide refuses to see their enemy as like themselves – to truly look at them. With perpetrator cinema, though, we can look hard at people with whom we would like to share nothing – and say we are both human, however monstrous that also makes us.

NAZA is in cinemas worldwide and will screen on the Guardian’s website from late November

‘Can We Get That Back?’ After School Shooting, Bend Questions Its Identity.

The New York Times October 17, 2026

Oregon School Shooting

Advertisement

Supported by

Days after the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School, the community is questioning its resilience — and safety.

By Anna Griffin and Maia Spoto

Anna Griffin reported from Bend, Ore., and Maia Spoto from New York.

Residents of Bend, Ore., like to think of their community as a small town, though this high-desert city in the shadow of the Cascade Mountains is home to more than 107,000 people and among the fastest-growing places in the Pacific Northwest.

People move to neighborhoods like the one surrounding Silver Rail Elementary School because they’re escaping something: the grittiness of Portland, Ore.; the higher prices of California; the asphalt, anonymity and poor air of urban America.

“We like to think we’re different,” said Savannah Patton, a mother of two students at the school. “Now this.”

Investigators still have numerous questions about the school shooting in Bend on Thursday, during which a 16-year-old former special education student at Silver Rail shot through a side entrance and attacked a special education classroom, killing three children and a teacher.

The police have said he used a pump-action shotgun. The gun belonged to the shooter’s mother, according to a law enforcement official who was granted anonymity to discuss details of the case.

Authorities have not explained how the teenager gained access to the gun, what motivated the attack or whether his mother or anyone else might face criminal charges.

Answers may come faster than a sense of safety can return to Bend, a former paper mill town that has been transformed over the past two decades into a hub for outdoor sports.

The Silver Rail shooting is the second recent major act of gun violence here: Four years ago, a 20-year-old carrying an AR-15-style rifle and a shotgun killed two people at a grocery store a few miles from the site of Thursday’s shooting.

“My kids have been asking me, is Bend safe still?” said Jeff Eager, a former mayor of Bend. “I’m telling them, yes, it’s safe. These horrible things do happen. They happen here, and they happen elsewhere, but Bend is still comparatively, I think statistically speaking, a safe place to live.”

The school shooting broke the tranquillity in the southeast Bend neighborhood around Silver Rail, a collection of new apartments, town homes and Craftsman-inspired houses built along neat street grids around a park and the school, which opened 11 years ago. The community feels suburban, still affordable at a time when Bend housing prices are skyrocketing, and built to mimic the slower pace of small-town life in a city that has doubled in size since 2000.

“Everyone wants to be here — in some cases they’ve made sacrifices in their life to be here, so everyone is really eager to make friends and create their little villages and their friend families,” said Christy May, the parent of a kindergartner and a fourth-grader at Silver Rail who moved to Bend from Portland 11 years ago.

“I’m not going to say it’s paradise, but it’s pretty close,” she said.

Parents, she said, are almost too eager to help out with field trips and other volunteer activities. “We’ve had to literally draw names out of a hat before,” she said.

Now they’re lining up for other ways to help: Meghan Standish, a stay-at-home mom in the neighborhood, said that when she went online to sign up for a meal train to help the family of Rhoam Summer, a 5-year-old killed in the shooting, every night until Christmas was booked.

Beyond looking to help, she was debating other plans as well.

“I know a lot of friends are interested in getting their concealed carry permits after this,” Ms. Standish said. “I know I am.”

On Saturday morning, a group of dads, coffee cups in hand, straightened a roll of drawing paper left for mourners to write messages at a makeshift memorial by the school’s front entrance. A pack of teenage boys taped tissue boxes to street signs near the entrance of the school. Chickadees chirped in the park across the street and, behind the yellow police tape, children’s bicycles still crowded the school bike rack.

“It’s all so new and all so peaceful, or it was,” Ms. Patton said. “How do we get that back? Can we get that back?”

She and her husband moved to Bend from Vancouver, Wash., nine years ago because they had always loved visiting. They “just left everything,” she said, when the opportunity to relocate arose.

“I wanted to live here forever with our kids or at least raise them here,” she said. “I don’t know now.”

She was home Thursday when shotgun blasts and police sirens broke the calm. Like dozens of other parents, she ran the few blocks to the school, then spent hours waiting to find out whether her children, ages 6 and 9, were safe.

Along with the four people killed, another student and a teacher were injured in the shooting.

Police say the attack could have been far worse without the intervention of a teacher who threw her phone at the shooter and tackled him, and a father who, driving by on his lunch break, saw the attack begin, chased the shooter into the school and then shot him.

“Even the fact that you had so many people rush out there says something,” Ms. May said, noting that neighbors who didn’t have students at the school brought out coolers with drinks and snacks for parents waiting for news about their children. “The instinct here is to take care of each other.”

Neighbors say that sense of togetherness could be what gets them through the next few weeks.

Ms. Patton and friends closed off their cul-de-sac Friday night and gave the kids ice cream and glow sticks. Other neighbors held pizza parties and movie nights. At a memorial by the school’s front entrance, a middle school volleyball team announced a fund-raiser. Dozens of messages left in chalk and marker encouraged survivors to pray, heal, “hug each other” and remember: “This Neighborhood Is Love.”

Officials with the Bend-La Pine School District say students at other campuses will return to class Wednesday. Silver Rail will remain closed until further notice. Ms. May’s children have already begun asking her whether the parent-teacher conferences scheduled for later this month will take place and if they’ll still get to go to the school’s annual “trunk or treat” parking lot Halloween party.

“They have very harrowing stories about what they saw and heard, and they still want to go back,” she said. “So I want that for them.”

Grace Benninghoff contributed reporting.

Anna Griffin is the Pacific Northwest bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of Washington, Idaho, Alaska, Montana and Oregon.

Maia Spoto is a reporter covering disability issues for The Times and part of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Man Fatally Shot in Midtown Manhattan Subway Station

The New York Times October 17, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The shooting occurred on Saturday at the 7th Avenue Station on 53rd Street, near Times Square. The Police Department said there have been no arrests.

By Maia Coleman and Wesley Parnell

A man was shot and killed inside a subway station several blocks from Times Square in Midtown Manhattan on Saturday afternoon, according to the police.

The man, who has not been publicly identified by the authorities, was standing on a northbound platform in the 7th Avenue Station on 53rd Street, where the B, D and E trains run, not long after noon, the police said.

According to a law enforcement official with knowledge of the matter, the man then got into a dispute with another man on the platform. It was not immediately clear what had sparked their fight or whether the men had been physical with each other, but the argument soon escalated, moving from the platform, onto a train, and then back on the platform again, the police said.

At some point in the encounter, the second man then drew a gun and shot the first man once in the chest before fleeing the area and heading north on 7th Avenue, the police said.

Officers were alerted to the episode just before 12:30 p. m.

The injured man, who the police said was in his 30s, was taken by emergency medical workers to Bellevue Hospital in critical condition. He was later pronounced dead by hospital staff, according to the police. Officers have not made any arrests connected to the shooting, but on Saturday afternoon, the police said they were seeking a man wearing a red tracksuit, a black vest and a face mask.

The spasm of violence drew a swarm of patrol cars and ambulances to the heart of Manhattan on Saturday, according to videos posted on social media, interrupting a gloomy October day.

Francia Navela, who operates a Nuts 4 Nuts cart near the subway, said she heard a commotion down inside the station. Seconds later, a rush of riders, some of whom were shrieking, spilled onto the bustling street.

“People were coming out running, crying,” Ms. Navela said. “But after that I didn’t want to look anymore because it was too awful.”

Not long after, Ms. Navela said, paramedics arrived and wheeled a body away on a gurney. She watched first aid workers deliver lifesaving measures as they rushed the victim into the ambulance.

“They were trying to resuscitate him but they couldn’t,” she said. “You could tell he was in a bad state.”

Major crime in the city’s transit system has risen slightly so far this year compared to last year, though offenses on the subway have been trending down after a period of turmoil following the Covid pandemic.

As of Oct. 11, there have been 1,697 crimes in the transit system since the start of the year, 27 more than the same period in 2025, according to the Police Department. Felony assaults, including those against police officers and M. T. A. employees, and thefts have driven crime up, the police said. Officers have made 51 gun arrests in the system this year, the highest number since they began recording such data.

Still, this year remains the second safest in the transit system in 15 years, not including the pandemic years when ridership was especially low.

By 3 p. m. on Saturday, service on the C, D and E trains in Manhattan was disrupted in both directions, according to an alert issued by the M. T. A., scrambling weekend travel as officers responded to the shooting.

A handful of police officers kept watch outside the blocked-off station entrance. Tourists gawked as they walked by.

Annette Russo, 52, who is visiting New York with her family, said she was on her way to Famous Original Ray’s Pizza when she stumbled upon the crime scene.

“I came to get a slice of pizza and someone happened to just die on the subway,” Ms. Russo said. “Is that a New York moment?”

Chelsia Rose Marcius contributed reporting.

Maia Coleman is a reporter for The Times covering the New York Police Department and criminal justice in the New York area.

Unrest Mars Day of Protest in France, as Student Movement Turns National

The New York Times October 17, 2026

Student Protests in France

Riots broke out in several French cities alongside peaceful marches of tens of thousands of people demonstrating against rising living costs and poor school conditions.

Riots broke out in several French cities alongside peaceful marches of tens of thousands of people demonstrating against rising living costs and poor school conditions.

A tourist office in Lyon, France, that was set on fire during unrest on Saturday. Many rallies stayed peaceful as weeks of student-led protests evolved into a national display of discontent. Credit... Jeff Pachoud/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Supported by

By Catherine Porter

Reporting from Paris

Unrest flared across France on Saturday amid demonstrations against rising living and fuel costs that built on weeks of high school protests, heightening a sense of fiscal and social crisis in the country.

More than half a million people joined 110 marches throughout the country, according to the interior ministry, making it the biggest day of protest since unrest began to surge nationally roughly a month ago. One of France’s main unions, the C. G. T., estimated a higher number of 800,000 protesters.

The protests marked a convergence between a student-focused movement that has spurred demonstrations out of hundreds of schools, and a broader social movement that appeals to French citizens of different ages.

In many places, the protests were overtaken by violent confrontations between rioters and police officers, including in Marseille, France’s second-largest city, where people briefly broke into the city hall and knocked over a bust of Marianne, a symbol of the French Republic, before the police cleared them out. By nightfall, roughly 400 people, most of them adults, had been arrested across the country, according to the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez.

A tourism office in Lyon was also broken into and set on fire by rioters, many of them dressed in black clothes, masks and goggles. In Paris, where more than 100,000 people marched peacefully in the streets, a few hundred rioters also faced off against riot police, mostly in the Place de la République, a central square, according to the police. Cars were burned and storefronts smashed, the police said.

President Emmanuel Macron said the culprits would be “prosecuted and punished.”

In a post on social media, he added: “We will all stand united against the sowers of chaos, who seek only to bring down our institutions and prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing so.”

Since the student protests began last month, highlighting poor conditions in French schools, hundreds of people have been injured amid escalating clashes with riot police. Many of those injured have been young people, including a 15-year-old whose left hand was blown off by a stun grenade, and thousands have been arrested, most of them minors, law enforcement officials said.

On Saturday, that youth-led movement evolved into a wider display of anger at the government of President Emmanuel Macron, who leaves office next year after a decade in power that has come to be defined by political crisis and economic stagnation.

The protests came as the government tries to pass a belt-tightening budget and as France approaches presidential elections in 2027. The French government has acknowledged that some of the students’ demands are legitimate but has condemned “urban violence.” It has also accused a leading far-left party, France Unbowed, of stoking the demonstrations, a contention that the party has rejected.

On Saturday, as images of rioters surging into buildings and setting cars on fire played on loop on French news channels, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu condemned the violence, saying on X that it was sparked by “ultraleft groups” who “clearly want to use these acts of violence as a “warm-up” before the presidential election.”

He lauded the police, saying they had “faced violence of extreme intensity to protect our fellow citizens.” He added: “We will not be intimidated. No one will impose their political agenda through violence.”

The leader of France Unbowed, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, replied by posting photos of peaceful protests from around the country and blamed the government for giving orders to “relentlessly” direct tear gas at protesters in Paris. “The confrontation seems to be the goal of this ‘maintaining order’ strategy,” he wrote on social media.

The interior minister, Mr. Nuñez, said that by late afternoon the police were no longer confronting ultraleft groups. He said that they were instead facing off against “opportunistic delinquents” who were looting stores in many cities across the country.

In Paris, the looting and damage went on long after nightfall. Emmanuel Grégoire, the city’s mayor, said the cost of the damage, once it was finally tabulated, would be “immense” as “entire streets have been methodically ravaged” along with public squares and many monuments.

Throughout the day, the rioters targeted many symbols of the state.

In Bordeaux, the official residence of the prefect — the region’s top civil servant — was damaged. In Marseille, a municipal police station was damaged, along with the city hall. Rioters also set fire to the city hall in Limoges, a town in central France renowned for its porcelain, and attacked the city hall in the northern city of Lille, breaking its door and many windows.

“These acts are particularly shocking,” said Charlotte Brun, a vice-mayor of Lille, on French television. “It’s the common house of all the citizens. To attack public services while we are thousands in on the road, with message against the high cost of living — it conflicts with the main message of today.”

Still, many marches across the country ended peacefully.

“We sang, we saw people dance, funny signs, no rioters,” said Solène Millon, 35, a photographer chatting with friends at the end of the march in Paris. “The mood was great. What we see on TV, with people breaking things, is a minority.”

Estelle Grandidier, a nonprofit worker who joined the march to protest degrading public services in France, agreed. She called the movement a “convergence of struggles.” And she, like many in the country, wondered what would come next.

“There are no clear guidelines. Everyone comes with their own demands,” said Ms. Grandidier, 41. “So the question is, ‘What is the next step?’”

Ségolène Le Stradic contributed reporting.

Catherine Porter is an international reporter for The Times, covering France. She is based in Paris.

The New York Times October 17, 2026

Supported by

Senator Darline Graham, appointed to fill the Senate seat of her late brother, Lindsey, gently disagreed with the president’s decision to exempt Russia from the sanctions legislation.

By Michael Gold

Reporting from Washington

Senator Darline Graham, Republican of South Carolina, gingerly criticized President Trump on Saturday for exempting Russia from a sanctions law that was championed by and named after her late brother, Lindsey.

“Personally, I would choose to put the pressure on Russia to end the war and get gas prices down,” Ms. Graham told reporters at a campaign event. “Because I don’t trust Putin, and I don’t trust Russia.”

It was a small break from Mr. Trump, and one that may put Ms. Graham, who was appointed in July to replace her brother after his death, in an awkward position as she campaigns for a full term with the president’s backing.

Over her short time as a senator, Ms. Graham’s legislative record is understandably thin. But she has cited her role in the sanctions package, a major part of Mr. Graham’s legacy, as a top achievement.

“I was so proud to get the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act passed,” Ms. Graham said during a debate this week. “It gives the president tools he can use if he so chooses to end the war through economic sanctions. So that is up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else.”

Mr. Trump chose something else. By waiving the sanctions, he essentially handed President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia a financial lifeline that Mr. Graham had been eager to cut. The Trump administration has also pitched European officials on resuming purchases of Russian gas, another move that would boost Moscow’s standing.

Ms. Graham said that she would speak to Mr. Trump about the sanctions decision next week in South Carolina, where he is set to appear at a rally to help boost her campaign. She also acknowledged that her brother and Mr. Trump had not always seen eye to eye, including on foreign policy.

“Lindsey — he disagreed with the president sometimes. They had that relationship where they could agree to disagree sometimes,” Ms. Graham said.

Other Republican senators have blasted the decision more forcefully. Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina called Mr. Trump’s move “beyond irresponsible.”

“It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day,” Mr. Tillis wrote on Saturday on social media. Mr. Tillis announced last year that he would not run for re-election, and has since become increasingly critical of Mr. Trump.

Senator John Cornyn of Texas said in a social media post that “Lindsey would be appalled.”

Mr. Trump did not explain why he chose to waive the sanctions, a top priority for Mr. Graham before his sudden death. But he did so a week after his administration temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel, the price of which has skyrocketed and become a central issue in the midterm elections.

Democrats in South Carolina hope, despite tough odds, that anger over energy prices may help put Ms. Graham’s seat in deeply conservative South Carolina in play. Dr. Annie Andrews, the Democrat running against her, has accused Ms. Graham of being overly beholden to Mr. Trump and a rubber stamp on pieces of his agenda that have raised costs for voters.

In a video on Saturday endorsing Ms. Graham in the general election, Mr. Trump said that he had asked her to run, and acknowledged his close friendship with her brother.

“She's going to be an incredible, really an unbelievable senator,” Mr. Trump said. “And like her brother — it’s good genetics. Her brother was a great politician who really helped me a lot.”

The sanctions measure, signed into law in September, was aimed at Russia’s energy sector, a key source of revenue helping finance the country’s war on Ukraine. It targeted Russian oligarchs, officials and financial institutions, and extended sanctions against Iran for five years.

But under the law, the White House has broad authority to issue exemptions or waivers. The measure required Mr. Trump to notify Congress only if he opts against imposing the economic restrictions on Russia.

Mr. Graham, a Russia hawk, spent more than a year building support for the measure. He died just hours after returning to Washington from a trip to Ukraine, where he said he had reached an agreement on imposing sanctions targeting buyers of Russian oil.

Ms. Graham, who had never held elected office before being appointed to the Senate, has sought to distinguish herself from her brother by saying she would focus on domestic policy issues. During a primary debate, she acknowledged that she was “not that informed on national security.”

But at her debate against Dr. Andrews this week, Ms. Graham was asked about Mr. Trump’s foreign policy decisions in Iran and Russia and their connections to gas prices.

She pointed both times to the sanctions bill.

Michael Gold covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on immigration policy and congressional oversight.
