Trump Offers Putin Economic Relief in Hopes That Russia Will Return the Favor

The New York Times October 17, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

The Trump administration is ignoring the will of Congress and waiving new Russia sanctions amid fears that high energy prices will cost Republicans in next month’s elections.

By Alan Rappeport

Reporting from Washington

For years, critics of President Trump accused him of welcoming help from Russia to tilt elections in his favor. Now, with midterm elections in the United States two weeks away, Mr. Trump is explicitly seeking economic support from Russia.

A week ago, the Trump administration announced that it was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Late on Friday night, the White House released an executive order exempting Russia from a sanctions law that Congress passed last month. The moves were a last-ditch effort to lower the soaring gas prices in America that polls show are turning voters against Mr. Trump and Republican candidates.

Ukraine has frustrated Mr. Trump in recent months with its attacks on Russian oil refineries, which he blames for high global energy prices. Although the attacks have disrupted global energy supplies, oil prices have been climbing since the United States attacked Iran at the end of February, leading to violence across the Middle East and clogging the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz. Gas prices on Saturday averaged $4.31 a gallon in the United States, according to the AAA motor club, up nearly 45 percent since the start of the war.

The crumbling of years of work by the United States to put economic pressure on Russia to end its war in Ukraine raises questions about the Trump administration’s strategy to broker a peace deal. Mr. Trump’s executive order on Friday comes as the administration is pushing for Europe to resume buying more Russian gas, as part of the peace deal.

Mr. Trump’s waiver of the sanctions also casts doubt on why Congress passed legislation that was intended to punish Russia but made imposing the sanctions optional.

On Saturday, Mr. Trump’s decision was hailed by Russia and assailed by Ukraine.

“The suspension of some of the provisions of the Graham Act marks an important and truly historic moment,” said Kirill Dmitriev, who is Mr. Putin’s special envoy for investment and economic cooperation. “These provisions could have effectively brought all economic cooperation between Russia and the United States to a complete halt, inflicting serious damage primarily on the U. S. economy and global markets.”

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, who has maintained that Ukraine has a right to defend itself against Russia, condemned the sanctions relief for Russia and predicted that there would be more of that to come.

“I want to thank both Democrats and Republicans who supported his bill,” said Mr. Zelensky, who posted a photograph on social media of him with Senator Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican who died in July after working for more than a year to build support for the legislation. . “That was a major victory: this truly bipartisan support. And now, the decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me. And it definitely helps only the Russians.”

Skeptics of the law said that they were not surprised that Mr. Trump was ignoring the will of Congress. The sanctions in the law, which was named after Mr. Graham, were intended to target Russian officials, oligarchs and financial institutions. But the law also said that Mr. Trump could decline to impose the sanctions if he sent a letter to Congress explaining that they were not in the “national interest.”

The law also gave Mr. Trump new powers, which he has yet to deploy, to impose high tariffs on buyers of Russian energy products.

Some top Republican lawmakers who have recently run afoul of Mr. Trump criticized the president’s executive order on Saturday as letting President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia off the hook.

“Congress Must Investigate Trump’s Aid and Comfort to Putin,” Senator John Cornyn, a Texas Republican, wrote in a post on social media.

Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican, called the decision “beyond irresponsible.”

“It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day,” Mr. Tillis said in a social media post. “If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin.”

But it appears that Congress has little recourse. Even when Congress mandates sanctions, the executive branch has broad discretion on whether to deploy them based on what it believes is best for national security.

“Presidents have always sort of bridled at congressionally mandated measures,” said Adam M. Smith, a former senior adviser to the director of the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control in the Obama administration.

Mr. Smith said that he was surprised that Mr. Trump had opted against imposing any of the sanctions and noted that it gave the appearance that the president was turning away from Ukraine and toward Moscow.

“This plus the diesel deal will make some people concerned about where the president’s head is in this space,” Mr. Smith said.

Alex Zerden, the founder of the risk advisory firm Capitol Peak Strategies and a former official in the Treasury Department’s Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence, said that Mr. Trump appeared to be adhering to the sanctions law as it was written. He was perplexed by the political calculus of seeking economic assistance from Russia after Congress demonstrated bipartisan support for crippling Russia’s economy.

“The optics around this are confounding given the bipartisan and presidential support for the Lindsey Graham legislation,” Mr. Zerden said. “But the president maintains wide discretion with this Congress.”

During the Biden administration, the United States imposed more than a thousand sanctions on Russian targets and corralled allies to put a cap on the price of Russian oil. The Trump administration has been lenient in enforcing many of those sanctions and so far has only imposed new sanctions on Lukoil and Rosneft, Russia’s two largest oil companies.

The decision to offer Russia relief from sanctions because of fears about energy prices also represent an about-face for Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

At his confirmation hearing last year, Mr. Bessent said the Biden administration’s sanctions on Russia were not “fulsome” enough and described Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as one of the greatest tragedies of his adult life. He warned any Russian officials who were watching the Senate hearing that he would gladly ratchet up sanctions pressure to force Russia to the bargaining table.

“I believe that the previous administration was worried about raising U. S. energy prices during an election season,” Mr. Bessent said.

Alan Rappeport is an economic policy reporter for The Times, based in Washington. He covers the Treasury Department and writes about taxes, trade and fiscal matters.

The New York Times October 17, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

With midterm elections approaching, organizers of the demonstrations known for their anti-Trump sentiment are urging people to vote early.

By Corina Knoll

A fresh round of “No Kings” events took place across the nation on Saturday, drawing participants determined to show the collective power of free speech and demonstrate the tenets of a democracy.

In the past, those who showed up did so to protest myriad issues. Immigration raids, budget cuts, government layoffs — the list was long and varied. The central goal was to publicly and vehemently denounce the Trump administration.

But this time, the message was singular. Get out and vote. And do it early.

The national “No Kings” coalition had said the gatherings would be nonpartisan and focused solely on voter participation. But many participants ignored that directive as they expressed their frustrations with much of the second Trump administration’s agenda, echoing sentiments in earlier rounds of nationwide “No Kings” rallies.

Instead of mass mobilizations, multiple “hyperlocal” gatherings were encouraged. More than 2,500 U. S. events were planned, including a virtual option.

With the midterm elections approaching, organizers urged people to become proactive and cast their ballots at an early voting site or send in an absentee ballot.

“Voting early is how we use our power,” they declared on the website for the coalition, which includes about 200 organizations, including the American Civil Liberties Union and the League of Women Voters.

Here is how gatherings looked across the country.

At Piedmont Park, speakers made pleas for voter mobilization as well as declarations of how large numbers of voters could create change.

“In the spirit of these civil rights icons and the nameless foot soldiers, it’s our time,” said Gerald Griggs, a civil rights lawyer, nodding to Martin Luther King Jr., John Lewis and other leaders. “So go vote early, contact five of your friends, and tell them go vote early.”

The crowd reflected a particular anxiety specific to the area, with attendees recalling how President Trump tried to overturn his 2020 election loss in Georgia.

For Felicia Murray Jackson, who led participants in a march from the park to a church, the moment was personal. Her older sister was killed in February when a man fleeing immigration agents smashed into her car.

“I don’t want to hear you tell me how sorry you are for my loss — I want to hear you say, I took your loss straight to the ballot box,” she declared to the crowd. “We’re going to take human trafficking, child rape and the Epstein files straight to the ballot box.”

Dozens of people turned out in Oklahoma City at Mayflower Congregational Church, although voter registration in the state ended Oct. 9. The day’s rally was limited to holding signs outside along Portland Avenue or filling out voter reminder postcards.

“We can send them to voters who need an extra nudge, and a reminder that voting in the midterms is just as important as voting in the presidential election,” said Nina Lawrence, an organizer who hoped to combat Oklahoma’s low voter turnout.

Lu Eyerman, a spokeswoman for Indivisible, a grass-roots voter movement, said the focus on the election was to prepare voters for anything that could come in the run-up to November’s election. “We want to be prepared to help in whatever way we can,” Ms. Eyerman said.

Near Pacific Plaza in downtown Dallas, Stephanie Williams with the Black Voters Matter Fund led the crowd in a vibrant chant.

“Our democracy is under attack!” she shouted. The crowd replied, “We fight back!”

Ms. Williams then addressed the crowd and listed how government policies showed up in their daily lives, from health care costs to SNAP funding to their electricity bills: “We have marched. We have rallied. We said, ‘No Kings.’ Today, we’re going to move from protest to power.”

Across the lawn, a steady stream of people held signs ranging from “Save democracy” to “Be a hero, vote!”

Among the attendees were Pam and Royce Mitchell, both 73 and married 51 years, who were attending their first “No Kings” rally. Ms. Mitchell, a retired kindergarten teacher, said the two had been George W. Bush supporters but were now Democrats. The political climate now, she said, was no longer about Democrats versus Republicans.

Reporting was contributed by Sean Keenan, Ben Fenwick and Deah Berry Mitchell.

Corina Knoll is a Times correspondent focusing on feature stories.

The New York Times October 17, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Ken Paxton’s bus tour of Texas comes as polls have shown the race for Senate is increasingly close. His rival, James Talarico, is scheduled to kick off a similar tour on Sunday.

By Jesus Jiménez

Reporting from Rockwall, Texas

Ken Paxton, the Republican Texas attorney general who is running for Senate against James Talarico, started a statewide bus tour on Saturday, looking to shore up support in what has become a close race.

Mr. Paxton kicked off the tour with a stop at an airport hangar in Rockwall, a Dallas suburb where President Trump won in 2024 by about 40 percentage points. After remarks from current, former and hopeful Texas officials, the AC/DC song “Thunderstruck” played as the hangar door slowly opened to reveal the arrival of Mr. Paxton’s bus.

The start of Mr. Paxton’s road trip comes as several polls have shown a tight race for the Senate seat in Texas, while other polls have given Mr. Talarico a slight edge at becoming the first Democrat to win a statewide election since 1994.

In remarks that lasted about 19 minutes, Mr. Paxton touted his record as the Texas attorney general and took jabs at Mr. Talarico. Mr. Paxton also acknowledged that the polls have been close, and urged his supporters to vote early and encourage others to vote as well.

“While you might think you have one vote, just one vote, the consequences of that vote will determine what the future of America looks like,” Mr. Paxton said. “We’re on a knife’s edge, but the difference is thousands of miles apart. That’s why this race is about more than just me and James Talarico.”

Among those who spoke at the rally were Jace Yarbrough, a Republican running for Congress who has been endorsed by President Trump, and Katrina Pierson, a Texas state representative running for re-election who had previously served as a Trump campaign adviser.

Mr. Paxton was also joined by Nate Schatzline, a former Texas state representative and an adviser to Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas. Mr. Schatzline told those at the rally that Mr. Paxton had recently been endorsed by dozens of pastors.

“This is not a political battle for him,” Mr. Schatzline said. “This is, in fact, a spiritual battle in the state of Texas and really across the country.”

Mark Linane, 60, who attended the event, said that the endorsement resonated with him and was one reason he planned to vote for Mr. Paxton.

“I’m a man of faith,” Mr. Linane said. “This is an important fight. We got a lot of things going on, and I think we have to put our faith first.”

After the rally, many attendees took turns signing messages on the campaign bus, and others took pictures by the bus. Mona Jam, 38, said that she had been door-knocking and making calls for Mr. Paxton.

Ms. Jam, who moved to Texas from Iran in 2016, said she supported Mr. Paxton because she believed he could help bring regime change in Iran.

“I think that’s what he stands for, too,” Ms. Jam said. “He is looking for freedom.”

The event in Rockwall was the first of two scheduled stops on Saturday. In all, Mr. Paxton’s bus tour will make more than 30 stops across the state before a final stop at the Alamo in San Antonio the night before Election Day.

Mr. Talarico is also planning a statewide bus tour that is expected to begin on Sunday. It is scheduled to make 21 stops across Texas, beginning in Plano, a Dallas suburb, and ending on Nov. 2 in Austin.

Jesus Jiménez is a Times reporter covering North Texas. He is based in Dallas.

Ms. Collins, a Republican running in a crucial race, said the debate remark by Troy Jackson reflects how he treats women. Mr. Jackson has defended his comment, and his campaign said Ms. Collins had run a campaign based on personal attacks.

By Tim Balk

Senator Susan Collins, Republican of Maine, criticized her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, over a debate moment when he told her to “shut up,” suggesting the remark reflected how he treats women.

“I was struck by how reflexive the response, ‘Oh, shut up,’ was,” Ms. Collins, the longest-serving Republican woman in Senate history, told Fox News on Friday, adding that “the fact that it seemed like such an automatic, quick reply was very telling.”

She said the exchange brought to mind what she described as the “reputation” that Mr. Jackson, a former State Senate president, had when he was a state lawmaker, “particularly when he’s dealing with women with whom he disagrees.”

“So in some ways, it didn’t surprise me,” said Ms. Collins, whose race could be critical in the battle for control of the Senate.

A spokeswoman for Mr. Jackson, Maggie Amjad, said in a statement that Ms. Collins had run a campaign “based on personal attacks” and was twisting the debate exchange.

On a debate stage Thursday night, Mr. Jackson, speaking in a low voice, told Ms. Collins to “shut up” after she said that a heckler disrupting the debate — by yelling about data centers — was a supporter of Mr. Jackson.

“This is obviously one of Troy’s supporters,” Ms. Collins said.

He replied: “Oh, shut up. I did not — I didn’t — I don’t even know that kid.”

The protester, Henry Elgie, 19, a student at Bowdoin College in Brunswick, Maine, said in an interview Saturday that he’d had “zero coordination” with the Jackson campaign but that he would vote for Mr. Jackson.

“I do not know Troy Jackson personally or at all,” Mr. Elgie said. “But I think he should be winning.”

Mr. Jackson has defended his response to Ms. Collins in the debate.

“She accused me of setting that up, which is completely untrue,” Mr. Jackson told WGME-TV in an interview published Friday. He added that he had sought to treat Ms. Collins with respect, but that she had “spent millions of dollars attacking” him in “a way that I don’t think is professional either.”

His spokeswoman, responding to Ms. Collins’s interview with Fox News, compared Mr. Jackson’s record with Ms. Collins’s on issues affecting women.

Ms. Amjad said in her statement that Mr. Jackson had responded in the debate to a false accusation from Ms. Collins, and that her “campaign’s attempt to turn that exchange into anything else is baseless.”

Ms. Amjad noted Mr. Jackson’s support for abortion rights and paid family and medical leave, and Ms. Collins’s vote to confirm a Supreme Court justice, Brett M. Kavanaugh, who later helped overturn a federal right to abortion.

During the race, Ms. Collins’s campaign has accused Mr. Jackson of bullying women when he was a state lawmaker.

Mr. Jackson was known to have a temper during his time in the State Legislature. In 2021, during an argument with Heather Sanborn, a state lawmaker, he threw a water bottle across a room. He has said that he regrets the episode, but that he will not apologize for “being passionate,” and that he fights hard for issues he believes in.

U. S. Floats Another Lifeline to Russia: Allowing It to Sell More Gas to Europe

The New York Times October 17, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

The Trump administration is pitching the idea as part of a peace deal with Ukraine, but Europe is wary and critics say Russia would be strengthened.

By Anton Troianovski and Jim Tankersley

Anton Troianovski reported from Washington, and Jim Tankersley from Berlin.

A key element in the Trump administration’s broad plan for securing peace in Ukraine is a proposal that would turn years of American energy policy upside-down.

Europe, the U. S. pitch goes, should resume buying more Russian gas — a move that would be an economic boon for Moscow and give it renewed influence in the region.

President Trump’s peace envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have brought up the idea in talks with Ukrainian and European officials, including with President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv last month, according to people familiar with the talks. To help entice Russia to end the war in Ukraine, the Americans have argued, Ukraine should consider restarting pipelines that used to carry Russian natural gas to Europe.

European officials in the talks have recoiled at the idea, which would undo the European Union’s years of efforts, backed by Washington, to rid itself of Russian gas. But Trump officials see Russian gas exports as a potential part of a peace settlement, given the revenues that would flow to Ukraine and what they see as the inevitable desire for cheaper energy by European voters, the people said, discussing sensitive diplomacy on the condition of anonymity.

The disconnect underscores the unusual — and, critics say, fatally flawed — nature of Mr. Trump’s renewed diplomatic effort to end Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Rather than pressure President Vladimir V. Putin or try to strengthen Ukraine’s war effort, the administration has spent significant time exploring economic incentives for Russia and raising them in talks with Europe and Ukraine.

U. S. and Russian officials have been talking about potential business deals since last year, but their prospect has not appeared to do anything to get Mr. Putin to budge from his core demands. And given how much European and Ukrainian leaders oppose returning to a reliance on Russian gas, the proposal may end up further complicating the Trump administration’s efforts to end the war.

In a statement, the White House said that the war was “driving up energy prices across Europe and creating significant economic hardship in both Russia and Ukraine.”

“The United States has been working closely with Ukraine and our European partners on a comprehensive peace proposal that includes economic incentives for both Russia and Ukraine as part of a final settlement,” the statement said. “Our objective is not simply to end the fighting, but to create the conditions for lasting peace, economic recovery and greater stability across the region.”

Mr. Trump on Friday exempted Russia from new sanctions passed by Congress, a week after lifting sanctions on Russian diesel, his most significant steps yet in easing economic pressure on Russia. Mr. Putin’s economic envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, described the diesel deal as just the beginning of what could result from his talks with Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff.

“I think we will be announcing some important initiatives in the near future,” Mr. Dmitriev said at an energy conference in Moscow on Friday. “The ice has finally broken, after all.”

Mr. Dmitriev said Russia and the United States were discussing a wide range of projects, including data centers running on Russian nuclear power. The sale of the international assets of the Russian energy giant Lukoil to an investor group that includes the U. S. government is also part of the talks, The New York Times reported this month.

But the proposal to bring back Russian gas exports to Europe, which Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff see as a potential part of a final peace package, may be the most audacious and divisive part of the plan. For American companies, it could reduce demand for U. S. liquefied natural gas in Europe. For European governments, it could boost populist politicians already urging an end to aid to Ukraine and a renewal of ties with Russia.

“We want natural gas and crude oil from Russia to relieve German consumers and German businesses,” Alice Weidel, a leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany, said in Parliament in Berlin this week. As Washington and Moscow negotiated deals “to their mutual advantage,” she said, sanctions on Russia were “ruining our own economy.”

Mr. Zelensky, who has attacked Mr. Trump in recent days for pulling back support for Ukraine and doing deals with Mr. Putin, alluded to the negotiations in an interview with The Financial Times this week.

“The question will be when will the next deal be?” Mr. Zelensky said. “Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas.”

Ukraine stopped transporting Russian gas in January 2025, losing around $1 billion in annual transit fees. The European Union has pledged to end all Russian gas imports by next year. Last year, 13 percent of the E. U.’s gas imports came from Russia, compared to 45 percent in 2021.

But as the White House has grasped for new ideas to end the war in Ukraine, and as Mr. Trump frets over high energy prices ahead of the midterm elections, the administration has been increasingly considering deals that would ease Russia’s ability to export its fossil fuels.

Enabling Russia to restart gas exports to Europe, the people involved said, is a longer-term plan being discussed by Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff. The envoys see such exports as among the economic incentives in a broader settlement that would involve negotiations over the future Russia-NATO relationship, security guarantees for Ukraine and an agreement over territorial control.

Some European and Ukrainian officials expect the United States to seek a stake in Russian gas exports, giving American companies or the government a cut of the profits, according to people familiar with the talks.

An American investor, Stephen P. Lynch, has sought to buy a sabotaged Russian undersea gas pipeline to Germany, Nord Stream 2, starting in the Biden administration. U. S. control of the pipeline, he argued, would benefit American interests and European security when, sooner or later, Russian gas flows through it are restored.

Mr. Lynch said he was not currently part of any Nord Stream negotiations and did not have a Treasury Department license to be involved. But Nord Stream has also come up in the discussions between the United States and Russia, people familiar with the talks said. Reuters reported this month that U. S. and Russian officials had discussed bringing a U. S. investor into Nord Stream.

The White House, in its statement, said that Nord Stream had not been “a subject of recent discussions.” It added that “any arrangement involving it would require close coordination with our European partners as part of a comprehensive peace agreement.”

One of the people familiar with the talks said the Trump administration sees restarting the undersea pipeline as “low-hanging fruit” in the event of a peace deal. European officials may have forsworn Russian gas publicly, the person said, but European voters, like American voters, will eventually want cheaper energy.

It is an echo of the Kremlin’s position. Mr. Putin’s spokesman, Dmitri S. Peskov, said in a voice message in response to questions about the gas talks: “Resuming energy cooperation in whatever form is in our interest, but right now, it may even more be in the interest of the Europeans themselves.”

The German government has been at the forefront of pushing back against restarting Russian gas pipelines, even though Germany had been the biggest buyer of Russian gas before Mr. Putin’s 2022 invasion. When the idea came up again in Ukraine talks hosted by Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner in Florida last week, Günter Sautter, the top security adviser to Chancellor Friedrich Merz of Germany, was particularly forceful in his opposition, according to two people familiar with the meeting.

A European official familiar with the Germans’ stance said this week that the German government views Russian gas sold through an intermediary as indistinguishable from gas straight from Russia — and thus, off-limits as part of peace negotiations.

Germany’s energy costs have soared since 2022, and current and former German officials acknowledge that buying Russian gas again would bring those prices down. But they say doing so would cost Germany and Europe dearly in security terms, including by making it vulnerable to a future gas cutoff by Moscow.

“Europe, and especially Germany, should never again be dependent on Russian gas,” Robert Habeck, who was the German economy minister when the war began and managed the transition off Russian gas, said in an interview. “Because we have seen how unreliable Russia was.”

But German leaders are under pressure at home over the war — and over gas imports in particular. The Alternative for Germany, or AfD, which leads national polls with close to 30 percent support, has pitched a renewal of Russian gas imports as a way to fight inflation and boost the German economy.

In the state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD this month elected the first far-right speaker in a German statehouse since 1945, lawmakers passed a largely symbolic measure this week that calls on the federal government to end sanctions against Russia and cease military aid to Ukraine. AfD representatives voted for the bill, along with lawmakers from a Russia-friendly party founded by a former leftist, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance.

European leaders are increasingly worried about the similar messages coming from their countries’ populist parties, Mr. Trump and the Kremlin. Mr. Merz and other European leaders have publicly criticized Mr. Trump’s lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel, saying the move broke the West’s economic pressure campaign against Moscow.

Mr. Habeck, the former economy minister, said it was possible Germany could live with the resumption of a relatively small amount of gas imports from Russia. But he said that it was crucial for Europe to own and operate its own energy infrastructure in the years to come, and that it would not matter — in security terms — if an American intermediary transported Russian gas.

“In the old days, I would be glad if an American company would be part of the ownership,” Mr. Habeck said. “Now I’m afraid, because we see that Trump seems to have more sympathies with Vladimir Putin than he has with the Ukrainians.”

Anton Troianovski writes about American foreign policy and national security for The Times from Washington. He was previously a foreign correspondent based in Moscow and Berlin.

Jim Tankersley is the Berlin bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of Germany, Austria and Switzerland.

Weak Links Start to Show in A. I. Borrowing

The New York Times October 17, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Debt trouble at CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank raises questions about whether there are broader problems with the data center build-out.

By Maureen Farrell and Rob Copeland

Maureen Farrell and Rob Copeland cover finance from New York.

Trillions of dollars in borrowed money have powered the A. I. boom. But now there is growing uncertainty around just how easily more money can be obtained — and how much of it will be paid back.

Those questions burst into the forefront this week when investors rapidly lost confidence in one debt-laden data center company, CoreWeave. Prices of its bonds — the company has accrued $72 billion in liabilities to operate 51 data centers — crashed, and investors placed a more than 60 percent likelihood CoreWeave would fail to meet its obligations.

Investors have sold off bonds for other A. I. giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s.

At the same time, Wall Street investors have been bidding up the price of some complicated financial instruments that insure corporate debt against default, such as those insuring SoftBank, the Japanese technology colossus that has borrowed heavily to bet its future on a partnership with OpenAI.

The recent market moves could spell losses for investors that own the companies’ existing bonds and could mean the companies will be forced to pay higher interest rates when they borrow again, raising the costs of their already wildly expensive A. I. projects.

The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the A. I. build-out.

The spread, or extra premium that investors demand to put their money into risky A. I. debt investments, has shot up more than 50 percent over the past six months, according to Barclays, the investment bank.

“The market is on a knife’s edge everywhere,” said Alexandra Coleman, founder of Azraq, a data center risk researcher.

A lot is riding on the continuation of the borrowing binge. Every week lately, economists, banks and private equity firms project higher and higher amounts of debt that they say will be needed to finance the artificial intelligence systems that their boosters assert will run the world in a few years.

Virtually every major mutual fund company, insurer and private equity firm has been buying up the A. I. debt, to say nothing of the scores of individual investors who have poured money into skyrocketing A. I. companies.

Not every data center developer worries bond investors equally. The larger so-called hyperscalers, such as Meta and Alphabet, which continue to borrow heavily, have been forced by investors to pay only modestly more in interest in recent debt deals. Investors have also sold out of some these companies’ existing debt, though the drop in bond prices has been less steep than for CoreWeave.

Some of this can be attributed to the Federal Reserve’s recent decision to begin raising interest rates in an effort to control inflation, which is being caused, in part, by the data center boom.

David Munves, head of credit strategy at the researcher AIR Platforms, said there was a “collective realization” this week that the risks of the artificial intelligence surge were greater than anticipated.

“The market’s waking up to the fact that there is potentially a mismatch between the money they have to commit today and borrow today and the ability to generate revenues down the road,” he added.

This week, the yield on CoreWeave’s bond eclipsed 15 percent, well into “junk bond” territory, and the company’s stock dropped 24 percent, including a 12 percent fall on Friday alone.

CoreWeave’s business model defies easy description. Its financial arrangements have been compared by some investors and analysts to that of the troubled office-space provider WeWork.

First, CoreWeave buys Nvidia and other A. I. chips. Then, as with WeWork, which leases space inside office buildings owned by others, CoreWeave contracts with data center owners to use the structures for A. I. computing for 15 years or more. CoreWeave then subleases the space to customers, including Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI, for a shorter time frame.

The rub is that CoreWeave is on the hook for costs on both ends: It must pay to assemble and operate the facilities before any tenant is in place, and it is committed to the space for longer than its customers may stick around.

Several investors said they were worried about whether hyperscalers such as Meta and Microsoft would even need to lease space from CoreWeave in the future. Alternately, they’re wary of whether the data centers could become dated or even obsolete as their existing contracts expire.

A CoreWeave spokeswoman, Lia Davis, said the company disagreed with the WeWork comparison. In a statement, she said that “the complexity of our financing reflects discipline, which is a point of pride for us.” CoreWeave’s chief executive, in a note to employees on Wednesday, called the recent market moves “irrational.”

In a March presentation to potential lenders, CoreWeave said it would earn enough from a five-year lease to cover its related expenses for twice that time.

“We are confident in our business model, our customers, the extraordinary quality of our execution and the relentless discipline around the financial engine we have built,” CoreWeave’s chief executive, Michael Intrator, told employees in his note.

Another worry: the increasing number of data centers that are being delayed by permitting issues, and in some instances falling through.

Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects. Last year, the company easily borrowed $38 billion from a group of banks to build, with the help of project developers, a pair of data centers, one in Texas and another on 2,000 acres of farmland in Port Washington, Wis.

Oracle planned to pay back the borrowed money on the Texas facility helped by profits from the latter complex, called Project Lighthouse, which it expected to be operational by 2028.

Since then, Project Lighthouse has run into local hurdles, including from state power regulators who have pushed back their time horizon to approve the construction of a power grid critical for the data center to operate.

Aterio, a data center researcher, said it was looking less likely that Project Lighthouse’s four data centers would start operating before 2029.

That’s just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due. Some of the debt has traded around 90 cents on the dollar or below that, according to two traders, a steep drop for a relatively new loan.

An Oracle spokeswoman declined to comment.

Oracle faces similar permitting issues at a data center project in New Mexico. The project’s developer, the investment firm Blue Owl, has started construction on the facility, but Oracle is struggling to get state permits to provide enough power.

Some of the $18 billion in debt tied to the project has recently sold at steep discounts, roughly 80 cents on the dollar, according to two people familiar with the trades.

SoftBank has borrowed heavily to make one of the biggest bets — by dollar value — on OpenAI. The Japanese conglomerate, led by Masayoshi Son, wrote its first $500 million check in 2024 and a year later invested $30 billion more.

To get that money, Mr. Son sold off most of SoftBank’s holdings of Nvidia and T-Mobile and took out loans against his stake in the chip designer Arm Holdings.

This year, Mr. Son invested again. On Oct. 1, SoftBank completed another $30 billion investment in OpenAI. Before doing so, in late September, the company raised a record $11 billion in debt at interest rates of nearly 10 percent.

In response to questions about SoftBank’s increasing debt, Alex Clavel, chief executive of the SoftBank Vision Funds, said the amount of their debt as a percentage of SoftBank Group’s assets hadn’t changed.

“The assets we’ve owned have increased significantly,” Mr. Clavel said in an interview.

The cost of insuring against losses on SoftBank’s debt has spiked. It now costs more than $40,000 to insure against $1 million of SoftBank debt. At the beginning of this year, the cost was less than $27,000.

Some investors see a potential silver lining to the troubles. John Lloyd, the global head of multisector and corporate credit at the asset manager Janus Henderson, said slowing down the financing for projects “makes existing projects and existing A. I. infrastructure even more valuable.”

Maureen Farrell writes about Wall Street for The Times, focusing on private equity, hedge funds and billionaires and how they influence the world of investing.

Rob Copeland is a finance reporter for The Times, writing about Wall Street and the banking industry.

Trump’s Bubble Is About to Burst

The New York Times October 17, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Maureen Dowd

By Maureen Dowd

Opinion Columnist, reporting from Washington

Sometimes a candid photograph captures a moment in a presidency, and the essence of the officeholder, so tellingly that you get a penetrating portrait of an era.

It happened when L. B. J. yanked up his beagle by the ears for photographers and demonstrated his domineering leadership style.

It happened when a photographer captured W. being told, while reading to children in a Florida classroom, that a second plane had hit the World Trade Center. His look of shock raised questions about whether, after his decades of winging it, a parlous rendezvous with destiny might be too much for him to handle.

It happened in 2009 when every living president gathered in the Oval Office and Jimmy Carter so obviously kept his distance from Presidents Obama, Clinton and both Bushes that his sense of superiority was made clear.

It happened when Obama was photographed bending over in the Oval to let a Black child touch his hair, to see if it was the same texture as his own, capturing the historic nature of his election.

It happened again when Doug Mills, The Times’s dazzling White House photographer, took a picture on Tuesday of President Trump on Marine One with his blond aides/acolytes Katie Zacharia, his wobbly new press secretary, and Natalie Harp, his special assistant for floofing.

Mills took the shot from far away with a long lens, but it bristles with intimacy.

The president is leaning in to talk to the two Ivanka knockoffs, who look like sorority-sister clones, four eyes glued on the man they adore, two fervent smiles glazed with pink lip gloss.

It is a snapshot of Trump’s hunger for adulation that has dragged us to this fraught moment in America.

He desperately craves being the center of attention, and seeing blind devotion mirrored back at him as that devotion wanes with an increasingly disgusted, exhausted public.

Trump was on a trip, part of a self-affirming odyssey to red states, which seemed to be designed not only to boost his unappetizing slate of candidates but also to let him bask in applause from the last fanatical members of his dwindling fan base.

In Mills’s photo, Marines are at attention beside the curved open doors of the helicopter, giving the impression that we are peering inside a bubble — at the very moment that Trump’s White House bubble is getting smaller and more ingrown and fractious than ever. Here he is in a cozy huddle with his most essential type of staff member: obedient helpmeets who help construct and perpetuate his absurd alternative reality and paranoid worldview.

Zacharia, the inept propagandist, and Harp, the so-called Human Printer, who trails — and sometimes sprints — behind the president with a portable printer, giving hard copies of soft coverage to Trump, offering him validation for his delusions and lies.

Zacharia reposted Mills’s photo with the caption, “Best President in U. S. History!!!” But it really should have been the classic Henry Kissinger line: “Power is the ultimate aphrodisiac.”

Wags on X had their own captions, imagining Harp thinking homicidal thoughts about Zacharia.

But actually, the two women — scorned by colleagues eager to anonymously trash talk them — were cloistered on the edge of the playground, clinging to each other and to their orange prophet who told them to hang in there.

But it didn’t last, and by Friday, he was easing Zacharia out. “Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider,” Trump told her, as he later recounted to reporters. Soon after, she got the boot.

They were trying to fight back against their in-house critics. Harp showed Trump the Politico Playbook story on Thursday reporting that the president is shopping around for a new chief of staff. It also named the advisers who have cashed in. The right to cash in, in Trump’s eyes, is for him and his family only.

“Trump has bristled at recent reports showing several longtime advisers are profiting from foreign consulting business,” Playbook said, noting that Susie Wiles’s daughter Katie is working for a firm representing Republika Srpska, a pro-Russian Bosnian Serb territory.

The Daily Beast headline about the Wiles report blared, “Natalie Harp Knifes Ice Maiden and Sparks Trump ‘Freakout.’”

Tellingly and perhaps prophetically, Susie Wiles is in Mills’s picture, but mostly cut out of the frame. You can see her legs in red pants and the Louis Vuitton bag on her lap.

We can’t see the expression on Wiles’s face, but we know that she is no fan of the two gushing young women in the picture.

Alarmed by Harp’s fixation on the president, and her emotionally raw letters to him in 2023, Wiles attempted — in vain — to curb her access. Trump’s decision to appoint Zacharia to a critical job where she was doomed to flounder and likely end up in an “S. N. L.” cold open blindsided Wiles, according to news reports.

Even Trump seemed taken aback by the press gaggle after Zacharia’s debut news conference debacle and when The Times’s Shawn McCreesh, before the president and his aides took off for Alaska, asked Zacharia where she had passed the bar.

“When I moved to China,” she said, as Trump — who described her as an attorney when he announced her appointment — snapped his head around. The story unspooled that she hadn’t passed the bar anywhere.

But by the time they got to Alaska eight hours later, she was beaming at her boss and doing damage control.

(She told a far-right Pizzagate conspiracist in an interview that she wanted to be played on “S. N. L.” by “a Scarlett Johansson-type character.”)

Zacharia tried to fight back on “Hannity,” no doubt assuming she would be in friendly territory.

But she wasn’t. Sean Hannity asked her why she had put up 15 media posts identifying herself as an attorney. She lamely protested that they were “retweets of a title that had been given.” (Mistakes were made.)

Hannity pressed on: “Why didn’t you just say ‘I never practiced law’?” and asked about her first news conference, “Why only three questions in 14 minutes?”

Zacharia looked unnerved, as though she had been sandbagged by her foes in the White House.

As his hold on the country seems to be slipping through his pudgy fingers, Trump needs the unqualified love from his blond Praetorian Guard.

Not only do Democrats seem headed for success in the midterms, fueled by a swell of Americans who see Trump as a crook, enriching himself while costs rise for everyone else, but the president’s inner circle is going up in flames. Aides are turning on one another and sinking in a cauldron of corruption and boneheaded policies.

This week has been a cascade of embarrassing stories: Kimberly Guilfoyle getting iced as ambassador to Greece after a donor revealed that just before her Senate confirmation hearing, she tried to shake him down to pay her $100,000 American Express bill; the Trump loyalist Ric Grenell, who was the head of the ill-fated Kennedy Center, accused by the Trump loyalist Alina Habba Mildon and her new billionaire husband of misallocating a $5.6 million donation marked for the center; and our ally Volodymyr Zelensky saying he felt betrayed by Trump’s sordid deal with Vladimir Putin over diesel oil and the restricted access to Elon Musk’s Starshield amid Russian bombardment. Trump even had to cancel the nitwit plan of his frat boy Pentagon chief to livestream an execution.

Instead of running the country and dealing with the world he has set on fire, the president is focused on settling petty squabbles and a web of corruption in his incompetent — and dangerous — court.

Doug Mills has proved once again that a picture is worth 1,000 words, or in my case, 1,283.

An old saying has it that first-rate managers hire first-rate managers, and second-rate managers hire third-rate managers. Thanks to Trump, we now know what kind of managers third-rate managers hire.

Just like sometimes we need a close call to realize how important something is, I hope that the Trump lesson to Americans will be one that will last for generations: that choosing a leader cannot be done lighlty, that character (some of it, at least) matters, that rules are needed and cannot be left to a handshake, and that commitment to friends and allies count. The US has lost the trust of the world and I hope it will not take a global war or another 9/11 for it to regain the respect it once had. Perhaps the American Century is over for good at this point, sadly.

I appreciated how you provided historical context for singular photographic moments that have defined presidencies. Trump's reality-TV performance of a U. S. presidency especially seems like a gold mine of revelatory nuggets. It does seem like Trump is in his Norma Desmond era, insisting his star shines brightly while the lights dim and the adoration fades away.

Maureen Dowd is an Opinion columnist for The Times. She won the 1999 Pulitzer Prize for distinguished commentary. She is the author, most recently, of “Notorious.” @MaureenDowd • Facebook

How a Teacher and a Dad Stopped the Slaughter in Bend

The New York Times October 17, 2026

Oregon School Shooting

Advertisement

Supported by

The city of Bend, Ore., is praising those who worked to stop the gunman at Silver Rail Elementary School. The authorities are searching for answers.

By Anna GriffinAaron WestNicholas Bogel-Burroughs and Chelsia Rose Marcius

Anna Griffin and Aaron West reported from Bend, Ore.

The 16-year-old who killed three children and a teacher with a shotgun at an Oregon elementary school blasted his way through a side entrance before a teacher’s heroism and a father’s quick thinking prevented even more carnage.

As the makeshift memorial in front of Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., grew Friday, with donations of flowers, stuffed animals and candles, police and school officials began offering a clearer picture of how the attack unfolded — and how much worse it could have been.

They identified the shooter as Griffin J. John II, a former special education student at Silver Rail who lived with his mother, Shauntai May Nickerson, a half-mile away from the school. He carried a 12-gauge pump-action shotgun that was registered to Ms. Nickerson, according to a law enforcement official who was granted anonymity to discuss details of the case.

The teenager approached the school on foot a little before 1 p. m. Thursday — picture day at Silver Rail — from an undeveloped and partially wooded lot on the side of the 11-year-old building, which featured modern school safety features at the front entrance.

A man in a red pickup truck was driving by and saw the teenager throw his shotgun over the fence and start to climb it, the police said. The driver “verbally confronted” the gunman, who paused to open fire at him, pelting the truck with shots. The man was not injured.

The teenager then got over the fence, shot through glass panes in a set of doors on the playground side of the building and went into a special education classroom just inside the school.

Inside, he killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher, Megan Lambert, who family members described as a young educator thrilled to be working in her hometown. He also wounded a 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher.

Another teacher in the room threw her cellphone at the shooter and then tackled him, Chief Mike Krantz of the Bend Police Department said.

Outside, Kaylub Giamanco, a father of two girls at the school, had seen the red pickup get shot while driving by on his lunch break. He swerved onto the sidewalk and ran inside.

He found the gunman wrestling with the teacher who tried to stop him and shot him several times with a .40-caliber handgun that had been legally secured in his truck, the police said. The suspect, who died, was carrying 44 more rounds of ammunition.

At a Friday afternoon news conference, Chief Krantz confirmed the I. D. of the suspect and then pledged that he would “not say his name again.”

He said the Bend community should give thanks to everyone who worked to stop the shooter.

“I don’t think we can underestimate or underappreciate that courage,” Mr. Krantz said. “When someone is willing to risk their own lives for others? A teacher who is willing to stand and fight for her children? Incredible.”

News of the heroism didn’t do much to soften the pain in Bend, a fast-growing city in central Oregon known for mountain biking, beer making and the ski slopes of nearby Mount Bachelor. The city is also familiar with gun violence: In 2022, a 20-year-old man killed two people and himself at a grocery store just three miles from Silver Rail.

“It’s awful that we know what this is like already,” said Michael LaMaita, the father of a preschooler who lives across the street from Mr. Giamanco. “It’s so weird to have it happen twice.”

Many Bend schools, miles away from Silver Rail, went into lockdown briefly on Thursday after the shooting, and thousands of people attended a candlelight vigil that night. School and recreational activities were canceled citywide Friday, so libraries and businesses that cater to families offered special programs for residents seeking community.

Carissa Honeycutt brought her 9-year-old son, Wallace, to a local park to practice skateboarding in an effort to “keep him busy, keep our minds occupied with other positive things today.”

Wallace attends Ponderosa Elementary but has still asked if it was safe to return to his own classroom. Ms. Honeycutt has reassured him, she said, even though she is also nervous.

Many parents talked of finding counseling for their children, and almost 200 people showed up at the city’s main library Friday morning seeking mental health support.

Sean Fink’s 10-year-old daughter is a fifth grader at Silver Rail and said she was in a classroom one floor above the attack.

“She told me she heard the teacher screaming for her life,” Mr. Fink said, adding that he’ll lean on the close-knit community around the school and its collection of young families to help her.

Derek Cox, another father of a Silver Rail student, said he planned to seek a therapist for his daughter in fourth grade, whose classroom was almost directly above the special education room where the shooting occurred.

“She heard it all,” he said, of his daughter. “I think she’s handling it as well as you could at that age right now, but this is going to have a long-term impact for sure.”

Brian Jolly, the grandfather of Rhoam Summer, a 5-year-old boy killed in the attack, said “the whole thing is senseless, and a shock.”

Mr. Jolly lives in Bend and said he saw his grandson often. “He was in my house a lot, and in my garden with me, and wrestling with me on the couch,” he said. “He was very bright and very mischievous and very fun-loving, and totally without fear.”

Investigators plan to keep the school roped off as a crime scene into early next week, and they still have a number of questions they are trying to answer. Among them: What motivated the shooter, and how did he gain access to the shotgun and ammunition?

The suspect’s mother, Ms. Nickerson, told a local television station in September 2020 that she was grateful her son, then 10, could return to in-person instruction following the Covid-19 school closures. He had struggled with learning from home, she said.

On Friday morning, Ms. Nickerson sat on the deck of her second-floor apartment, smoking and weeping. In a brief conversation, she said that her son “was a good boy,” and that she had seen no warning signs that he might commit violence.

“If I could have prevented this, I would have,” she said.

Investigators have searched the apartment, according to the law enforcement official who spoke anonymously. His mother was cooperative, the official said, and investigators seized the boy’s electronic devices under a search warrant.

The police said the shooter had attended Silver Rail for at least some of elementary school, though they were not able to provide details of when he was a student there or whether he knew any of the teachers he shot. He was not enrolled in the Bend-La Pine school district at the time of the shooting.

Superintendent Steve Cook said the school district will conduct its own investigation to determine how the shooter entered the building, which parents said had an updated front entryway designed to prevent just this kind of attack. Silver Rail had a school resource officer, but the officer was responsible for a half-dozen campuses and was not at Silver Rail on Thursday afternoon.

“Rest assured,” Mr. Cook said Friday, “we will take a hard look at everything we have done.”

The 7-year-old girl who was shot was in serious but stable condition after being airlifted from Bend to a children’s hospital in Portland, Ore., officials said.

She was also the beneficiary of a teacher’s bravery: Heidi Penington, a friend of the girl’s family, said another special education teacher, identified as Becky Drury by Ms. Drury’s husband, threw herself on top of the child as the gunman fired.

A shot went through Ms. Drury’s arm and the girl’s face, Ms. Penington said. Both are expected to survive.

Jacey Fortin, Livia Albeck-Ripka, Madison Malone Kircher and Mimi Dwyer contributed reporting.

Anna Griffin is the Pacific Northwest bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of Washington, Idaho, Alaska, Montana and Oregon.

Nicholas Bogel-Burroughs reports on stories across the United States, including natural disasters, protests, unsolved mysteries, high-profile criminal cases and more.

Chelsia Rose Marcius is a criminal justice reporter for The Times, covering the New York Police Department.
