50 Years In, What’s the Point of U2? Bono and the Edge Have Answers.

The New York Times October 17, 2026

Trump Administration

The Interview

The Interview

Credit... Philip Montgomery for The New York Times

Supported by

By David Marchese

U2, as I’m sure you’re well aware, is one of the biggest bands of all time. The Irish quartet has released iconic albums like “The Joshua Tree” (1987), “Achtung Baby” (1991) and “All That You Can’t Leave Behind” (2000); staged some of the highest-grossing and most innovative tours ever; and won 22 Grammys, among myriad other achievements. Still, there are other rock artists on that level. Not many, but a few. Where U2 may truly be unparalleled is that all that success was earned by the same four guys.

The four members of the band — Bono on lead vocals, the Edge on guitar, Larry Mullen Jr. on drums and Adam Clayton on bass — still occupy the same positions they did when they first played together in suburban Dublin in September 1976 — 50 years ago this fall. (And from what I understand, they all still like one another, too.) Especially in the tempestuous world of rock ’n’ roll, that longevity and stability is to be celebrated.

Which is exactly what the band has done. On Sept. 25, U2 celebrated its golden anniversary with performances in front of giddy students at Mount Temple Comprehensive School in Dublin, where the members first met, and then, as a surprise, from a balcony of a former rock club in front of an instant crowd of thousands in the city’s center. Next month, on Nov. 13, U2 will release “Carnaval De Luz,” the band’s first full-length album of new material since 2017. (It follows two EPs, “Days of Ash” and “Easter Lily,” both released this year.)

On the day after those commemorative events, I spoke with Bono and the Edge, the band’s two principal songwriters, about their long working relationship, friendship, and what U2 still means — both to them and to the world.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Amazon | iHeart

I think of U2 as wanting to be the best and biggest band in the world. But it probably shouldn’t be the case that the best and biggest rock ’n’ roll band in the world is a band that’s been around for 50 years, comprising guys in their 60s.

Bono: That’s very, very hurtful, David.

The Edge: But fair.

So what do you think the purpose of U2 is right now? What should U2 be trying to be?

The Edge: We genuinely think that we might just write the best song we’ve ever written next week, or do the best show we’ve ever done next tour. When we talk about the best, we’re not thinking about rock ’n’ roll. We’re thinking about our favorite bands and what, if I’m in the audience at a show, would I want to see and hear. So it’s where rock ’n’ roll collides with activism, where rock ’n’ roll collides with ideas from fine arts. And I suppose a transcendent aspect as well. We’ve never thought it was necessary to hold back our own spiritual quests and questionings from our work. They are all expressed. And when we hit a song that has a transcendent quality, that’s the peak for me. I really think we’re in with a shout of the best songs we’ve ever written, the best tours we’ve done, still. That’s why I’m still in this band.

Bono: And therefore, the shout of the best songs anyone’s ever written. That’s where U2 gets really annoying. That grandiosity, which, by the way, is in all the artists that want to go there — the Beatles, Nirvana. I’m jealous when we’re left out of the pop charts. That’s a personality flaw, but deep down, it’s because I don’t want those ideas to be left out of the mainstream. My favorite artists stormed the mainstream. David Bowie, I think of his best work as being experimental and innovative, but even into his 40s, 50s, he could throw out a perfect pop song.

When you say there are ideas that you want to be in the mainstream, what are they?

Bono: The metaphysical thing, the gospel side of U2 — that was only allowed in rock ’n’ roll if you were Black. You can’t be white people talking about God, because generally white people who talk about God make our audience very nervous, you know? But not in the Black church in America. Coming to the United States, we’d just seen those televangelists, and we were like, Wow, these people are in deep trouble. Then you walk into a Black church and you hear the abandonment of the singing and that feeling — it’s fervor, but not freaky fervor. So being able to sing songs of faith and devotion and songs of doubt, to put the gospel with the blues, which is rock ’n’ roll. There’s nowhere you can’t go, including the pop charts. My constant argument is don’t cede the charts to just those pop mechanics. Hip-hop did it and got revolutionary ideas on the radio. But a lot of indie stuff just gave up. They weren’t even bothering.

You said that talking about God in your music can be a little uncomfortable for your audience, but I would argue that U2’s religious impulse is hugely important to your audience. It’s a big part of why people feel so connected to the band.

The Edge: I mean, yes, but we weren’t seeing it as a selling point. We were seeing it as the thing we have to speak about because it’s where we’re coming from. But people have said that we’re the band that people who don’t know that they believe in God like. It’s in the work in such a natural way. There’s no polemic there. It’s just our search, our inquiry. And it involves so much doubt. It has to, I think. Because if it’s not dogma, then it’s constantly in flux. I would say I’m agnostic about half of the week, and then the rest of the week I’ve got an incredibly strong faith. But it’s always changing, ready to be upgraded.

I want to ask about failure and success. Obviously, U2 had enormous successes. But there have been failures, too.

The Edge: A lot you wouldn’t even have seen or heard of.

So what does success or failure for the new album look like?

The Edge: I feel it’s already a success myself, because of the degree of time and effort and dedication to the work. I don’t really care that much what happens now because I know it’s really great.

Bono: I could say that, but I wouldn’t believe it. It’s a bit like you’re a comedian, you’ve got a routine, your punchline arrives, and if no one laughs, it’s not quite the same. Some of the songs, I would love to see even another artist take them somewhere. We were just talking about gospel music a minute ago. There is a song called “Glorify” on the album. We really ended up putting what’s like a demo on the album. It’s really minimal, the expression of the song. But that’s a screaming dance-floor hit. That’s how I imagine it. There’s a part of me that goes, [expletive], I want to do that version. I’m not sure we can. Somebody else should do that to help it cross over.

We’re speaking almost exactly 50 years ago to the day that you guys practiced for the first time in drummer Larry Mullen Jr.’s kitchen. Edge, in Bono’s memoir, “Surrender,” he writes that when you were teenagers, you and your brother, Dik, had a reputation as weirdos — pleasant weirdos but weirdos nonetheless. This was in reference to you and your brother blowing up your family’s garden shed?

The Edge: Quite likely.

Do you remember having any sense of Bono’s reputation before you all started playing together?

The Edge: First of all, that was an absolutely valid comment from Bono. Myself and my brother, there is some neurodivergence there of some sort. I’m not sure exactly what. A. D. H. D., autism, whatever. So socially speaking we were always a bit on the fringe. But, yeah, fascinated with explosives. I know way too much about how to blow things up than I ought to. But Bono’s reputation preceded him because one of my best friends growing up, Shane Fogarty, went to Mount Temple a year ahead of me, so I quizzed him about school, and he says, “It’s all right, you don’t have to wear uniforms, people are very nice, and there’s some fun heads there.” I said, “Like who?” He says: “This mad [expletive] head called Paul Hewson. He’s mental, but he’s good fun.” So even before I went, I’d heard about this character. I guess Bono’s always been that extrovert, exhibitionist performer, and he had that at age 13 already.

You guys have documented your career together in a bunch of different ways: in documentary films, in the “U2 by U2” book, in countless interviews. But are there ways in which your memories and understanding of how you came together has been superseded by the legend and the lore?

Bono: You’re suggesting we are not superheroes? [Laughs] I always saw us in some sort of mythological sense, if I’m honest. The names — think about it. We wished to escape suburbia and discover these other selves, and we gave those other selves names. The Ramones were key for us, and they are really well-drawn characters.

What you just said about coming up with the fictional names — this always killed me about the band. Bono! Edge! And then … Adam and Larry. Was there any discussion that they should have names too?

The Edge: We need to explain the whole name thing. We laughed a lot at that age. We would laugh at each other and ourselves and that was the deal. So the names were not necessarily designed for their heroic aspect. Bono’s very first name was in fact Steinrich Van Haitian Bang Bang Bang, and then I was Inchicore for a while before I became the Edge. Adam for a while was known as Mrs. Byrnes, and Larry for some reason was the Jam Jar. We were borrowing a lot from Monty Python.

Bono: It’s about inventing who you want to be rather than who you were given when you were born at a certain point, place and time.

Bono, when you and I spoke last, around the time of your book, you told me that U2 had been working on the album “Songs of Ascent,” but then thought you needed an album of “unreasonable” guitar music instead. Then I saw somewhere you, Edge, said that the band had been working on an album of “sci-fi Irish folk” with Brian Eno. And yet we’ve arrived at “Carnaval De Luz.” So in a practical way, can you describe when the concept for new music changes? Does Bono show up one day and say: “Guys, we’re scrapping sci-fi Irish folk. We’re doing ‘Carnaval’!”? How does that actually work?

The Edge: Really, the music tells you. As we were working on those projects, it was pure creative experimentation and exploration. There was no deadline, nothing booked or committed to. I had also spent the whole pandemic lockdown just working on music. So we had this beautiful opportunity to create with no agenda and just see where it took us. But what we had decided is that the album should be a countervailing mood to the times. The times are anxious, despondent. People are really a bit lost, and we were like, What is it that we can help with here? And we thought an album that’s a party, a celebration, a sort of bringing people together, a gathering around our common aspirations, would be the thing to do.

Bono: There’s a defiance to this, too. There’s a Dan Savage quote about when he was an AIDS activist in San Francisco in the middle of that crisis. He said: In the morning, we would bury our friends. In the afternoon, we’d go out to protest so we’d have less people to bury. Then, in the evenings, we would go out and dance, because the dance was what we were fighting for. I loved that so much. That is not surrendering to the melancholy. That’s the defiance. Sorry to do this as an Irish person, but again, if you go to the Black church during civil rights, they’re up. Sly and the Family Stone, no minor chords. It’s like, wow, “Dance to the Music.” That’s “Carnaval.” Defiant joy is the thing we were looking for.

Where’s the line between the defiance you’re describing and fiddling while Rome burns?

Bono: What do you think, Nero?

The Edge: Well, one is to be in denial, and one is to be fully aware, to stare darkness in the face and to still choose joy. That’s the difference. I think technology’s a big problem right now. Social media — people are in their heads too much. They’re in their part of the echo chamber of their own algorithm. What’s really important is the reset. We are so much more capable than we are led to believe, and by being isolated and by allowing the wave of negativity to go on unchallenged, people are feeling disempowered and dejected. They don’t understand that they can be part of something great. That’s what’s really positive about rock ’n’ roll shows and festivals. It gives people that sense of agency again.

Bono: Can I just say, rage is part of this. Rage is part of the right response. Anger is OK. To surrender to the melancholy is what we’re trying to avoid.

One could almost think of “Carnaval De Luz” as a protest album, but it’s a protest album without proper nouns. You’re not saying who you’re protesting against or naming anyone explicitly. And I’m thinking of this in the context of some of your peers at the top of the rock ’n’ roll pyramid. Bruce Springsteen was out on the road this year giving speeches railing against Trump and his administration and its policies. On the other side, I spoke to Mick Jagger earlier this year, and I asked him a question about the function of rock stars, and he basically said, Hey, I’m here to help you have a good time. Nobody wants to be lectured. And I wondered if making an album, like you did, of politically galvanizing, defiantly joyful protest music without actually mentioning politics, was your way of trying to walk a middle path there.

Bono: No. It’s picking the fight with the author of all of this mess. I found believing in God — or that God is love — unusually easy in my life. But the concept of evil was tricky for me. It wasn’t as easy to digest. So in the new song “If the World Is at War We Better Not Be,” the line goes:

I wanna speak to the spiritYou can feel it, but you can’t fear itBe ye kings or queens or emperors of despairWe’re not arguing the tossWe got some words for your bossWe’re speaking to who speaks through youTo the prince of the power of the airAll these shimmers and these glimmers, mirrors that must crack, all the neon fizzing flickers, we’re grateful for some of thatThe fiction of a nation, the stories we don’t tellWe need the light of illumination so you can go right back to hellIf the world is at war, we better not be.

That’s what this album’s about. We should be grateful that evil is out in the open. And on [the band’s February EP] “Days of Ash,” we name names. You know, I spoke to Renee Good’s family.

The woman killed by ICE in Minnesota.

Bono: We wrote a song about it a week later, and we had this line, “America will rise up against the people of the lie.” Edge had given me this book 30 years ago by M. Scott Peck called “People of the Lie.” It’s about the nature of evil, and a study of malignant narcissism. Anyway, I was explaining to the family, before we used the lyric, asking them for permission. They’re on Zoom, and when I get to the bit about “America will rise against the people of the lie,” the father said, “I have the book ‘People of the Lie’ right here.” I said, “The book Edge gave me 30 years ago?” He says: “Yeah, it’s right here. Just a month ago, I took it out to explain some of what’s going on to my son.” So with those songs in “Days of Ash,” we did go to names. But for “Carnaval De Luz,” we didn’t want to. There’s a line in the song “Midnight Sunshine” that goes: “Catastrophizing is the glamorizing of the world’s pain. If you don’t want to make a devil bigger, stop repeating his name.” Can I go on here for just a second?

You’ve never stopped before.

Bono: [Laughs] I know. I’m so sorry about that. But if you can separate a discussion about this administration from a discussion about the left and the right and conservatives and liberals, then I’m fine to go ahead with it. Because I think this is the most extraordinary moment. I mean, this is the greatest heist in the history of the world: stealing America. And it’s not a caper movie. It’s real, and it’s happening. I don’t want to put off good people who vote conservative, who vote Republican. Their party’s been hijacked, and it’s an aggressive takeover. I want to invite them back. I want them to return. People vote conservative for all kinds of reasons that are OK. So if we can talk about it without getting to the usual loggerheads — but this is a serious problem and I have serious personal dealings with this because of 25 years of work in development.

That development work has been decimated by DOGE and, by proxy, Elon Musk, and the Trump administration. Do you see evil in that?

Bono: For general clues on evil, look at the abuse of children. That’s always a clue. I don’t know how many fatalities will eventually be attributed to the DOGE cuts. There are many different estimates. If you go to, say, The Lancet, they suggest, I think, up to 2030, maybe five million children under 5. And let’s say they’re half wrong. What Christian household, what Catholic household, what Jewish household, anyone of faith, in fact anyone of conscience, would allow the hemorrhaging of human life that is going to happen as a result of these DOGE cuts? It’s unconscionable.

Well, here’s the test-of-faith question. I was listening just this morning to “Glorify,” and there’s a line that goes, “You spit in my eye, you’re a barefaced lie, and there’s nothing you can do to keep me from loving you.” It’s the idea of having love for your enemies. Do you have love for the people doing the things that you’re calling unconscionable?

Bono: Yeah, I love these people because I believe God loves them and Christianity calls us not only to love our neighbor but to love our enemies. But what’s going on with the man whose name shall not be mentioned is something way bigger than the man. It’s going on all over the world. This greatest heist in the history of the world? It’s the crown jewels. It’s freedom. It’s democracy. It’s like the [expletive] Enlightenment. Anyway, that’s it. Edge is just sitting here looking at me.

Edge, you have had the experience many times of being in situations like this and having Bono field questions of the kind that I’m asking. What is that like for you?

The Edge: I mean, look, we don’t mind getting deep and serious, but you want to keep some balance as well. That is why U2 pivoted so heavily after “Joshua Tree” and “Rattle and Hum” to “Achtung Baby,” because we realized we were being robbed of aspects of who we were. It just wasn’t reflected in the work and therefore in people’s understanding and perception of us. So the thing to remember about us is, yes, we can get very heavy and very deep, but actually we have a lot of fun, and when we’re together working, we laugh a lot and we fail a lot and we’re happy that we’re comfortable with failure. So, yeah, I share a lot of Bono’s views on these things and we feel a responsibility, I suppose, to address what we see going wrong with the world, but you can’t do it incessantly. So on our album we touch on it lightly, and then, as you say, we’re not mentioning names because we don’t want to get into finger wagging. What we want to do is draw attention to something that’s a kind of antidote, something that is better. And I think that’s the way people operate. You tell somebody they shouldn’t do something, it’s going to be a struggle. If you show somebody a better path, they’re going to go there.

So when you’re in the studio with Adam and Larry — you guys have known each other for 50 years — there have got to be things that make the rhythm section look at the front-line guys and go, “This drives me nuts!” What are they?

The Edge: Bands are weird things, let’s be honest. We are brothers in arms, for sure, but we don’t agree on everything by any means. We end up making decisions by consensus because we’ve learned over the years that if we’re arguing about something, there’s a problem. When everybody just goes, “That’s it!” we know we’re onto it. So we do argue, but generally speaking, it’s when something’s not quite right. And then it’s just a difference of opinion, like what road we take. So, yeah, I’m sure I’m very annoying at times.

Bono: I don’t think Edge is — and that’s annoying, by the way — because he’s a person of great reason. I would have the annoying gene the most. But it’s a thing about performers. The same portal that you open up to fit a whole stadium inside is maybe not a portal you can close enough in time to protect yourself from the outside world. You think about stadium-sized egos like myself, and you think about self-aggrandizement and much worse, but what happens is the opposite. It’s the collapse of the ego. Singing itself is a vulnerability if you’re any good.

I was reading the trades, as I do, and I saw an item not that long ago about you guys hiring a woman named Sulinna Ong as part of your management team. She had previously been at Spotify doing global curation. And Jeff Azoff, who manages Harry Styles, is one of your managers now. When U2 starts working with new management, presumably those people make an argument for what their value to you is. So what did they tell you that you didn’t already know about how U2 can find new listeners or move forward at this point in the band’s career?

Bono: You must have had surveillance on us, because just in the last couple of weeks we’ve been sitting around listening to people tell us to do things that we hadn’t thought of. Sulinna said it is almost impossible, the way people live now and listen now in their separate communities, to do something that everyone will be aware of. The amount of advertising you would have to spend, the amount of concerts you would play in every college town or around the world — people still might not know that you’ve put out a new album. So you should turn up in unexpected places. And they were suggesting some of them. Some of them were not things that we would have considered. And we were laughing, the four of us, and going, Are we still going to have to break into the charts? Nothing’s changed since we were kids. We were sitting around with Larry, who doesn’t normally like to do this kind of thing, and I was saying: “Are we ready to go out and meet people that may not know who we are? I’m used to it as an activist, but are we as a band?” I was surprised that all four of us were like, OK, give us another suggestion. Including Larry, who was like: “I’m listening. I’m suspicious, but I’m listening.” I thought that was good. For us, it’s still something we have to prove.

Maybe it feels gauche to get into the specifics, but are they suggesting licensing a song in a show you hadn’t thought of? Are they suggesting you play a pop-up at a Raising Cane’s?

The Edge: That’s a great idea! I’m going to write that down.

Bono: You’re going to get on very well at the corporation. You had some very good ideas during the interview. [Laughs]

The Edge: I think also this album, and where we’re going to take the tour, lends itself to some almost Dada-like opportunities to play around with the absurd, to do some crazy stuff no one was expecting. I’m looking forward to that. It’s hard to surprise yourselves as much as your audience, having done it so many times before.

I’ve always been curious about what your old manager Paul McGuinness said to you after the whole iTunes mess, where you put the then-new album [“Songs of Innocence” (2014)] on people’s iTunes without asking. Paul must have had something to say about that.

Bono: He said pretty much the same thing that Tim Cook said when I pitched him the idea, which is: You spent your whole life getting people to pay for music. Why would you want to give something away for free? I mean, we were experimenting. We wanted to see if we could get Apple or another company to pay for our music and then they distribute it. And look, it’s going to take some experimentation to fix the music [business]. It’s astonishing how little other musicians are paid and it’s frightening. But yeah, that was all on me.

Was it a reputational error for you?

Bono: I went too far on that one.

The Edge: We take risks. We have to. So you fail, you fall on your face at times. That’s part of the gig.

Edge, you alluded to playing live. Are there plans to go on tour next year?

The Edge: There are.

Your tours are always conceptual in some way. What is the new concept?

Bono: Well, the album title’s a clue.

The Edge: We can’t go too much into it because the plans are still forming, but we are interested in this intersection between shamanism and show business. All of the great showmen have, to some extent, to pull off a magic trick, which gets into a mysterious place. And it works both ways: The great politicians of this moment, who unfortunately in a lot of cases are supremely dangerous, are very shamanistic. They are dazzling people with an act. It’s the snake oil salesman aspect. And we’re living in a post-truth era because, unfortunately, there are so many opportunities to put fake narratives out there, and that’s being taken advantage of. Our buttons can easily be pushed, particularly when fear is the weapon that you’re taking advantage of. So we’re exploring these things in a good way and a bad way. The lyric of the song “Silencio” [from “Carnaval De Luz”] encapsulates those two extremes. The two types of silence. Contemplative, meditative, reflective silence is a beautiful thing. But the other kind of silence is when you are cowed and you’re afraid to speak because if you say the wrong thing, you will be punished, you might go to jail, you’ll be ostracized, and that’s super dangerous.

Bono: There’s a poem by Michael Leunig. [Pulls out his phone to read the poem] “There are only two feelings, love and fear. There are only two languages, love and fear. There are only two activities, love and fear. There are only two motives, two procedures, two frameworks, two results, love and fear. Love and fear.” There’s a lot of love at our shows, and it’s not an “up with people,” “let’s all give each other a hug” type of love. I think there’s a level of depth at a U2 show where people who genuinely don’t normally agree with each other’s politics feel safe. I’m very proud of that. If they’re in America, we want people to feel really good about their choice to probably pay too much to see us. But we are going to challenge them.

Presumably you have some say in the ticket prices.

Bono: Well, the whole problem with the live business is, very little. But what we do in our band is we take the best seats in the house and make sure that they’re often the most affordable. We also have no problem separating rich people from their money.

Let me wrap up with a holistic question. Even just in the course of this conversation, it’s obvious that U2 thinks about the story that we’re all living in and what the band can offer to that story. But you’ve been around for 50 years. This doesn’t go on forever. So where is U2 in its own story right now, and do you have some sense of how you want that story to end?

The Edge: We’re still creatively extremely inspired and active, and there are lots of songs that have yet to be released, yet to be finished. So I can’t see that ending anytime soon.

Bono: Edge, I think he might be interested in your speech to the band the other day about if you had to find another band.

The Edge: That’s the other thing about why I’m still in U2. Occasionally early on I would think, This is too difficult, I should really get out of this band, and I would start the inner dialogue. [Talking to himself] “So, what do you want to do with your life?” And I would say, “Well, I’m a creative person, and music is kind of my main thing, so I’d stay in music.” “OK, do you want to sing?” And I’m like: “I really don’t want to be the singer. I’m happy being a guitar player.” “So who’s the singer you most like to work with?” And I’d be like, “Well, clearly Bono.” So, OK, I’ll be doing a solo thing but Bono will be the singer. So then, “What’s the best rhythm section for you guys?” I’d be like, “That’s Adam and Larry, isn’t it?” OK, so it’s going to be a solo band with Bono on vocals, I’ll be the guitar player, and Adam and Larry will be the rhythm section. I basically would redesign U2. So yeah, there’s no doubt about it. This is where I belong.

Bono: More likely, I think, is that people tire of you and that we tire of going the distance to meet them, resulting in them tiring of you. I think if we keep playing live till we drop, there will always be people. But we have one problem in this regard, which is that we pledged to each other when we were 18, 17, 16, that we would never, ever walk onto a stage without it being everything. We haven’t betrayed that yet. We’ve had fistfights onstage, we’ve had them backstage, we’ve had madness, but we’ve never betrayed that.

The Edge: Yeah, it never was entertainment to us, ever. It was always something with a lot more importance and meaning. Some of the early shows we saw were the Clash on their first tour, the Buzzcocks, the Jam and Talking Heads. So when you’re around that kind of sense of urgency and the ideological aspect, it’s like you can’t take this stuff lightly. It’s way more than just entertainment.

Bono: It’s the thing they say about football: It’s not a matter of life and death. It’s something much more serious than that.

This interview has been edited and condensed. Listen to and follow “The Interview” on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, iHeartRadio or Amazon Music. Follow us on Instagram and TikTok.

Director of photography (video): Benjamin Breading

As an aging GenXer, it was humbling to learn U2 just turned 50. It’s a big reason I was so eager to hear my colleague David Marchese interview Bono and The Edge about how the band views its future and strives to stay relevant. (Stars: They’re just like us! — a reference only old people will get, I know.) I loved watching these lifelong friends and collaborators tackle David’s questions, bounce ideas off each other, and still genuinely crack each other up.

David Marchese is a writer and co-host of The Interview, a regular series featuring influential people across culture, politics, business, sports and beyond.

This Is One of the Saddest Facts About the Cornell Rape Case

The New York Times October 17, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Emily Bazelon

Ms. Bazelon is a staff writer at The Times Magazine and in Times Opinion.

One of the saddest facts about the alleged sexual assault rocking Cornell is the departure from campus of the young woman at the center of it, known as Jane Doe. She left school some time after she reported that she was raped at a fraternity party in October 2024, when she was a 20-year-old sophomore.

In the two decades I’ve been writing about campus sexual assault, it has been all too common for students to drop out of school after experiencing or reporting such an assault. It’s one reason that at various points I’ve questioned requiring schools to investigate sexual assault based on Title IX, the statute that prohibits sex-based discrimination in federally funded education. Are universities really equipped to do this? Students who make accusations often come away unsatisfied with the process or the outcome, and students who are the subjects of those accusations often complain of being railroaded.

But cases like this one lead me to conclude that, for all its flaws, Title IX and the disciplinary procedures it requires colleges to undertake are necessary. Without them, allegations like Jane Doe’s would be entirely in the hands of police and prosecutors to address, and that option is often worse. A mountain of evidence over the years shows how the criminal justice system struggles to address sexual assault effectively and fairly — or doesn’t really try at all, as in the Cornell case. Title IX fills a void: If sexual misconduct prevents a victim from taking full advantage of her education, then the institution has to address it. That responsibility is an awkward fit in some ways, but it reflects the reality that colleges are not just classrooms; they are a very particular kind of community in which all members have a duty of care toward one another. The Cornell case shows how hard it can be for universities to enforce Title IX well and also why they have to keep trying.

Congress enacted Title IX in 1972. Twenty years later, the Supreme Court ruled that students whose Title IX rights were violated could sue for compensation. I was in college then. I remember going to Take Back the Night marches, hearing women’s stories of what we called date rape and not imagining the university would do anything about it.

The civil rights office of the federal Department of Education has long instructed schools to establish a grievance procedure for students who said they were assaulted and harassed. But people who made reports often found themselves brushed off. In 2009, the Center for Public Integrity investigated Title IX discipline nationally and found that many campus processes were slow, confusing and secretive, and often resulted in little or no punishment. Survivors organized to demand more from schools. They wanted accountability for perpetrators, and they wanted services like counseling and academic accommodations.

The Obama administration stepped in on behalf of victims. By 2014, the Office for Civil Rights in the Department of Education was investigating 55 colleges and universities over their handling of sexual misconduct complaints. The department also issued new guidance, discouraging schools from allowing accused students to directly question their accusers, a process the office said could be traumatizing or intimidating, and emphasized that schools should use a lower standard of proof for finding an accused student “responsible,” the term schools use to mean guilt. Universities hired more staff for Title IX investigations and support services. They started operating what amounted to sex crimes units.

Was there less rape and more justice? I couldn’t tell. In surveys, students continued to report high rates of assault. And the cases that captured public attention presented dueling narratives of injustice. In November 2014, Rolling Stone published a false story of gang rape at a fraternity at the University of Virginia, showing that the press could rush to judgment without verifying the facts.

Two months later, a Stanford student named Brock Turner drew public outrage over what men still apparently thought they could get away with on campus. Mr. Turner had been found on top of an unconscious woman after they’d each been drinking at a party. Prosecutors brought criminal charges, and he was tried and convicted. But the judge sentenced him to only six months in jail.

The Turner case was not, though, a failure of Title IX enforcement. Within two weeks of the assault, Stanford had investigated the allegations and barred Mr. Turner from campus. He withdrew before he could be expelled.

In May 2015, I wrote about a Title IX investigation at Columbia University that split the public in ways that are similar to the Jane Doe case. When Emma Sulkowicz reported that her fellow undergraduate Paul Nungesser raped her, the university investigated and found he was not responsible for assault — in other words, not guilty. Columbia also gave Ms. Sulkowicz credit in an art course for a monthslong performance project in which she carried a mattress around campus to symbolize her trauma. Her performance art made her a symbol of the wronged survivor. Mr. Nungesser, however, argued that he was the victim, and sued Columbia for gender discrimination.

Lots of people saw the Columbia case in black and white, as either a rape or a lie. But talking to Ms. Sulkowicz, Mr. Nungesser and other students filled me only with uncertainty. I couldn’t even settle the factual disputes about what had happened during Columbia’s Title IX process, because those proceedings were confidential.

It’s true that student privacy laws limit the information schools can disclose, but schools sometimes have gone further than the law requires. The lack of information about the conclusions they reach, and why, breeds mistrust — as we are seeing again at Cornell.

Also in the mid-2010s, feminists, some of whom were the mothers of college-aged children, started dividing over what Title IX had become. Some thought the Obama administration’s rules were pushing schools to railroad accused students, who were almost always men. Others believed that women were still being shortchanged. I wrote about that debate. As frustrations mounted, critics on the right and left called for sidelining or abandoning campus investigations, and instead requiring schools to report accusations of sexual assault to the police. Despite often being among the biggest critics of the universities, survivors and their supporters resisted. They argued that forcing students to go to law enforcement would make them less likely to report assaults at all, eliminating a mechanism with which to hold perpetrators accountable and to provide survivors with accommodations and mental health services. “The fact that two institutions” — universities and the police — “mistreat survivors is not an argument for forcing students to choose between reporting to both or to neither,” argued Alexandra Brodsky, a co-founder of the advocacy group Know Your IX.

More recently, the first Trump administration, saying the Title IX process had become unfair to accused students, rolled back some of the Obama-era guidance. The new standards allow schools to use a higher standard of proof for a finding of responsibility and require live hearings with the opportunity for cross-examination.

When Jane Doe filed a lawsuit against Cornell in September, the university became the target of outrage and protest. One of the complaints was about Cornell’s lack of transparency in the two years since the alleged assault took place. In the wake of the suit, many facts have spilled out. Hundreds of pages of the university’s investigation in 2024 and 2025 have been disclosed to The Times and other news outlets. But I don’t think we know enough to fully judge Cornell’s response.

Here’s what stands out to me in the record. As in many cases like this one, the judgment of the students involved was clouded by drugs and alcohol. In her interview with a Cornell police officer and a Title IX investigator in November 2024, three weeks after the alleged assault, Jane Doe says she drank a lot over three hours at her sorority and a bar before walking to a party at the Chi Phi fraternity to meet a frat brother she was interested in, Matthew Ingalls. After they danced, Mr. Ingalls asked her to have a three-way with him and another fraternity brother, Jonathan Newell. Jane Doe said yes. The three students went upstairs to a shared bedroom and social space called the alumni room. The men drank and snorted ketamine. Jane Doe said she had ketamine and alcohol, too.

The night took a much more extreme turn at 1:42 a. m. That’s when Mr. Newell sent a message on Snapchat to dozens of Chi Phi brothers advertising “free pussy” in the alumni room. As men began responding, Mr. Ingalls wrote, “Like you can walk in and whip it out.”

The Snapchat exchange was grotesquely dehumanizing. Jane Doe didn’t know about it. She didn’t understand that Mr. Newell and Mr. Ingalls had apparently set her up as a group of men entered the alumni room. In her lawsuit, she says she was incapacitated by alcohol and ketamine. I think it’s equally important that she did not know she was essentially being prostituted on Snapchat — 53 minutes after Mr. Newell’s message, one man on the thread asked, “shop still open?”

Afterward, when Jane Doe heard that frat brothers were bragging about an “eightsome,” she was shattered. “My reputation is destroyed and i’m utterly ashamed,” she wrote to Mr. Ingalls. “All i do is sleep and cry all day.” When she heard rumors about the Snapchat messages, she asked the investigators to subpoena them.

There’s one more dark part of this story that matters for assessing the institutional response. After leaving the alumni room, Jane Doe went to a small room with Mr. Ingalls and another fraternity member, Winston Lee. Jane Doe said that they asked her for another three-way. She told the investigators she said she was too tired and didn’t have it in her. The men had sex with her anyway. “I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped,” she said.

Is Jane Doe’s account enough to press rape charges in the criminal justice system? Aspects of it make the case difficult to prosecute. That does not, however, prevent a district attorney from asking a grand jury for an indictment. At the least, these facts should have triggered a serious criminal investigation. But the Cornell police officer left Jane Doe’s definitive statement about being raped out of the six-page summary that was given to the county’s district attorney, Matthew Van Houten. Prosecutors took no action. After the lawsuit was filed in September, Mr. Van Houten said Jane Doe’s statement “described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual.” That’s not what she told the police, and it shows why survivors have so little faith in local law enforcement. Early this month, Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed the New York attorney general, Letitia James, as a special prosecutor in the case. Two of the accused men have asked the judge to remove Ms. James because before her appointment, she issued a statement expressing sympathy for Jane Doe.

In contrast to the district attorney, Cornell took significant action. The university closed Chi Phi in November 2024, and put the students Jane Doe had accused on interim suspensions, according to the lawsuit. Over the next few months, Cornell investigators conducted over 50 interviews and collected evidence, including the Snapchat messages and dozens of texts among students.

In May 2025, a disciplinary panel at Cornell met over 12 days to review the evidence against the seven men, all of whom denied any wrongdoing. Based on the panel’s findings, Mr. Ingalls and Mr. Newell were expelled, Mr. Lee was suspended for two years and a fourth student who Jane Doe said had nonconsensual sex with her in the alumni room was suspended for three semesters. The other three men received relatively light punishments. (One had already graduated, and two played lesser roles, though they did go to the alumni room after receiving the Snapchat invitation and participate in the messaging rather than expressing concern about it.)

In her lawsuit, Jane Doe said the penalties were insufficient. In the record, the reasons for the panel’s findings are heavily redacted, which means that, once again, a secretive process makes it hard to evaluate a university’s decision-making in an explosive case. Cornell has named a former acting U. S. attorney general, Sally Yates, to lead an independent review of its response. Whatever Ms. Yates finds, I hope she makes the information public in a way that allows us all to assess comprehensively the outcomes Cornell reached, and allows other schools to learn from this disastrous case. This week, the university said it would work with trauma-informed investigators from the state police and suspended frat parties for the rest of the academic year, a step toward prevention — another facet of Title IX.

In a case like this, publicity is its own form of punishment. “I’m being labelled as an assaulter in the public eye,” Matthew Ingalls texted Jane Doe in the days after the frat party. Because of Title IX, Cornell found that he deserved the label. That’s some form, at least, of deterrence.

This case is hard to write about — it is so contested and emotions are running high. I wanted to separate the role of universities from the role of police and prosecutors. Why do universities investigate sexual assault and what would students lose if they stopped?

Emily Bazelon is a staff writer at The New York Times Magazine. @emilybazelon • Facebook

How Pennsylvania Explains the Forces Shaping the Midterms

The New York Times October 17, 2026

Rachel Wisniewski for The New York Times

To see the dynamics shaping the midterms, look no further than Pennsylvania.

Trump and Republicans dominated this quintessential swing state in 2024.

But this year, Pennsylvania offers clues for how House Democrats might run up the score — and how they might not.

Supported by

Four battleground congressional districts in the state reveal fault lines that are echoing nationwide.

By Shane Goldmacher

Shane Goldmacher interviewed seven congressional candidates in battleground districts and reported from Allentown, Bethlehem, Green Lane, Hazleton, Langhorne and Nazareth, Pa.

No single state in America better captures the forces and fault lines shaping the coming midterm elections than Pennsylvania.

Just two years ago, Pennsylvania was at the epicenter of a nationwide Republican revival. President Trump swept its electoral votes. His party ousted an entrenched Democratic senator. And it was the only state where Republicans flipped two House seats.

Now the pendulum has swung. Mr. Trump’s support has crumbled. And Democrats are targeting four bellwether House districts in the state that together would give them the congressional majority.

What makes Pennsylvania so revealing is how emblematic those races are of the candidates, issues and demographic shifts that will determine outcomes across the country.

A Republican is clinging to power in sprawling suburbs that have otherwise turned blue. Democrats are trying to reclaim fast-growing Hispanic areas that swung to the right two years ago. White, working-class voters in aging industrial towns and rural areas have lost patience with the president’s promises.

“Pennsylvania runs the whole gamut of the midterms in four races,” said Jesse Ferguson, a national Democratic strategist involved in House elections. “If Democrats can win every kind of fight there, there is no district safe for Republicans in this moment.”

One race features the House’s most outspoken moderate Republican; another includes the former leader of the hard-right House Freedom Caucus. Stock trading and corruption is a recurring theme in advertising. Accusations of socialism are flying.

Yet for all the differences between these districts, there is a commonality to the G. O. P.’s troubles.

His name is Donald J. Trump.

The president’s approval rating had dwindled to 34 percent in the most recent Times/Inquirer/Siena poll of Pennsylvania voters. Three-quarters of voters disapprove of his handling of the cost of living.

Manpower and money are pouring into the state. More than $105 million in advertising on broadcast, cable and streaming is blanketing screens of all sizes in those four districts.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader, kicked off his 100-day sprint to the speakership in Pennsylvania over the summer. He returned last weekend for a rally in one district and made appearances in Black churches in another. A few days earlier, the man whose job he is trying to take, Speaker Mike Johnson, blitzed through the state’s battlegrounds in a single day on behalf of all four Republican incumbents.

Polls show that Democrats are heavily favored to flip the House. What the size of that majority, and its shape and direction, are likely to depend on are the results in places like Pennsylvania.

A flip in all four would signal a Democratic wave; a flip in none would represent an unexpected Republican revival.

Here’s a closer look at each of those races and what they tell us about what might happen on Nov. 3.

With his dismal approval rating, Mr. Trump appears to be a drag for Republicans across Pennsylvania. But in no race does his unpopularity loom larger than in Pennsylvania’s First District, on the outskirts of Philadelphia.

The district voted against Mr. Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024. Yet each time Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a moderate Republican, managed to win anyway — the only member of Congress in his party to do so.

On paper, the suburban seat should be the easiest to flip of the four top battlegrounds. In reality, strategists in both parties say it is the toughest — because of Mr. Fitzpatrick’s unique staying power. He is a moderate Republican who counts the support of typically big Democratic organizations, including labor unions and some big environmental groups.

Mr. Fitzpatrick for years has been something of a white whale for national Democrats. But party officials believe the combination of Mr. Trump’s lowly standing and the popularity of the Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, has opened a door of opportunity. Mr. Shapiro had a 60 percent approval rating in the same Times/Inquirer/Siena poll.

Mr. Fitzpatrick’s Democratic challenger in 2026, Bob Harvie, told a crowd of Democratic activists earlier this month in Green Lane, a small borough in suburban Montgomery County, that he hopes to be swept into office with a Shapiro blowout.

“All of us who are running are going to be clutching both hands, white knuckles, onto those Josh Shapiro coattails,” Mr. Harvie said in a speech. “Because they’re going to take us somewhere.”

Mr. Shapiro has endorsed Mr. Harvie. He has appeared at events with him over two consecutive weekends. But he notably did not mention Mr. Fitzpatrick’s name in either, instead speaking narrowly about the implications of the race for congressional control.

“Not a coincidence,” Mr. Fitzpatrick said over coffee at a diner two days after the first event.

Mr. Fitzpatrick, who has not endorsed the Republican running for governor, called Mr. Shapiro a “friend.” He invited him to his wedding over the summer, though Mr. Shapiro did not attend. “He sent a lovely note,” Mr. Fitzpatrick said.

National Democrats recently started using images of Mr. Fitzpatrick, in black tie, toasting at his wedding in attack ads.

“I respect whatever Josh does, and I want him to do well,” Mr. Fitzpatrick said. “And he knows that.”

If Pennsylvania is a swing state, then Northampton, nestled in the Lehigh Valley along the New Jersey border, is one of its swingiest counties. Northampton has alternated between the two parties in every presidential election since 2012, voting with the winner each time: Obama, Trump, Biden, Trump.

Most recently, in 2024, Representative Ryan Mackenzie ousted a Democrat on the strength of a Republican resurgence in Allentown, which is majority Hispanic and the district’s biggest city. Some of its more diverse precincts swung 20 percentage points or more in that year’s presidential race. After he won, Mr. Mackenzie said he hired a Spanish-language outreach coordinator on “day one” for his congressional office.

Victor Martinez, the host of a popular Spanish-language radio show in the Lehigh Valley, had warned Democrats in 2024 about Mr. Trump’s rising appeal. This year, he said, local Republicans should brace for a Hispanic revolt.

“Here we are two years later and the sentiment is, ‘Wait a minute, it got worse!’” Mr. Martinez said of Latinos who gave Mr. Trump a chance on the economy. “Gas is more expensive! Groceries are even more expensive! Electricity is more expensive!”

Bob Brooks, his Democratic challenger and a union leader for firefighters, has his own Hispanic outreach effort. It is branded “Bombero Bob” — Spanish for firefighter — though he said the Latino community’s concerns are largely the same as those of the union members he represents.

“They have the same problems as everybody else,” he said. “They feel lied to.”

Today, the seat is generally seen as one of the most likely of the four to flip.

As Mr. Mackenzie took a seat inside the lodge of the Fraternal Order of Police in Bethlehem last week, he set out to make the case for why, as a freshman Republican he, might buck both parties’ history of midterm losses.

Just down the road, a billboard yoked Mr. Mackenzie to the president. But Mr. Mackenzie bragged about solving 10,000 constituent cases and securing federal funding for a firehouse in Alburtis and an upgraded emergency communications system in Carbon County. “It’s not just about the climate,” Mr. Mackenzie insisted. “It’s much more about individual candidates.”

Yet even some supporters fear the opposite.

“Unfortunately, I think people aren’t voting for the individuals,” said Lucy Lennon, 63, who owns a real estate company in Bethlehem, and came to a recent Mackenzie event. “They’re voting party. And there is some backlash on the Republican Party, for whatever reason.”

Just to the north, Pennsylvania’s Eighth District has become a national symbol of the Democratic Party’s steady decline in the Trump era among blue-collar workers. Centered around the city of Scranton, voters in the district knocked off a longtime Democratic incumbent in 2024 in favor of a Republican, Rob Bresnahan.

Mr. Bresnahan’s re-election campaign has been shaped by some of the same issues dominating races across America: congressional stock trading and grocery prices.

In 2025, Mr. Bresnahan emerged as one of the most prolific stock traders of that year’s congressional freshman class, after campaigning against the practice the year before.

In an interview, he said he explored putting his assets in a blind trust, but he concluded that it was unworkable. He said his financial advisers made trades independently. His individual stock trading has slowed, if not stopped entirely, since all the attention.

“The whole message that they’ve been running against me is over my stock trading,” Mr. Bresnahan said in an interview after a rally in a warehouse in Hazelton, denying he oversaw his own trades.

Accusations of insider trading among members of Congress have flooded races nationwide. In the Eighth District, Paige Cognetti, the mayor of Scranton and Mr. Bresnahan’s Democratic challenger, has made it a centerpiece.

She has also linked it to affordability, another major issue on voters’ minds.

“There is a clear line now between corruption and costs,” she said in an interview.

Democrats are trying to make this connection for voters all across the country.

Ms. Cognetti recorded a commercial recently in her husband’s grocery store, lashing prices and stock trading in the same spot. “Making that bread for themselves,” she said of Congress as she smushed a loaf of bread, “while the middle class gets squeezed out.”

Mr. Trump has carried the district all three times he has been on the ballot, so Ms. Cognetti is trying to run as a different kind of Democrat. She is leveraging past skirmishes with local Democrats and using the catchy tagline “Paige Against the Machine” from her mayoral run.

“There’s certainly frustration about the cost of groceries and the kitchen table issues,” Mr. Bresnahan acknowledged. He said his grandmother calls him almost daily to talk about rising prices.

“I’m asking for another chance to continue to move that ball,” he added.

Yet Mr. Trump still boasts a potent base in the region.

Dwayne McDavitt, a founder of Bikers for Trump Pennsylvania, came out to see Mr. Bresnahan at a rally with Mr. Johnson, the House speaker, at a warehouse in Hazleton. He said with disdain that the Democrats had only one message this year.

“What they’re running on,” he said, “is hating Trump.”

Two years ago, Janelle Stelson, a former television newscaster, lost Pennsylvania’s 10th Congressional District to Representative Scott Perry, a Republican, by just over 1 percentage point.

In an interview, Ms. Stelson, a Democrat, described the central Pennsylvania region she hopes to represent as Republican, but she said Mr. Perry, the former chairman of the House Freedom Caucus, was too far right even for the 10th District.

“The most extreme of the extremes,” she said.

In her rematch, Ms. Stelson has run ads embracing parts of Mr. Trump’s agenda, such as cutting taxes on tips and overtime.

Republicans have tried to cast her as a “smooth talker” and hammered her as “too liberal for Pennsylvania,” comparing her to socialists and progressives in their ads: former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of California, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York, Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont.

Yet even in a district that Mr. Trump carried, Democratic groups have run ads urging Mr. Perry, a staunch Trump ally, to “stop voting with Trump” — a potential sign that politics are shifting even there.

“He has been a very willing acolyte for the president and we have seen the president’s poll numbers drop precipitously,” Ms. Stelson said. “You can’t stand up for somebody like that all the time and expect that you’re not going to be affected.”

Mr. Perry’s campaign did not make him available for an interview.

In recent days, the Trump administration further jolted the race. The Department of Homeland Security announced the arrest last week of a Nigerian man on charges of indecent exposure — and included in its announcement a scathing political attack on the Stelson campaign, alleging that he had worked for her.

“It’s unbelievable that Janelle Stelson would employ an illegal alien,” Charles Wall, deputy director of I. C. E., said in the news release.

The Stelson campaign said it wasn’t true. The man had neither worked for nor volunteered for the campaign or its vendors, the campaign said.

According to a police report, law enforcement found fliers for Ms. Stelson in the suspect’s vehicle. A watchdog group has since called for an investigation into whether the Department of Homeland Security had improperly engaged in partisan politics.

Meanwhile, on his recent swing through Bethlehem and Nazareth, Mr. Johnson noted that it was his seventh visit to that district — more than any other swing seat in America.

“The entire country is watching,” Mr. Johnson said, “what happens in about four districts of Pennsylvania.”

Shane Goldmacher is a Times national political correspondent.

Corporate Tax Revenue Falls Even as Profits Soar Under Trump

The New York Times October 17, 2026

U. S. Economy

Advertisement

Supported by

The annual decline was about $70 billion. Companies are writing off billions in A. I. investments, taking advantage of tax cuts that President Trump signed into law.

By Andrew Duehren

Reporting from Washington

Corporate tax revenue has fallen precipitously under President Trump even as companies’ profits have surged to record highs, a divergence that began after Republicans approved tax breaks allowing firms to write off the cost of their investments more quickly.

Revenue from the corporate income tax, which applies to the profits made by the largest and most sophisticated companies in the United States, fell roughly 15 percent, to $381 billion, in the fiscal year that ended on Oct. 1, according to data released on Friday by the Treasury Department. The roughly $70 billion drop followed a similar decline the previous year. Corporate tax revenue is down more than quarter from 2024, the last full fiscal year of the Biden administration.

Note: Data is for fiscal years, which begin in October.

Source: Treasury Department.

Andy Duehren/The New York Times

Note: Data is adjusted for seasonality at annual rates, as well as inventory valuation and capital consumption

Source: Bureau of Economic Analysis, via the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

Andy Duehren/The New York Times

Behind the decrease are the tax cuts that Republicans passed and Mr. Trump signed last year. That law lets companies claim larger deductions in the year they make new investments, a change made as many of the country’s largest technology firms began pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into artificial intelligence projects, including data centers.

The cuts have reduced corporate tax revenue even more sharply than analysts projected. Company leaders, locked in a frenzied race to build more powerful A. I. models, have said they plan to keep increasing their investment spending, potentially depressing corporate tax revenue for years to come. The additional investment may also supercharge firms’ profits, enlarging the gap with the taxes collected from those earnings.

“It’s very unusual to see a divergence of that magnitude, but it’s not surprising in the sense that we know what’s causing it,” said Peter Berezin, the chief economist at BCA Research, an investment research firm. “A. I. spending is projected to increase for the next few years, so these companies will be able to write off even more of their spending. If they didn’t have huge profits, that would be one thing. But they do.”

The fall in corporate tax revenue is just part of the deterioration in the nation’s fiscal situation. The difference between government spending and revenue neared $2 trillion last fiscal year, as military spending increased and higher interest rates raised the cost of payments on the federal debt. The debt held by the public, more than $32 trillion, is now nearly equivalent to the annual output of the economy, a level not seen since the years after World War II.

The deficit is growing even though the economy remains relatively strong and unemployment low. Corporate profits have only swelled in recent years, powering stock indexes to record highs, a development that might be expected to increase corporate tax receipts. Revenue from the individual income tax grew last fiscal year.

But in their tax cut, Republicans made a series of changes allowing companies to reduce the amount of earnings subject to tax. They changed the timeline over which companies can write off the cost of new investments, as well as research and development costs. Rather than deducting the cost of new computing equipment over several years, for example, companies can now write it off immediately.

Businesses aggressively lobbied Congress for this seemingly minor accounting tweak because it improves the economics of new investment. Academic researchers found that the tax break, when previously in place, did help generate additional investment, which can help power the economy overall.

That was before the competition to dominate A. I. technology unleashed hundreds of billions of dollars in spending on chips, data centers and the electrical systems that power them. Major companies like Microsoft, Google and Meta appear so committed to sharply increasing their investment that the tax break may not be having much of an effect on their plans.

“These companies’ leaders aren’t really acting as if they’re feeling constrained in their investment behavior right now,” said Matt Gardner, a senior fellow at the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a liberal think tank. “It seems pretty uncontroversial to say that we are rewarding these companies for what they were going to do anyway.”

The tax break applies to investment spending broadly, not just to data centers and other A. I.-related expenses. While the tax change could encourage additional business investment in other sectors, the A. I. rush is so significant that it may be crowding out other capital expenditures. Financing the build-out of A. I. infrastructure has helped push up interest rates, making borrowing for new investments more expensive across the economy, while the prices of other business inputs have also increased.

“It looks like we are at a point for the macroeconomy of having about as much investment as we can,” said Gabriel Chodorow-Reich, a Harvard economics professor who co-wrote a paper finding that the tax break helped increase investment. “In that circumstance, increasing the marginal incentive to do investment may end up ultimately increasing the price of investment, rather than producing more total investment.”

On the campaign trail, some Democrats have started to attack Republicans for voting to approve the tax break, painting it as subsidy exclusively for data centers. Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, has proposed excluding components for data centers from the investment incentive.

That has worried proponents of the tax incentive, which has historically enjoyed a measure of bipartisan support. They argue that the accelerated write-offs will, over a longer time frame, still spur additional business investment. The drop in tax revenue should be temporary, they said, as companies exhaust the deductions they can claim on their investments.

“To the extent that we think this investment is occurring because there are very large profits to be had, when those profits are had, they will be taxed, and that’s how we should want the tax system to work,” said Erica York, a senior economist at the Tax Foundation, a think tank that generally supports lower taxes.

But the government’s payday may be years away if the A. I. investment cycle continues unabated. One economist, Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh at Columbia University, has estimated that total spending on A. I. infrastructure between 2025 and 2032 will exceed $10 trillion.

Then there is the question of whether the A. I. investments will actually become profitable.

“If we realize data processing is a commodity, and we can have open-source models that charge way, way less, then there’s a big bubble and the whole thing bursts,” said Jeff Hoopes, a professor of accounting at the University of North Carolina.

“You end up not generating as much revenue,” he said, adding that the revenue would not have materialized in that case under the previous tax approach, either.

The decline in corporate tax revenue is an early indicator of how A. I. could reshape the tax system. As companies and investors profit off A. I., those earnings would, under current law, face lower tax rates than the wages paid to workers, who may also be displaced by the technology. That could, in the long run, curb tax revenue overall.

On Wall Street, excitement about A. I. is tempered by concerns about the deficit. Beyond the tax cuts passed through Congress, the Trump administration has taken several regulatory steps that could reduce tax payments for companies, including by weakening a measure aimed at limiting corporate tax avoidance.

David Kelly, the chief global strategist at J. P. Morgan Asset Management, said the economy didn’t need the business tax breaks that Republicans passed last year.

“If you’ve just drunk five cups of coffee, a sixth cup of coffee isn’t going to do you much good,” he said. “You’re stimulating something that doesn’t need stimulating.”

Andrew Duehren covers tax policy for The Times from Washington.

Trump Aides Admit the House Is a Lost Cause

Wired October 14, 2026

Trump White House aides see almost no paths to Republicans keeping control of the House in the midterm elections and are more focused on redoubling their efforts to save the Senate majority.

That has been the takeaway for officials in GOP groups who have been discussing the state of play with White House aides in recent weeks, according to three sources familiar with the situation.

It all comes as the White House moves into damage-control mode after contemplating for the first time earlier this month, as Inner Loop previously reported, that Republicans could possibly lose both chambers of Congress.

The general expectation is that the House has become a lost cause. Races that Republican congressional leadership once thought they could flip in order to offset Democratic gains are no longer considered attainable.

The Congressional Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Speaker Mike Johnson, has now pulled ad buys in Democratic districts in Michigan and Ohio they were hoping to flip, as well as in the Republican seat being vacated in Nebraska by the retiring Don Bacon. The fund also started canceling remaining ad reservations in two House races where Republicans are seeking reelection in New Jersey and Iowa.

White House aides have shifted their focus to pushing an all-out defense of the Senate majority, which is also looking problematic but to a lesser degree than the House, the sources say. (Polling models and prediction markets agree.)

The aides see the Senate as still in play in large part because early returns for mail ballots have been relatively strong and comparable to 2024 presidential election levels in key Senate battleground states, sources say.

Trump officials at MAGA Inc. have also privately discussed how if Republicans can win some combination of senate seats in Alaska, Iowa, and Ohio, that would form a firewall that complicates Democrats' path to snatching control of the Senate.

Still, Trump officials appear to have conceded they are unlikely to win in North Carolina. Senate Republicans’ campaign arm has paused ad spending in North Carolina since the start of October, mirroring pullbacks by other outside groups.

“President Trump is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in both the House and Senate,” says White House spokesperson Liz Huston in a statement.

The state of play—retreating from a state like North Carolina, where Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chair is on the ballot—would have been unthinkable just a few months ago.

But it speaks to the torrid political climate for Republicans heading into the last stretch of the midterm cycle, which appears to worsen by the week as high gas and living prices caused by the Iran war remain sticky in voters' minds.

With 20 days until the election, sources say, Trump officials are looking to get maximum turnout from the MAGA base in November, rather than trying to capture swing voters who polls show are not breaking for Republicans.

"Republicans remain laser focused on winning and protecting and expanding President Trump's majorities,” says Republican National Committee spokesperson Natalie Baldassare in a statement. “We're thinking outside the box to fight the typical midterm precedent.”

The effort has manifested in a direct voter outreach play with the president crisscrossing the country to reach out directly to his supporters, showing up at rallies in states that should have been reliably Republican.

Trump started the week by hitting the trail in Ohio, where Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown has been polling consistently ahead of Republican Jon Husted, who has weathered negative ads branding him as "the face of data centers."

On Tuesday, the president flew to Wasilla, Alaska—once the home of former governor and vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin—to help the Republican Senate incumbent Dan Sullivan, who has been trailing Democrat Mary Peltola.

And after stumping in Arizona and Kentucky later this week, Trump is set to host a $1 million-per-plate fundraiser dinner for MAGA Inc. at his Mar-a-Lago club, replenishing a war chest that is being emptied at an increasing rate.

Trump has remained steadfast in his belief that he can drive his supporters to vote in November if he hits the trail, as he did in the 2016 and 2024 presidential elections, a person familiar with his thinking tells Inner Loop.

But Trump, whose polling continues to be among the worst on record for any president, is not always wanted at rallies. To date, the president has not done a rally in Iowa with Republican candidate Ashley Hinson, who recently began to buck the president and called for measures that would help end the Iran war altogether.

AI Came for Math. Now It’s Chasing the Rest of Science

Wired October 14, 2026

Last week, I attended a talk at MIT by Neil Thompson, who studies progress in computing and artificial intelligence. Over the course of just half an hour, Thompson made a convincing case that several scientific fields are about to be upended by AI.

As mathematicians reel from the way AI is automating their field, Thompson’s latest study suggests that probability, statistics theory, economic theory, high-energy theory, gravitation and cosmology, and quantum physics may be next, thanks to the rapidly evolving capabilities of frontier models. Between mid-2024 and mid-2026, the study shows, the best AI models went from being able to correctly solve about 2 percent of theoretical problems in these fields to about 35 percent of such problems. And there are no signs that this progress will slow down.

“Within just a few years, we expect a lot of theory questions to be totally transformed in terms of AI's ability to do them,” says Thompson.

Broadly, Thompson’s lab digs into how advances in computer science impact society and affect innovation. This study—which Thompson conducted alongside Gabriel Manso, a PhD student, and Claudio Mayrink Verdun, a research scientist—took problems stated in research papers posted online between December 2025 and May 2026, and then tested whether different OpenAI models—o1, o3, GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.5—could solve them.

Crucially, solutions to these problems were found in papers published after the training cutoff for GPT-5.5 and preceding models. This means that the models they tested had to work out solutions for themselves, rather than relying on answers fed in as training data. (Such papers served as ground truth for testing the models’ solving skills.) The researchers also blocked internet access, which prevented the models they tested from looking up solutions online.

The areas covered by the study were limited—the trio focused on fields in which AI models could figure things out without needing to run simulations or experiments. But the work suggests that the kinds of shock waves currently being felt in math are likely to ripple out to other math- and theory-heavy areas of scientific inquiry.

In September, OpenAI rocked the math world by announcing that an unreleased model had solved a long-standing, grand challenge in mathematics known as Navier-Stokes, which concerns equations that explain the behavior of fluid motion. The episode proved extra controversial after a mathematician at NYU—who had been working with another academic associated with Anthropic—accused OpenAI of gazumping them after learning of their progress.

OpenAI and others have since announced hundreds more solutions to longstanding math problems, triggering something of a crisis in the field. Some mathematicians have called for limits on the use of AI, warning that the process of solving problems is often as useful as having the final answer.

As with math, Thompson says, we should expect advances in other areas to have both positive and negative effects. He notes that theoretical advances sometimes drive practical advances in science and suggests that greater use of AI may mean that more progress happens this way.

Some prominent AI researchers have already founded new labs focused on AI for science, and the big AI labs are all ramping up scientific research. These efforts explore how AI could be empowered to conduct real experiments alongside theoretical analysis. AI may mean that theorists are no longer required to solve key problems, but the researchers say that doesn’t mean that experts won’t be needed to make sense of solutions and to make sure they’re sound.

“We are still going to need people to generate good ideas to connect the dots,” says Manso. He adds that for very complex problems, it’s possible that AI might make mistakes. (OpenAI, in fact, withdrew several solutions in its latest dataset post-publication.) “We also need ways to verify what was done, because it's very easy for a model to tell you ‘this is the right answer,’ and when you look at the entire solution, you start to see maybe it is not.”

Earth’s Condition Is ‘Serious and Getting Worse’ as Climate Change Intensifies

Wired October 14, 2026

The climate just got its annual checkup, and the results aren’t looking so hot.

“If Earth were a patient coming in for an annual physical, I would say its condition is serious and getting worse,” Oregon State University researcher Bill Ripple says.

Ripple is the lead author of a new paper chronicling the state of the climate, published on Wednesday in BioScience. The findings show that seven of the 16 planetary vital signs tracked by the researchers have never been in a more extreme state.

That includes the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, which is 50 percent higher than preindustrial levels due to burning fossil fuels, as well as symptoms of burning all that oil, coal, and gas. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets have shrunk to record lows, while ocean heat has soared to record highs.

Climate change has already quickened the pace of warming from about 0.05 degrees Celsius per decade from 1880 through 1970 to 0.36 degrees Celsius per decade since 2010, according to the analysis. While the global average temperature, including land, isn’t at a record extreme, that may change by the end of the year as El Niño strengthens. The natural climate pattern is characterized by a hotter-than-normal Pacific Ocean, but it also boosts global heat levels by pouring more energy into the atmosphere. This year’s El Niño is shaping up to be one for the record books.

“A strong El Niño could temporarily push global temperatures even higher, while bringing additional heat and drought to vulnerable regions,” says Ripple. He adds that “El Niño is a natural phenomenon, but it's now occurring on top of a much warmer planet. That makes its impacts potentially more dangerous.”

Of particular concern are ecosystems such as coral reefs and tropical forests. The spread of ocean heat is likely to fuel a mass coral die-off, known as coral bleaching. With each successive wave of bleaching, reefs become less resilient. Corals are among the ecosystems most threatened by climate change; if the planet warms beyond 1.5 degrees Celsius, most of the world’s coral will be unlikely to survive.

Tropical forests also face pressure from El Niño. This is especially true of the Amazon, which tends to see dry weather during this climate pattern. The timing couldn’t be more dire: The region, dubbed “the world’s lungs,” is already under intense pressure from logging and mining interests and the possible return of a right-wing government in Brazil that prioritizes extraction and land clearing over conservation.

The new report also warns that the Amazon is among the ecosystems at risk of crossing a tipping point—that is, reaching a threshold where it shifts from a tropical rainforest into something more resembling savanna. It’s highly unlikely that crossing that tipping point is imminent, let alone something that will happen this year. But this year’s blast of El Niño–influenced weather will edge it closer.

“Warming, drought, and deforestation could push the Amazon toward widespread forest degradation,” Ripple says. “My concern is that these changes could interact, making them increasingly difficult to stop.”

The report is an avalanche of bad news for the climate, though it does note that carbon-free forms of energy are playing a bigger role in the power grid. The report calls it a sign we’re in the “Age of Electricity.” Despite that, annual greenhouse gas emissions are at record highs. In other words, the world is still smoking a pack a day, even at the risk of losing a lung.

“There are some encouraging signs, especially the growth of renewable energy, but they aren't yet enough to reverse the overall deterioration,” Ripple says. “The climate emergency is not something waiting for us in the future. We are already living through it.”
